title: מבנה הסוגיות – Nazir
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: formulations that make one a nazir
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: formulations that make one a nazir
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various verbal expressions (kinnuyim and explicit phrases) that render a person a nazir, and records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding the phrase 'I take upon myself birds.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all kinnuyim (substitute expressions) for nazirite vows are treated like nazirite vows, and lists several verbal formulations that make one a nazir.
The Mishnah lists explicit phrases like 'I will be' and 'I will be handsome' that render one a nazir.
The Mishnah lists kinnuyim (substitute expressions) like 'nazik', 'naziach', and 'paziach' that make one a nazir.
The Mishnah lists yadot (indirect expressions) like 'I am like this' and 'I am growing hair' that make one a nazir.

sub.text: Mishnah's dispute: Rabbi Meir and Sages
sub.text_en: Mishnah's dispute: Rabbi Meir and Sages
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that saying 'I take upon myself birds' makes one a nazir, while the Sages hold it does not.

items.text: Gemara's question: why Nazir in Seder Nashim?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: why Nazir in Seder Nashim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the tractate Nazir is placed in Seder Nashim, given that the Tanna is discussing women's matters. It answers that the Tanna is expounding on the verse about the sotah, and the connection is that wine leads to adultery, so one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should vow to abstain from wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna, who is discussing Seder Nashim (women's matters), includes the tractate Nazir.

The Gemara answers that the Tanna is expounding on the verse about the sotah (סוטה, suspected adulteress), explaining that wine caused her transgression, so one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should vow to abstain from wine.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah is missing a clause
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah is missing a clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah opened with kinnuyim but then explained yadot (introductory phrases). Rava (or Kedi) says the Mishnah is actually missing a clause: it should have stated that both kinnuyim and yadot are effective, and then it lists examples of yadot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah opened with kinnuyim (substitute terms for nazirite vows) but then explains yadot (introductory phrases), creating an apparent inconsistency.
Rava (or Kedi) resolves the inconsistency by stating that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it should have stated that both kinnuyim and yadot are effective, and then it lists examples of yadot.

items.text: Objection: why not explain kinnuyim first?
items.text_en: Objection: why not explain kinnuyim first?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Tanna should have explained kinnuyim first. It brings examples from other mishnayot where the Tanna first mentions the prohibited items and then explains them, but also counterexamples where the permitted items are explained first. The Gemara shows inconsistency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Tanna should have explained kinnuyim (substitute terms for nazirite vows) first, before yadot (introductory phrases).
The Gemara answers that the Tanna follows the pattern of the previous mishnah, explaining the prohibited items first, citing the mishnah in Shabbat about what may be used for lighting.
The Gemara brings another example from the mishnah in Shabbat about covering hot food, where the prohibited items are explained first.
The Gemara brings a third example from the mishnah in Shabbat about what a woman may wear outside, where the prohibited items are explained first.
The Gemara objects by citing counterexamples from the mishnayot in Shabbat about animals and in Bava Batra about inheritance, where the permitted items are explained first.

items.text: Final resolution: the Tanna sometimes explains either way
items.text_en: Final resolution: the Tanna sometimes explains either way
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Tanna sometimes explains the first item and sometimes the second. The distinction is that when the prohibition pertains to the person himself (as in Nazir), he explains the prohibition first; when the prohibition comes through an animal, he explains the permission first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the inconsistency by stating that the Tanna sometimes explains the first item and sometimes the second, and then distinguishes: when the prohibition pertains to the person himself (as in Nazir), he explains the prohibition first; when the prohibition comes through an animal, he explains the permission first.

items.text: Why the Mishnah begins with substitutes before the main topic
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah begins with substitutes before the main topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists substitutes (kinuyei) before the main term 'nazir', and answers that since substitutes are derived through exegesis, they are beloved to the Tanna and thus mentioned first. It further explains that the Tanna begins with the essence of the vow but then explains the substitutes first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists substitutes (kinuyei) before the main term 'nazir', given that in the parallel case of 'Yesh Nochalin' the Tanna explains the essence of inheritance first.
The Gemara answers that substitutes are beloved to the Tanna because they are derived through exegesis (midrash), so they are mentioned first.
The Gemara objects: if substitutes are beloved, why does the Tanna not open the Mishnah with them entirely, rather than placing the main term first?
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna begins with the essence of the vow (the main term) but then explains the substitutes first because they are beloved.

items.text: The case of 'I will be' and Shmuel's explanation
items.text_en: The case of 'I will be' and Shmuel's explanation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I will be' becomes a nazir. The Gemara objects that perhaps he meant 'I will be in a fast.' Shmuel answers that the case is when a nazir was passing before him. The Gemara then clarifies that when a nazir is passing, there is no doubt about another meaning, but otherwise we suspect he meant a fast.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'אֱהֵא' (I will be) becomes a nazir.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the speaker meant 'I will be in a fast' rather than becoming a nazir.
Shmuel answers that the case is when a nazir was passing before him, clarifying the intent.
The Gemara objects: does Shmuel hold that an ambiguous expression (יָדַיִם שֶׁאֵינָן מוֹכִיחוֹת) is not a valid indication of intent?
The Gemara resolves: when a nazir passes before him, there is no doubt about another meaning; otherwise, we suspect he meant a fast.

items.text: Further clarification: what if he meant to exempt from offerings?
items.text_en: Further clarification: what if he meant to exempt from offerings?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another possibility: perhaps he meant to exempt the nazir from his offerings. It answers that he said it in his heart. The Gemara then asks why this needs to be stated, and concludes that it teaches that we require his mouth and heart to be in agreement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the speaker might have meant to exempt the nazir from his offerings.
The Gemara answers that he said it in his heart, implying a silent intention.
The Gemara asks why this clarification needs to be stated at all.
The Gemara resolves that the statement teaches that we require his mouth and heart to be in agreement.

items.text: The case of 'I will be beautiful' and Shmuel's explanation
items.text_en: The case of 'I will be beautiful' and Shmuel's explanation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I will be beautiful' becomes a nazir. The Gemara objects that perhaps he meant to beautify himself before God with mitzvot, citing a verse. Shmuel answers that the case is when he was holding his hair and said 'I will be beautiful.' The Gemara then questions whether nazir is a matter of sin, and we call it 'beautiful'?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I will be beautiful' becomes a nazir.
The Gemara objects that perhaps he meant to beautify himself before God with mitzvot, citing a baraita about beautifying the sukkah, lulav, tzitzit, and Torah scroll.
Shmuel answers that the case is when he was holding his hair and said 'I will be beautiful,' indicating nazirite intent.
The Gemara questions how nazirite, which involves sin, can be called 'beautiful.'

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who calls a nazir a sinner, only applies this to a defiled nazir who might violate his vow, not to a pure nazir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's characterization of a nazir as a sinner applies only to a defiled nazir who might violate his vow, not to a pure nazir.

items.text: The phrase 'I am like this'
items.text_en: The phrase 'I am like this'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how 'I am like this' can be a valid nazirite vow, since the speaker does not explicitly say 'I am a nazir'. Shmuel answers that it refers to a nazir passing before him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the speaker was holding hair, the phrase 'I am like this' does not explicitly mention naziriteship.
Shmuel answers that the case is where a nazir was passing before the speaker, so 'like this' refers to that nazir.

items.text: The phrase 'I am salsel'
items.text_en: The phrase 'I am salsel'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how 'salsel' refers to hair, and proves it from a maidservant's statement. It then considers an alternative meaning from a verse about Torah, but Shmuel resolves that the speaker is holding his hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the term 'סלסול' (salsel) refers to hair.
The Gemara cites a maidservant in Rabbi's household who used the verb 'מסלסל' (salsel) in reference to hair.
The Gemara objects that 'סלסל' might refer to Torah study, citing the verse 'סַלְסְלֶהָ וּתְרוֹמְמֶךָּ' (exalt her and she will raise you).
Shmuel resolves that here too the speaker is holding his hair, so 'סלסול' refers to hair.

items.text: The phrase 'I am mekalkel'
items.text_en: The phrase 'I am mekalkel'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how 'kalkel' refers to hair, citing a Mishna about lime for hair removal. It then considers an alternative meaning of sustaining the poor, but Shmuel resolves that the speaker is holding his hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the phrase 'I am mekalkel' refers to hair, citing a Mishna about lime for hair removal and Rav's gloss.
The Gemara objects that 'kalkel' could mean sustaining the poor, citing the verse about Joseph sustaining his family.
Shmuel resolves that the speaker is holding his hair, so 'kalkel' refers to hair.

items.text: The phrase 'I take upon myself to let grow pera'
items.text_en: The phrase 'I take upon myself to let grow pera'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how 'shiluach' means growth, citing a verse about pomegranates. It then considers an alternative meaning of sending water, but resolves through a verbal analogy of 'pera' from the Torah and the priestly context, with an alternative answer that 'sending water' also implies growth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I take upon myself to let grow pera' is a nazirite.
The Gemara asks how we know that 'shiluach' here means growth.
The Gemara cites a verse 'שלחיך פרדס רמונים' (Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates) to prove that 'shiluach' means growth.
The Gemara objects that 'shiluach' might mean sending water, citing the verse 'ושולח מים על פני חוצות' (sending water upon the streets).
The Tanna derives through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'פרע' from the Torah and the priestly context, showing that 'pera' means hair growth.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: even 'sending water' implies growth, as Rav Yosef translates that when water is given to fruit, it grows.

items.text: The phrase 'I take upon myself tziporin'
items.text_en: The phrase 'I take upon myself tziporin'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir rules that one who says 'tziporin' becomes a nazir. Reish Lakish explains that 'tziporin' is juxtaposed to hair in a verse, and Rabbi Meir holds that one can be bound by something adjacent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's ruling that one who says 'tziporin' becomes a nazir.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's position.
Reish Lakish explains that Rabbi Meir interprets 'tziporin' as adjacent to hair, based on the verse 'until his hair grew like eagles' and his nails like birds'.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir holds that a person can be bound by something adjacent (to hair).

items.text: Rabbis' position on grasping adjacent matters
items.text_en: Rabbis' position on grasping adjacent matters
items.desc_en: The Rabbis hold that one does not grasp a matter that is adjacent to another, meaning that saying 'birds' does not automatically imply nazirite birds.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis hold that one does not grasp a matter that is adjacent to another, meaning that saying 'birds' does not automatically imply nazirite birds.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Meir's concern
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Meir's concern
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that everyone agrees one does not grasp adjacent matters; Rabbi Meir's concern is that the speaker might have accepted the birds of a nazirite who became impure. The Gemara raises and rejects alternative possibilities, such as birds of a freewill offering or a metzora, and concludes that the case involves a pure nazirite passing before him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that everyone agrees one does not grasp adjacent matters, and explains Rabbi Meir's concern is that the speaker might have accepted the birds of a nazirite who became impure.
The Gemara objects: if we are concerned about a freewill offering, the speaker should have said 'I take upon myself a nest'.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of a metzora's birds and concludes the case involves a pure nazirite passing before him.

items.text: Difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's positions. It answers that if one says 'birds that are adjacent to hair upon me,' according to Rabbi Yochanan it depends on a nazirite passing before him, while according to Resh Lakish it is valid even without a nazirite passing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the positions of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish.

The Gemara answers that the difference is in a case where one says 'birds that are adjacent to hair upon me': according to Rabbi Yochanan it depends on a nazirite passing before him, while according to Resh Lakish it is valid even without a nazirite passing.

items.text: Challenge to the principle of not grasping adjacent matters
items.text_en: Challenge to the principle of not grasping adjacent matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that one does not grasp adjacent matters, citing a baraita that saying 'right hand' constitutes a vow. The Gemara initially suggests this is because 'right hand' is adjacent to oath, but then answers that 'right hand' itself is called an oath, as derived from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that one does not grasp adjacent matters by citing a baraita that saying 'right hand' constitutes an oath, suggesting it is because 'right hand' is adjacent to oath.
The Gemara answers that 'right hand' itself is called an oath, as derived from verses, not because it is adjacent to oath.

items.text: Mishnah: Nazir from specific grape products
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazir from specific grape products
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'I am a nazir from pits' or 'from skins' or 'from shaving' or 'from impurity,' he is a nazir and all details of nezirut apply to him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one says 'I am a nazirite from חרצנים (grape seeds) and זגים (skins), from shaving, and from impurity,' he is a nazirite with all the details of naziriteship.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one is not liable unless he vows from all grape products. The Rabbis derive from 'from wine and strong drink he shall abstain' that even one item suffices. Rabbi Shimon requires the verse 'from all that is made from the grapevine' to include all, and uses the other verse to prohibit mitzvah wine like profane wine. The Gemara asks what that mitzvah wine is, answering kiddush and havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah does not align with Rabbi Shimon's position.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Shimon says one is not liable unless he vows from all grape products, while the Rabbis say even one item suffices to make him a nazirite.

The Gemara asks the reasoning: Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'from all that is made from the grapevine, from pits to skins', while the Rabbis derive from 'from wine and strong drink he shall abstain'.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Shimon also has the verse 'from wine and strong drink' — that verse is needed to prohibit יין מצוה (mitzvah wine) like profane wine.
The Gemara asks what that mitzvah wine is, and answers: קידושא ואבדלתא (kiddush and havdalah).

items.text: Gemara's objection: Already bound by oath from Sinai
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Already bound by oath from Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one is already under an oath from Sinai (e.g., not to drink wine), how can a new nazirite vow take effect? This sets up the need for Rava's resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a nazirite vow cannot take effect because the person is already bound by the oath from Sinai prohibiting wine.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Nazirite vow overrides oath
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Nazirite vow overrides oath
items.desc_en: Rava explains that if one first takes an oath to drink wine and then declares himself a nazirite, the nazirite vow takes effect and overrides the oath, because the nazirite prohibition is more stringent.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that a nazirite vow can take effect on top of an oath, using the example of one who first swears to drink and then declares naziriteship.

items.text: Rabbis' derivation: 'Shechar' teaches two laws
items.text_en: Rabbis' derivation: 'Shechar' teaches two laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the word 'shechar' (intoxicating drink) that the nazirite prohibition includes wine of mitzvah, and also that it teaches another law (about the Temple).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Rabbis need the word 'שכר' (intoxicating drink) if it is already used to forbid מצוה wine (wine of a mitzvah) like regular wine, and answers that it teaches two things.
The Gemara answers: If so, the verse should have said 'from wine'; the extra word 'shechar' teaches two laws.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's derivation: 'Shechar' for Temple analogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's derivation: 'Shechar' for Temple analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon uses the word 'shechar' to draw an analogy between nazirite and the Temple: just as a nazirite is only prohibited from wine, not other intoxicating drinks, so too in the Temple only wine is prohibited, excluding Rabbi Yehuda's view that other sweet drinks also render one liable.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rabbi Shimon's reason for the word 'שכר' (intoxicating drink) in the verse: to draw a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between nazirite and the Temple.

The gemara cites the verse 'יין ושכר אל תשת' (wine and intoxicating drink do not drink) to establish the analogy: just as for a nazirite only wine is forbidden but other intoxicating drinks are not, so too in the Temple only wine is forbidden, excluding other intoxicating drinks.
The gemara explains that the analogy also excludes the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one who enters the Temple after eating dried figs, honey, or milk is liable.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon rejects 'issur chal al issur'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon rejects 'issur chal al issur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rabbi Shimon holds that a prohibition does not take effect where another prohibition already exists, as illustrated by his ruling that eating neveilah on Yom Kippur is exempt from the karet penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon does not accept the principle of איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect where another prohibition already exists).

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that one who eats neveilah (a carcass) on Yom Kippur is exempt from the karet penalty, illustrating that the prohibition of neveilah does not take effect on top of the Yom Kippur prohibition.

items.text: Rabbis' derivation from 'mi-gefen hayayin' and Rabbi Shimon's rejection of combination
items.text_en: Rabbis' derivation from 'mi-gefen hayayin' and Rabbi Shimon's rejection of combination
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive from the verse 'mi-kol asher yei'aseh mi-gefen hayayin' that nazirite prohibitions combine. Rabbi Shimon, however, holds that there is no combination of different substances for lashes, only for the sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the Rabbis: but the verse 'מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר יֵעָשֶׂה מִגֶּפֶן הַיַּיִן' (from all that is made from the grapevine) is written, implying a different derivation.
The Rabbis answer that the verse teaches that nazirite prohibitions combine (מִצְטָרְפִים) with each other.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon does not hold of combination (צֵירוּף), as cited in a baraita.
The baraita quotes Rabbi Shimon: any amount suffices for lashes, and the olive's bulk (כְּזַיִת) was only stated regarding the sacrifice.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Nazirite like Shimshon
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Nazirite like Shimshon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various phrases that render one a nazirite like Shimshon. The Gemara explains why multiple formulations are needed: to exclude the possibility that one refers to a different person or a common name.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists phrases that render one a nazirite like Shimshon (שמשון).
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to list all these formulations.

The Gemara explains that each phrase is needed to exclude alternative interpretations: 'as Shimshon' might refer to another Shimshon, 'as ben Manoach' might be a common name, so the additional phrases clarify the intent.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Difference between permanent nazirite and Shimshon nazirite
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Difference between permanent nazirite and Shimshon nazirite
items.desc_en: The Mishnah contrasts a permanent nazirite (who may lighten his hair with a razor and brings sacrifices if defiled) with a Shimshon nazirite (who may not lighten his hair and brings no sacrifice for defilement). The Gemara notes that the Mishnah is missing the initial case of one who says 'I am a permanent nazirite'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what distinguishes a permanent nazirite from a Shimshon nazirite, and lists the differences: the permanent nazirite may lighten his hair with a razor and brings three animals, and if defiled brings a sacrifice for impurity.
The Mishnah continues by stating that a Shimshon nazirite may not lighten his hair and does not bring a sacrifice for defilement.

The Gemara questions who mentioned a permanent nazirite, implying the Mishnah is missing the initial case of one who says 'I am a permanent nazirite', and suggests the Mishnah should be read as if it first states that case.

items.text: Opening statement of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Opening statement of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a נזיר שמשון who becomes impure does not bring a purification offering, but the nazirite status still applies to him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a נזיר שמשון (Samson-nazirite) who becomes impure does not bring a purification offering, but the nazirite status still applies to him.

items.text: Identifying the author of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the author of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored this Mishnah, ruling out both Rabbi Yehuda (who permits impurity even ab initio) and Rabbi Shimon (who says the vow is void). It concludes that the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda's, but the phrase 'if he became impure' is borrowed from the case of a permanent nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, noting that it cannot be Rabbi Yehuda (who permits impurity even לכתחילה) nor Rabbi Shimon (who says the vow is void), and cites the baraita with their positions.
The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah were Rabbi Yehuda, he permits impurity even לכתחילה, yet the Mishnah says 'if he became impure'; if Rabbi Shimon, he says the vow does not take effect at all.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yehuda, and the phrase 'if he became impure' is borrowed from the case of a permanent nazirite (נזיר עולם).

items.text: Linking to a tannaitic dispute about דבר הנידר
items.text_en: Linking to a tannaitic dispute about דבר הנידר
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon parallels a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yosei regarding whether one can vow using a firstborn animal (בכור), which is already consecrated. Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Yaakov (who does not require a דבר הנידר), and Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei (who does).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding Samson the Nazirite parallels a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yosei about whether one can vow using a firstborn animal (בכור), which is already consecrated.
The Gemara explicitly proposes that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Yaakov (who does not require a 'דבר הנידר' — a thing that can be vowed) and Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei (who does require it).

items.text: Rejecting the parallel: all agree on דבר הנידר
items.text_en: Rejecting the parallel: all agree on דבר הנידר
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the parallel, arguing that all agree a דבר הנידר is required. The dispute about a firstborn is based on a different verse (לַה׳) and whether a firstborn can be 'captured' by a vow. Rabbi Yosei limits the verse to sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, while Rabbi Yaakov argues that a firstborn can be sanctified by a vow, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the parallel, arguing that all agree a דבר הנידר (something that can be vowed) is required, and the dispute about a firstborn is based on the verse 'לַה׳' which includes the firstborn.
Rabbi Yosei responds that the verse 'לַה׳' is needed to include sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, not the firstborn.

The Gemara objects: what reason does Rabbi Yosei have to include sin-offerings and guilt-offerings but exclude the firstborn? Rabbi Yosei answers that sin-offerings and guilt-offerings can be captured by a vow, while a firstborn cannot.

Rabbi Yaakov argues that a firstborn can indeed be captured by a vow, citing a baraita that there is a מצוה (commandment) to sanctify a firstborn, as it says 'הַזָּכָר תַּקְדִּישׁ' (the male you shall sanctify).
Rabbi Yosei objects: even if there is a מצוה (commandment) to sanctify it, if one does not sanctify it, is it not already holy by itself?

items.text: Applying the verse to nazirite and the story of Shimon HaTzaddik
items.text_en: Applying the verse to nazirite and the story of Shimon HaTzaddik
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse לַה׳ is not applied to nazirite, and answers that it is needed for a different teaching: the story of Shimon HaTzaddik, who never ate from a nazirite's guilt-offering except for one man who vowed to become a nazirite for the sake of Heaven, as per the verse 'איש כי יפליא לנדר נדר נזיר להזיר לה׳'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'לַה׳' (to the Lord) is not applied to the nazirite case as well.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for the story of Shimon HaTzaddik, who only ate from a nazirite's guilt-offering when the vow was made for the sake of Heaven, as per the verse 'איש כי יפליא לנדר נדר נזיר להזיר לה׳'.

items.text: Was Samson a nazirite? And proof of impurity
items.text_en: Was Samson a nazirite? And proof of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Samson was a nazirite, citing the verse 'כי נזיר אלהים יהיה הנער מן הבטן', but explains that an angel said this. It then seeks proof that Samson became impure to the dead, considering verses about killing with a jawbone and taking garments, but ultimately concludes that it is a tradition (גמרא גמירי לה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Samson was a nazirite, citing the verse that calls him a nazirite from the womb.
The Gemara answers that the verse was spoken by an angel, not by Samson himself, so it does not prove he was a nazirite.
The Gemara asks for proof that Samson became impure to the dead, rejecting the verse about killing with a jawbone as possibly referring to killing from a distance.
The Gemara proposes another verse about taking garments after killing, but rejects it as possibly referring to killing dying men.
The Gemara concludes that the proof that Samson became impure is a received tradition (גמרא גמירי לה), not derived from verses.

items.text: Source for a permanent nazirite: Absalom
items.text_en: Source for a permanent nazirite: Absalom
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says Absalom was a permanent nazirite, based on the verse about fulfilling his vow after forty years, and that he cut his hair once every twelve months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: where is a perpetual nazirite (נזיר עולם) written? The answer: a baraita teaches that Rabbi says Absalom was a perpetual nazirite, as he shaved only once every twelve months.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states that Absalom was a permanent nazirite, based on the verse about fulfilling his vow after forty years and cutting his hair once every twelve months.

items.text: Derivation of twelve months from walled cities
items.text_en: Derivation of twelve months from walled cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the duration of a nazir's vow from the phrase "yamim" used in the context of walled cities, where it means twelve months. This is the initial suggestion for the length of nezirut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'yamim' in walled cities to derive that a nazir's unspecified vow lasts twelve months.

items.text: Rabbi Nehorai and Rabbi Yosei's opinions on shaving frequency
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehorai and Rabbi Yosei's opinions on shaving frequency
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai states that a nazir shaves once every thirty days, while Rabbi Yosei says he shaves from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve, like kings. These opinions are cited as alternative views on the frequency of shaving during nezirut.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai states that a nazir shaves once every thirty days, implying a minimum nezirut of thirty days.
Rabbi Yosei states that a nazir shaves from Friday to Friday, like princes, implying a seven-day minimum.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi's derivation with his own principle
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi's derivation with his own principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi can derive twelve months from a gezeirah shavah when he holds that "yamim" minimally means two days. The answer is that this gezeirah shavah is learned due to the concept of "koved" (burden), which does not apply to two days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi can derive twelve months from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) when he himself holds that 'ימים' (days) minimally means two days.
The Gemara answers that this גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) is learned due to the concept of כובד (burden), which does not apply to two days.

items.text: Rejecting alternative derivations from other verses
items.text_en: Rejecting alternative derivations from other verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving the duration from verses that mention "yamim" with years or months, but rejects them because the gezeirah shavah must be from a verse where "yamim" stands alone without years or months. It also rejects a derivation from "miyamim yamimah" because the forms differ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the duration from the verse 'וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים' (two years of days), but rejects it because the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) must be from a verse where 'יָמִים' stands alone without years.
The Gemara proposes deriving the duration from the verse 'עַד חֹדֶשׁ יָמִים' (a month of days), but rejects it because the גזירה שוה must be from a verse where 'יָמִים' stands alone without months.
The Gemara proposes deriving from the verse 'מִיָּמִים יָמִימָה' (from days to days), but rejects it because the form 'יָמִימָה' is different from 'יָמִים' and cannot be used for a גזירה שוה.

items.text: Clarifying the principle of deriving from similar terms
items.text_en: Clarifying the principle of deriving from similar terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that when a term is repeated in the Torah, it is considered the same. However, this applies only when there is no closer parallel; here, since there is a closer parallel (walled cities), we derive from that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practical difference of the derivation, citing the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that repeated terms are equivalent.
The Gemara answers that the principle of deriving from similar terms applies only when there is no closer parallel; here, since a closer parallel (walled cities) exists, we derive from that.

items.text: Alternative opinions on shaving frequency and their implications
items.text_en: Alternative opinions on shaving frequency and their implications
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores the reasoning behind Rabbi Nehorai's thirty-day interval and Rabbi Yosei's weekly interval. It notes that for Rabbi Nehorai, the burden of hair justifies thirty days, while for Rabbi Yosei, the practice is like kings. The difference between Rabbi Yosei and other brothers is illustrated by cases of holidays falling mid-week.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know the shaving frequency is once every three months, suggesting alternatives like four times a year or every four or two months.
Rabbi Nehorai states that a nazir shaves once every thirty days, because just as the burden of hair justifies this interval for priests, so too for nazirites.
Rabbi Yosei states that a nazir shaves from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve, and the Gemara asks what difference exists between his practice and that of other brothers.
The Gemara resolves the difference: when a holiday falls mid-week, other brothers shave then, but Rabbi Yosei's nazir does not shave until the end of the Sabbath eve.

items.text: The forty years in the wilderness and the request for a king
items.text_en: The forty years in the wilderness and the request for a king
items.desc_en: A brief digression: Rabbi Nehorai in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua explains that the forty years in the wilderness correspond to the period until the people asked for a king, which occurred in the tenth year of Samuel's judgeship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the forty years mentioned in the context of the nazir's shaving refer to.

sub.text: Rabbi Nehorai in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rabbi Nehorai in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua answers that the forty years refer to the period until the people asked for a king, which was the tenth year of Samuel the Ramathite.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Deriving thirty days for standard nezirut
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Deriving thirty days for standard nezirut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that standard nezirut is thirty days. The Gemara derives this from the gematria of "yihyeh" (30) and from the count of the word "nazir" in the Torah. Bar Pada argues for 29, but Rav Mattana explains that the other instances are used for other halakhot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that standard nezirut is thirty days.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?
Rav Mattana answers: The verse says 'קָדוֹשׁ יִהְיֶה' — the gematria of 'יִהְיֶה' is thirty.
Bar Pada says: Corresponding to the instances of 'נָזִיר' and 'נִזְרוֹ' stated in the Torah, there are twenty-nine.
The Gemara objects: Rav Mattana too should derive from 'נָזִיר' and 'נִזְרוֹ'!
Rav Mattana replies: Those instances are needed for exposition — to forbid יין מצוה (wine of a mitzvah) like ordinary wine, and to teach that nezirut takes effect upon nezirut.

items.text: Bar Pada's response to the objection
items.text_en: Bar Pada's response to the objection
items.desc_en: Bar Pada counters that all the verses cited by Rav Mattana are indeed needed for exposition, but the one he uses for the count is the primary source; the others also teach the count.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada counters that all the cited verses are needed for exposition, but the one he uses for the count is the primary source; the others also teach the count.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah: Standard nazirite is thirty days
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah: Standard nazirite is thirty days
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that a standard nazirite period is thirty days. This is consistent with Rav Mattana, but poses a difficulty for Bar Pada, who derives the count from a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah that a standard nazirite period is thirty days, which is consistent with Rav Mattana but poses a difficulty for Bar Pada.

items.text: Bar Pada's answer: Because the thirtieth day is for shaving and offerings
items.text_en: Bar Pada's answer: Because the thirtieth day is for shaving and offerings
items.desc_en: Bar Pada explains that the Mishnah states thirty days because the thirtieth day is used for shaving and bringing offerings, so the count is thirty inclusive.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada explains that the Mishnah states thirty days because the thirtieth day is used for shaving and bringing offerings, so the count is thirty inclusive.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah: One who says 'I am a nazirite' shaves on the thirty-first day
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah: One who says 'I am a nazirite' shaves on the thirty-first day
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another Mishnah: one who simply says 'I am a nazirite' shaves on the thirty-first day. This fits Rav Mattana, but is difficult for Bar Pada.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that one who says 'I am a nazirite' shaves on the thirty-first day, which fits Rav Mattana's view but poses a difficulty for Bar Pada.

items.text: Bar Pada's answer: The latter clause supports him, the former is like saying 'complete'
items.text_en: Bar Pada's answer: The latter clause supports him, the former is like saying 'complete'
items.desc_en: Bar Pada responds: consider the latter clause of that Mishnah — if he shaved on the thirtieth day, he has fulfilled his obligation. This supports Bar Pada. The former clause is treated as if he said 'complete days'.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada responds to the challenge by directing attention to the latter clause of the Mishnah, which supports his position, and explains that the former clause is treated as if the nazirite said 'complete days'.

items.text: Rav Mattana's difficulty with the latter clause and his principle
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's difficulty with the latter clause and his principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the latter clause is difficult for Rav Mattana. He holds the principle that part of the day is considered as the whole day, so shaving on the thirtieth should be valid even for a thirty-day nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty for Rav Mattana from the latter clause of the Mishnah, which implies that shaving on the thirtieth day is not valid for a standard nazirite.

The Gemara explains that Rav Mattana holds the principle that part of the day is considered as the whole day (מקצת היום ככולו), so shaving on the thirtieth day should be valid even for a thirty-day nazirite.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah: Explicitly says 'thirty days' and shaving on the thirtieth is invalid
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah: Explicitly says 'thirty days' and shaving on the thirtieth is invalid
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where one says 'I am a nazirite for thirty days' and shaves on the thirtieth — he has not fulfilled his obligation. This is explained as referring to one who says 'complete days'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a Mishnah where one who says 'I am a nazirite for thirty days' and shaves on the thirtieth day has not fulfilled his obligation.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah refers to one who explicitly said 'complete days' (שְׁלֵימִין).

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah: Two nazirite periods
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah: Two nazirite periods
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who takes two nazirite periods shaves the first on the thirty-first day and the second on the sixty-first. This fits Rav Mattana, but is not addressed for Bar Pada here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about one who takes two nazirite periods, shaving the first on the thirty-first day and the second on the sixty-first, and notes that this fits Rav Mattana's view but is not addressed for Bar Pada here.

items.text: Objection to Bar Pada from the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Objection to Bar Pada from the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty for Bar Pada's position that 30 days are required, because the Mishnah's first clause allows shaving on day 30 for the first nezirut, implying day 30 counts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Bar Pada from the Mishnah's first clause, which implies that day 30 counts for the first nezirut, contradicting Bar Pada's requirement of 30 full days.

items.text: Bar Pada's resolution: the first clause refers to a case of 'complete days'
items.text_en: Bar Pada's resolution: the first clause refers to a case of 'complete days'
items.desc_en: Bar Pada explains that the Mishnah's first clause, which allows shaving on day 30, refers to a case where the nazir specified 'complete days' (30 full days), so day 30 is the 30th day after completion.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada responds by citing the Mishnah's latter clause, which supports his view, and explains that the first clause refers to one who explicitly said 'complete days' (שלמים).

items.text: Objection to Rav Mattana from the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Mattana from the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Mattana's position also faces a difficulty from the Mishnah's second clause, which says 'day 30 counts for here and there' — but Rav Mattana resolves it by citing that clause itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Rav Mattana from the Mishnah's latter clause, which says day 30 counts for both nezirut periods, contradicting Rav Mattana's position.
Rav Mattana resolves the objection by citing the Mishnah's second clause itself, which states that day 30 counts for both here and there.

items.text: Clarification: the novel teaching is for two consecutive nezirut periods
items.text_en: Clarification: the novel teaching is for two consecutive nezirut periods
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the principle of 'partial day counts as a full day' was already stated, but the Mishnah's repetition teaches that it applies even between two separate nezirut periods, not just within one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana responds by citing the Mishnah's latter clause, explaining that the principle of מקצת היום ככולו (part of the day counts as the whole) applies even between two nezirut periods, which is a novel teaching.

The Gemara answers: one might have thought this principle applies only within a single nezirut period, but for two consecutive nezirut periods it does not; therefore the Mishnah teaches us that it does.

items.text: Objection to Bar Pada from the Mishnah's third clause
items.text_en: Objection to Bar Pada from the Mishnah's third clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty for Bar Pada from a Mishnah that says shaving on day 59 (30 days minus one) is valid because day 30 counts — but Bar Pada requires 30 full days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita: if one shaved on day 59, he fulfills his obligation because day 30 counts, which is fine for Rav Mattana but problematic for Bar Pada, who requires 30 full days minus one.

items.text: Bar Pada's reliance on the first clause
items.text_en: Bar Pada's reliance on the first clause
items.desc_en: Bar Pada responds that he relies on the first clause of the Mishnah (which he interprets as requiring complete days), and the third clause is consistent with that interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada responds that he too relies on that baraita, implying it supports his position.

items.text: Final objection to Bar Pada from impurity on day 30
items.text_en: Final objection to Bar Pada from impurity on day 30
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a nazir who becomes impure on day 30 must restart entirely — this contradicts Bar Pada's view that day 30 does not count, but supports Rav Mattana.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a final objection from a Mishnah: if one said 'I am a nazirite' and became impure on day 30, he must restart completely, which is fine for Rav Mattana but problematic for Bar Pada.

items.text: Bar Padda's defense of Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Bar Padda's defense of Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Bar Padda argues that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling (only seven days are lost) is based on the principle that part of the day is like the whole day (מקצת היום ככולו), so the impurity on the final day counts as the entire day, leaving only seven days to be lost.

sub.desc_en: Bar Padda defends Rabbi Eliezer's ruling by invoking the principle of מקצת היום ככולו (part of the day is like the whole day), arguing that impurity on the final day counts as the entire day, so only seven days are lost.

items.text: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a nazirite for 100 days who becomes impure on day 100 loses everything according to the first Tanna, but Rabbi Eliezer says only 30 days. The Gemara questions: if Rabbi Eliezer holds מקצת היום ככולו, he should lose only 7 days; if not, he should lose all 100. This challenges Bar Padda's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a Mishnah: if Rabbi Eliezer holds מקצת היום ככולו, he should only require seven days to be lost; if not, he should require all days — yet he rules thirty days, which is inconsistent.

items.text: Resh Lakish's scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the principle of מקצת היום ככולו. Resh Lakish explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is based on a verse: "This is the law of the nazirite on the day of the completion of his naziriteship" — the Torah says that if he becomes impure on the day of completion, you give him the law of a nazirite (i.e., he starts a new term of 30 days, not the full original count).

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish rejects the principle of מקצת היום ככולו and explains that Rabbi Eliezer derives his ruling from the verse 'זאת תורת הנזיר ביום מלאת ימי נזרו' — the Torah says that if one becomes impure on the day of completion, he receives the full Torah of a nazirite (thirty days).
The Gemara asks: if so, why does Rabbi Eliezer not require him to restart the entire count?

Resh Lakish explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is based on the verse 'זאת תורת הנזיר ביום מלאת ימי נזרו' — the Torah says that if he becomes impure on the day of completion, you give him the law of a nazirite (a new 30-day term).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the minimum term
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the minimum term
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav Mattana and Bar Padda may correspond to a Tannaitic debate. Rabbi Yoshiyah learns from the verse "until the completion of the days" that the minimum nazirite term is 30 days (since growth of hair requires at least 30 days). Rabbi Yonatan argues that the phrase "days that need filling" implies 30 days, as other numbers (like 29) would not require filling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute about the minimum term of nezirut, citing Rabbi Yoshiyah who derives from 'עד מלאת הימים' and 'קדוש יהיה גדל פרע' that nezirut requires at least thirty days.
Rabbi Yonatan argues that no special derivation is needed; the phrase 'עד מלאת הימים' itself implies thirty days, as these are the days that require completion.
Rabbi Yonatan argues that the phrase 'עַד מְלֹאת הַיָּמִים' (until the completion of the days) itself implies 30 days, as other numbers like 29 would not require 'filling' (מַלּאוֹת).

items.text: Attribution of views to Rav Mattana and Bar Padda
items.text_en: Attribution of views to Rav Mattana and Bar Padda
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is it not that Rav Mattana holds like Rabbi Yoshiyah (who requires 30 days for the term), and Bar Padda holds like Rabbi Yonatan (who also requires 30 days but via a different derivation)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Mattana follows Rabbi Yoshiyah and Bar Padda follows Rabbi Yonatan in their respective positions.

items.text: Rav Mattana's rejection of the attribution
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's rejection of the attribution
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana responds that everyone agrees 30 days are required; the dispute between Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan is about whether the word "until" (עד) includes the endpoint or not. Rabbi Yoshiyah holds "until" does not include the endpoint, Rabbi Yonatan holds it does.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana explains that everyone agrees thirty days are required; the dispute between Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan is about whether the word 'עד' (until) includes the endpoint or not.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yonatan's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yonatan's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yonatan's statement: "What are the days that need filling? You must say 30." Why not say Shabbat (i.e., 7 days)? The Gemara answers: Is there a deficiency in Shabbat? (Shabbat is always 7 days, so it doesn't need filling; 30 days can be deficient if a month is 29 days.)

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yonatan's reasoning: why specifically thirty days? Why not a week (שבת), which also has a completion? The Gemara answers that a week has no deficiency (חסירותא) to be filled.
The Gemara objects: why not say Shabbat (7 days)? It answers: Shabbat has no deficiency (it is always 7 days, so it does not need filling).

items.text: Gemara's question about counting days for years
items.text_en: Gemara's question about counting days for years
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can count days for years, citing the rabbis of Caesarea who derive from the verse "for the months of the year" that months are counted for years, but not days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can count days for years, citing the rabbis of Caesarea who derive from the verse "for the months of the year" that months are counted for years, but not days.

items.text: Mishnah: Vague nazirite vows are for thirty days
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vague nazirite vows are for thirty days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says "I am hereby a nazirite, one large one" or "one small one," or even "from here until the end of the world," he is a nazirite for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I am a nazirite one large' or 'one small' or even 'from here until the end of the world' becomes a nazirite for thirty days.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the vow is only thirty days, given that the person said "until the end of the world." It explains that the person meant that the matter is as long to him as from here until the end of the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules thirty days despite the speaker saying 'from here until the end of the world', and answers that the speaker meant it feels as long.
The Gemara explains that the speaker meant the matter is as burdensome to him as a journey to the end of the world, not a literal duration.

items.text: Comparison with a vow based on distance
items.text_en: Comparison with a vow based on distance
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a vow from here to a certain place, where the number of days is estimated. It questions why that case is not similarly interpreted as a figure of speech. Rava answers that it is because he actually started traveling, and Rav Papa adds that it is in a place where parasangs are not counted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a vow from here to a certain place, where the number of days is estimated, and if less than thirty days, he is a nazir for thirty days, otherwise for the number of days.
The Gemara asks why this case is not similarly interpreted as a figure of speech, like the previous one.
Rava answers that it is because he actually started traveling.
The Gemara objects that each parasang should then be counted as a separate nazirite period.
Rav Papa answers that it is in a place where parasangs are not counted.

items.text: Objection from a perpetual nazirite vow
items.text_en: Objection from a perpetual nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one says "I am a nazirite like the dust of the earth," he becomes a perpetual nazirite who shaves every thirty days. The Gemara answers that any matter that has a limit is not taught in that context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one says 'I am a nazirite like the dust of the earth,' he becomes a perpetual nazirite who shaves every thirty days, so why not treat each thirty-day period as a separate nazirite vow here as well?
The Gemara answers that any matter that has a fixed limit (like thirty days) is not taught in the context of the Mishnah's rule about indefinite nazirite vows.

items.text: Distinction between perpetual nazirite and nazirite for life
items.text_en: Distinction between perpetual nazirite and nazirite for life
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita distinguishing between a nazirite for all the days of his life (perpetual) and a nazirite for a hundred years (not perpetual). Rabba explains that hairs are different because they are separate from each other, but the Gemara objects that days are also separate. The Gemara answers that days are not separate from each other in the sense that day and night are one unit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between a perpetual nazirite (נזיר עולם) who says 'all the days of my life' or 'perpetual nazirite' and a nazirite for a fixed term (e.g., 100 years), who is not a perpetual nazirite but merely a long-term nazirite.
Rabba answers that hairs are different because they are separate from each other, unlike days which are continuous.
The Gemara objects that days are also separate from each other, as the verse says 'and there was evening and there was morning, one day'.
The Gemara resolves that days are not truly separate from each other because day and night together form one continuous unit, and they never become completely separated from each other.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava offers a simpler explanation: the Mishnah's case is different because it explicitly says "one naziriteship," implying a single term of thirty days.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by noting that the Mishnah explicitly says 'I am a nazirite one', indicating a single term.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on adding days or hours to a nazirite vow
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on adding days or hours to a nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says "I am a nazirite and one day" or "and one hour," he is a nazirite for two terms. The Gemara explains that these cases are necessary to teach that there is no naziriteship for a single day, and that adding an hour does not extend the term to thirty-one days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases where adding a day, an hour, or a half to a nazirite vow results in two full terms.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach all three cases.

The Gemara explains that each case is necessary: the day case teaches that there is no naziriteship for a single day, and the hour case teaches that adding an hour does not extend the term to thirty-one days.

items.text: Gemara's concluding argument on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's concluding argument on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the Mishnah had taught 'one hour', it would not be precise, but since it taught 'one and a half', which is precise, one might think not to count two naziriteships; therefore the Mishnah teaches all of them — a nazirite of two terms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the Mishnah had taught 'one hour', it would not be precise, but since it taught 'one and a half', which is precise, one might think not to count two naziriteships; therefore the Mishnah teaches all of them — a nazirite of two terms.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one says 'I am a nazirite for thirty days and one hour', he is a nazirite for thirty-one days, because nezirut is not measured by hours.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who says 'I am a nazirite for thirty days and one hour' becomes a nazirite for thirty-one days, because naziriteship is not measured by hours.

items.text: Rav's distinction
items.text_en: Rav's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav says: The Mishnah's ruling applies only when he said 'thirty-one days', but if he said 'thirty days and one day', he is a nazirite of two terms (two separate nezirut periods).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when one said 'thirty-one days', but if one said 'thirty days and one day', he becomes a nazirite of two terms.

items.text: Explanation of Rav's reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav holds like Rabbi Akiva, who interprets extra language (לישנא יתירא) as adding meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav follows Rabbi Akiva, who interprets extra language (לישנא יתירא) as adding a separate naziriteship.

items.text: Supporting Tosefta from Bava Batra
items.text_en: Supporting Tosefta from Bava Batra
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Akiva rules that if one sells a pit but also specifies its depth and height, he must buy a path to it, because the extra language indicates he sold only the pit, not the path. The Sages disagree, and Rabbi Akiva concedes if the seller said 'except for these'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva rules that extra language in a deed requires the seller to provide a right-of-way, while the Sages disagree, and Rabbi Akiva concedes when the seller explicitly excludes those items.

sub.text: Sages' disagreement and Rabbi Akiva's concession
sub.text_en: Sages' disagreement and Rabbi Akiva's concession
sub.desc_en: The Sages disagree with Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller said 'except for these,' the buyer does not need to purchase a path.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of indefinite nezirut
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of indefinite nezirut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three types of nezirut declarations: 'like the hair of my head', 'like the dust of the earth', and 'like the sand of the sea' – all make one a permanent nazir who shaves every 30 days. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi distinguishes between 'I am hereby a nazir like...' (permanent) and 'I take upon myself nezirut like...' (shaves every 30 days). Additional cases include 'full of the house' (evaluated as if full of mustard seeds, making him a nazir forever) and 'from here to place X' (measured in days).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who declares nezirut 'like the hair of my head', 'like the dust of the earth', or 'like the sand of the sea' becomes a permanent nazir who shaves every 30 days.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects, distinguishing that only one who says 'I take upon myself nezirut like...' shaves every 30 days, not one who says 'I am hereby a nazir like...'.
The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'I am hereby a nazir full of the house' or 'full of the basket', where the basket is evaluated as if full of mustard seeds, making him a nazir forever.

The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'I am hereby a nazir from here to place X', where the distance is measured in days, and if less than 30 days he is a nazir for 30 days, otherwise for that number of days.

The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'I am hereby a nazir like the number of days of the sun', who counts nezirut for that number, and Rabbi Yehuda relates a story where such a person died after completing.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why not estimate leniently?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why not estimate leniently?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a basket is treated as full of mustard seeds (making him a nazir forever). Why not view it as full of cucumbers and gourds (which are larger, thus fewer items, allowing a finite nezirut)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah treats the basket as full of mustard seeds (making him a nazir forever) rather than as full of cucumbers and gourds (which would allow a finite nezirut).

items.text: Chizkiya's answer: It follows Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Chizkiya's answer: It follows Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Chizkiya answers that the Mishnah reflects a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Shimon holds that doubtful nezirut is stringent (so we do not give a lenient estimation), while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is lenient. The Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya answers that the Mishnah is taught in a dispute and follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a person enters a situation whose doubt is more stringent than certainty.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Shimon forbids a nazirite vow conditioned on a pile containing 100 kor that was lost, because doubtful nezirut is stringent.
Rabbi Yehuda permits in the same case, because doubtful nezirut is lenient.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection: Even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection: Even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, this case is different because the person has already entered into nezirut (by saying 'I am hereby a nazir'), so there is no way to release him leniently. The Gemara then asks: why not estimate with cucumbers and gourds? It answers that we initially thought he accepted nezirut upon himself (so leniency is impossible).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, here the person has already entered into nezirut (נזירות), so there is no way to release him leniently.
The Gemara asks: why not estimate the basket as if full of cucumbers and gourds, giving him a lenient way out?
The Gemara answers: we initially thought he accepted nezirut (נזירות) upon himself, so leniency is impossible.

items.text: Opening claim: Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi
items.text_en: Opening claim: Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Yehuda's view aligns with Rabbi's, citing a baraita where Rabbi says that one who vows 'like the hair of my head' etc. does not shave every thirty days, implying multiple naziriteships.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi says that one who vows 'like the hair of my head' etc. does not shave every thirty days, implying multiple naziriteships.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda really hold like Rabbi?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda really hold like Rabbi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assertion by citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda recounts a case of one who vowed 'as the number of days of the sun' and died after completing the count. If it were a single naziriteship, there would be no completion. This implies Rabbi Yehuda accepts multiple naziriteships, contradicting the claim that he holds like Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda truly holds like Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that one who vows 'like the number of days of the sun' died upon completion, implying a single naziriteship.
The Gemara explains that if the person accepted multiple naziriteships, completion makes sense; but if it were a single naziriteship, there would be no completion, thus supporting the challenge.

items.text: Second challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's baraita on 'minyan'
items.text_en: Second challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's baraita on 'minyan'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that one who vows 'as the number of summer fruits' or 'as the number of sheaves of the Sabbatical year' counts naziriteships accordingly. The Gemara deflects by saying that the word 'minyan' (number) is different, implying a specific count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further challenge: does Rabbi Yehuda really hold like Rabbi? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who vows 'as the number of summer fruits' or 'as the number of sheaves of the Sabbatical year' counts naziriteships accordingly.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by stating that the word 'מִנְיָן' (number) is different, implying a specific count.

items.text: Objection: Does 'minyan' differ for Rabbi?
items.text_en: Objection: Does 'minyan' differ for Rabbi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi himself does not distinguish 'minyan' from other formulations, as shown in a baraita where Rabbi requires explicit mention of 'naziriteships' for multiple vows, even with 'minyan'. Thus the distinction is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi himself does not distinguish 'number' (מנין), citing a baraita where Rabbi requires explicit mention of 'naziriteships' even when using 'number'.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yehuda agrees in one, disagrees in one
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yehuda agrees in one, disagrees in one
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with Rabbi in one respect (that the vow is for multiple naziriteships) but disagrees in another: Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes 'minyan' as indicating a count, while Rabbi does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with Rabbi in one matter (that one accepts multiple naziriteships) but disagrees in another: Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes 'number' (מנין) while Rabbi does not.

items.text: Baraita: Nazir for life vs. eternal nazir
items.text_en: Baraita: Nazir for life vs. eternal nazir
items.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between 'nazir for all my days' or 'eternal nazir' (which is a permanent naziriteship) and 'nazir for 100 years' (which is a regular naziriteship for that period).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who vows 'I am a nazir all the days of my life' or 'a perpetual nazir' becomes a perpetual nazir, but even 'one hundred years' or 'one thousand years' is not a perpetual nazir but a nazir forever.

items.text: Baraita: Counting with 'and one', 'and again'
items.text_en: Baraita: Counting with 'and one', 'and again'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one says 'I am a nazir and one', he counts two; 'and again' adds one more; 'and return' adds another. The Gemara clarifies that 'and return' does not add all previous ones, only one.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who says 'I am a nazir and one' counts two naziriteships; 'and again' counts three; 'and further' counts four, and the Gemara explains that this teaches that 'and further' does not imply all previous terms (which would make six).
The Gemara asks: is this not obvious? Why is a baraita needed?
The Gemara answers: one might have thought 'and return' adds all previous ones (making six), so the baraita teaches that it adds only one.

items.text: Baraita: Greek number prefixes for nazirite vows
items.text_en: Baraita: Greek number prefixes for nazirite vows
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Sumchos who rules that 'hen' (one) is one naziriteship, 'digon' (two) is two, 'trigon' (three) is three, 'tetragon' (four) is four, 'pontigon' (five) is five.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Sumkhos who says that one who says 'hen' (one) counts one naziriteship, 'digon' two, 'trigon' three, 'tetragon' four, 'pontigon' five.

items.text: Baraita: Shapes and impurity from leprosy
items.text_en: Baraita: Shapes and impurity from leprosy
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses that round, digon, trigon, and pontigon buildings are not susceptible to leprosy impurity, but tetragon (square) is, because the Torah mentions 'wall' and 'walls' both above and below, implying four walls.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a round, digon, trigon, or pontigon house is not susceptible to skin ailments (נגעים), but a tetragon house is, because the verse uses 'wall' and 'walls' both above and below, requiring four walls.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'I am hereby a nazirite from dried figs and dried fig cakes.' Beit Shammai rules he is a nazirite, while Beit Hillel rules he is not. Rabbi Yehuda adds that Beit Shammai only said this when he says 'they are upon me as a korban.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who says 'I am hereby a nazirite from dried figs and dried fig cakes,' and Beit Shammai rules he is a nazirite.
Beit Hillel rules that he is not a nazirite.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that Beit Shammai only ruled this way when the person says 'they are upon me as a korban.'

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Beit Shammai can rule that he is a nazirite, since the Torah restricts nazirite prohibitions only to products of the grapevine, not dried figs. It explains that Beit Shammai holds like Rabbi Meir, who says a person does not utter his words in vain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Beit Shammai can rule that one who says 'I am a nazirite from dried figs and cakes' becomes a nazirite, since the Torah restricts nazirite prohibitions only to products of the grapevine.

The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai holds like Rabbi Meir, who says a person does not utter his words in vain, so the nazirite vow takes effect and the specification of figs is treated as a mistaken condition.

items.text: Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel holds like Rabbi Yosei, who says a person is bound only by the completion of his words. Since he said 'from dried figs,' this is a vow and its opening together, so the vow is nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel holds like Rabbi Yosei, who says a person is bound only by the completion of his words, so the statement is a vow and its opening together, nullifying the vow.

items.text: Objection and resolution for Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Objection and resolution for Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to Beit Shammai, this is a vow and its opening together. It resolves that Beit Shammai holds like Rabbi Meir that a person does not utter his words in vain, and since he said 'I am hereby a nazirite,' he becomes a nazirite; the phrase 'from dried figs' is merely to seek a release. Beit Shammai follows their own view that there is no petition for release in consecrated items, and thus none in naziriteship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to Beit Shammai, the statement 'I am hereby a nazirite from dried figs' constitutes a vow with its opening together, which should invalidate the vow.

The Gemara resolves that Beit Shammai holds like Rabbi Meir that a person does not utter his words in vain, so the initial declaration 'I am hereby a nazirite' takes effect, and the phrase 'from dried figs' is merely seeking a release; Beit Shammai follows their own view that there is no petition for release in consecrated items, and thus none in naziriteship.

items.text: Beit Hillel's alternative reasoning
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's alternative reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that Beit Hillel holds like Rabbi Shimon, who exempts in a similar case because the person did not donate in the manner of donors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel holds like Rabbi Shimon, who exempts in a similar case because the person did not donate in the manner of donors.

items.text: Two versions of Rabbi Natan's baraita on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Two versions of Rabbi Natan's baraita on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita in which Rabbi Natan reports a dispute: Beit Shammai say the person is both a nazirite and has vowed (or is a nazirite but not vowed), while Beit Hillel say he has vowed but is not a nazirite (or neither vowed nor a nazirite). The two versions align Beit Shammai with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, and Beit Hillel with Rabbi Yosei or Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah does not align with the following Tanna, introducing Rabbi Natan's baraita.

Rabbi Natan reports the first version: Beit Shammai say the person is both a nazirite and has vowed, aligning with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda; Beit Hillel say he has vowed but is not a nazirite, aligning with Rabbi Yosei.

The second version of Rabbi Natan's baraita: Beit Shammai say he has vowed but is not a nazirite, aligning with Rabbi Yehuda; Beit Hillel say he neither vowed nor is a nazirite, aligning with Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Mishnah from Menachot about improper meal-offering vows
items.text_en: Mishnah from Menachot about improper meal-offering vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah from tractate Menachot: one who vows to bring a meal-offering from barley must bring wheat; if he says 'flour' he brings fine flour; if 'without oil and frankincense' he brings with them; if 'half a tenth' he brings a full tenth; if 'a tenth and a half' he brings two. Rabbi Shimon exempts him because he did not vow in the manner of donors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah from Menachot listing cases where improper meal-offering vows are corrected, with Rabbi Shimon exempting the donor.

items.text: Chizkiya identifies the mishnah as Beit Shammai's view
items.text_en: Chizkiya identifies the mishnah as Beit Shammai's view
items.desc_en: Chizkiya states that the mishnah in Menachot is disputed and follows Beit Shammai: just as Beit Shammai say that if one says 'from dried figs and cakes' he becomes a nazirite, so too if one says 'from barley' he brings wheat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that one who vows a barley meal-offering must bring wheat.
Chizkiya answers that the mishnah is disputed and follows Beit Shammai, drawing an analogy from their view on nazirite vows.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation: the person retracts
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation: the person retracts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that even according to all opinions, the mishnah refers to a case where the person says 'Had I known that one does not vow in this manner, I would not have vowed this way but that way.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that even according to all opinions, the mishnah refers to a case where the person retracts by saying 'Had I known that one does not vow in this manner, I would not have vowed this way but that way.'

items.text: Chizkiya's distinction between barley and lentils
items.text_en: Chizkiya's distinction between barley and lentils
items.desc_en: Chizkiya says the mishnah only applies when he said 'from barley', but if he said 'from lentils' he brings nothing at all.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya distinguishes the mishnah's ruling: it applies only when the vow specified barley, but if he said 'from lentils' he brings nothing at all.

items.text: Chizkiya retracts due to contradiction with Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Chizkiya retracts due to contradiction with Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Chizkiya holds the mishnah follows Beit Shammai, but lentils for a meal-offering are like dried figs for a nazirite, and Beit Shammai say he becomes a nazirite. This forces Chizkiya to retract.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Chizkiya holds the mishnah follows Beit Shammai, and since lentils for a meal-offering are like dried figs for a nazirite, Beit Shammai's ruling that he becomes a nazirite contradicts Chizkiya's position.
The Gemara concludes that Chizkiya retracts his position due to this contradiction.

items.text: Rava explains why Chizkiya retracted: the mishnah says 'barley' not 'lentils'
items.text_en: Rava explains why Chizkiya retracted: the mishnah says 'barley' not 'lentils'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the mishnah itself caused Chizkiya to retract: why does it teach 'barley' rather than 'lentils'? Chizkiya therefore concludes that Beit Shammai's ruling there follows Rabbi Yehuda (who holds that one can vow with unusual items).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Chizkiya retracted his earlier position.
Rava answers that the mishnah itself caused Chizkiya to retract: why does it teach 'barley' rather than 'lentils'?
Rava concludes that Chizkiya therefore holds that Beit Shammai's ruling there follows Rabbi Yehuda, who allows vowing with unusual items.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's response and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's response and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that even 'from lentils' applies, but the Gemara notes that this contradicts his earlier statement about retraction.
