The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking according to Chizkiya's reasoning. The Gemara then suggests that Chizkiya's retraction might be unnecessary: perhaps the mishnah only teaches 'barley' because it is a case where the person might be retracting, but lentils are even more obvious.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that even if one said 'from lentils,' he brings a proper meal-offering.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's current statement contradicts his earlier ruling that retraction is effective only if the person says 'I did not know that one does not vow in this way.'
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking according to Chizkiya's reasoning, not his own.
The Gemara asks Chizkiya why he retracted his earlier position, attributing it to the mishnah not mentioning lentils.

The Gemara suggests that Chizkiya's retraction may be unnecessary: the mishnah only teaches 'barley' because it is a case where the person might be retracting, but lentils are even more obvious and need not be stated.

items.text: Introduction to the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Introduction to the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case of a cow teaches that one brings a meal-offering from wheat, not barley, similar to the sotah offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'or like the meal-offering of the sotah' teaches that the offering must be brought from wheat, not barley.

items.text: Mishnah: Nazirite vows contingent on a cow or door
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazirite vows contingent on a cow or door
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where one says 'this cow is hereby nazirite if it stands' or 'this door is hereby nazirite if it opens.' Beit Shammai rule he is a nazirite, Beit Hillel rule he is not. Rabbi Yehuda adds that Beit Shammai only said this when the person says 'this cow is a korban upon me if it stands.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'this cow is hereby a nazirite if I stand' or 'this door is hereby a nazirite if I open,' with Beit Shammai ruling the person is a nazirite and Beit Hillel ruling he is not, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that Beit Shammai only said this when one says 'this cow is a korban upon me if it stands.'
The Mishnah presents a second case where one says 'this door is hereby nazirite if it opens.'

sub.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai rule he is a nazirite, Beit Hillel rule he is not.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that Beit Shammai only said this when the person says 'this cow is a korban upon me if it stands.'

items.text: Gemara's question and Rami bar Chama's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rami bar Chama's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does a cow speak? Rami bar Chama explains the case: a cow was lying before him, and he said 'since this cow is not standing, I am a nazirite from its flesh if it stands on its own.' It stood on its own. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel follow their respective opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a cow can speak to make a nazirite vow, and Rami bar Chama answers that the case involves a cow lying before him who says 'I thought this cow would not stand — I am a nazirite from its meat if it stands on its own,' and it stood on its own.
Rami bar Chama explains the scenario and notes that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel follow their respective established positions.
The Gemara concludes that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel follow their respective opinions in this case.

items.text: Comparison to the case of dried figs and cakes
items.text_en: Comparison to the case of dried figs and cakes
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares this to the earlier dispute about dried figs and cakes: Beit Shammai say he is a nazirite, and here too, since he said 'from its flesh,' he is a nazirite. Beit Hillel say he is not a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai, who rule that one who vows from dried figs and cakes becomes a nazirite, apply the same logic here when one says 'from its meat,' while Beit Hillel rule he is not a nazirite.

items.text: Rava's statement: multiple cases are taught
items.text_en: Rava's statement: multiple cases are taught
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: did Beit Shammai already state this once? Rava says they taught it twice or thrice, and Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya also taught it twice or thrice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai's ruling needs to be repeated, and Rava answers that it is stated two or three times, and Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya also taught it two or three times.
Rava explains that the repetition is necessary to teach multiple cases, and Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya also taught it multiple times.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya also taught it twice or thrice, supporting Rava's claim.

items.text: Necessity of multiple cases
items.text_en: Necessity of multiple cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why all three cases (dried figs, flesh, door) are necessary: each case might have led to a different ruling if only one were taught. The cases of dried figs and flesh are needed to show Beit Shammai's stringency, and the door case is needed to show Beit Hillel's leniency, and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all three cases (dried figs, flesh, door) are necessary to teach, because each alone might have led to a different conclusion.
The Gemara explains that the case of dried figs is needed because Beit Shammai might have ruled leniently for flesh, but the dried figs case shows their stringency due to confusion with grapes.

The Gemara explains that the case of flesh is needed because Beit Shammai might have ruled leniently for dried figs, but the flesh case shows their stringency due to the association of flesh with wine.
The Gemara explains that the case of the door is needed because without it, one might think Beit Shammai would concede to Beit Hillel in that case, but the Mishnah teaches they do not.

The Gemara explains that the cases of dried figs and flesh are needed because without them, one might think Beit Hillel would concede to Beit Shammai in those cases, but the Mishnah teaches they do not.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the earlier explanation: does the Mishnah say 'if it stood on its own'? Rather, Rava explains the case as one where a cow was lying before him and he said 'this is a korban upon me.' But a door is not fit for a korban! So Rava says the case is where a cow was lying before him...

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rami bar Chama's explanation, noting that the Mishnah does not say 'if it stands on its own,' and questions how a door can be a korban.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the case involves a cow lying before him who says 'this is a korban upon me,' and the Gemara begins to address the door case.
The Gemara objects: while a cow is fit for a korban, a door is not fit for a korban, so how can the case apply to the door?
Rava resolves the objection by reiterating the case of a cow lying before him, implying the door case is handled differently.

items.text: Initial case and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Initial case and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The man says 'I am a nazir from wine if it does not stand,' and the cow stands on its own. Beit Shammai holds the vow is void because the condition depends on his causing it to stand, which he did not do. Beit Hillel holds the vow is void because the condition depends on the cow not standing, and it stood.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case: a man says 'I am a nazir from wine if it does not stand,' and the cow stands on its own.
Beit Shammai holds that the man's loophole (תּוּרְפֵּיהּ) is based on his causing the cow to stand, which he did not do, so the vow is void.
Beit Hillel holds that the man's loophole is based on the cow lying down, and since it stood, the vow is void.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's objection and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's objection and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case: if so, consider the end of the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says Beit Shammai only spoke about a case where one says 'they are upon me as a korban.' But here, the man did not consecrate the cow itself, so how can the case be about a cow?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: if the previous interpretation holds, then consider the end of the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says Beit Shammai only spoke about a case where one says 'they are upon me as a korban,' but here the man did not consecrate the cow itself, so how can the case be about a cow?

items.text: Revised case: nazir from the cow's flesh
items.text_en: Revised case: nazir from the cow's flesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the case: the man says 'I am a nazir from its flesh if it does not stand,' and the cow stands on its own. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel again dispute whether the vow is void due to the man not causing it to stand or due to the cow standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the case to a man saying 'I am a nazir from its flesh if it does not stand,' and the cow stands on its own.
Beit Shammai holds that the man's loophole is due to his causing the cow to stand, and he did not cause it to stand, so the vow is void.
Beit Hillel holds that the man's loophole is due to the cow lying down, and the cow is standing, so the vow is void.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Beit Hillel holds that if the cow had not stood, he would be a nazir? But they said 'from its flesh' — one cannot become a nazir from flesh!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Beit Hillel's position: if they hold that one can become a nazir from the cow's flesh, their own statement 'from its flesh' contradicts this, since one cannot become a nazir from flesh.

items.text: Beit Hillel's response to Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's response to Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains: Beit Hillel is speaking according to Beit Shammai's reasoning. They say: according to us, even if it had not stood, he would not be a nazir. But according to you who say he would be a nazir, at least admit that the man's condition is due to the cow's standing, and it stood. Beit Shammai responds: no, the condition is due to his causing it to stand, and he did not cause it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel is speaking according to Beit Shammai's reasoning, arguing that even if the cow had not stood, he would not be a nazir according to Beit Hillel, but according to Beit Shammai's view, the condition is due to the cow standing, and it did stand.
Beit Shammai objects that the man's condition is due to his causing the cow to stand, and he did not cause it, so he is not a nazir.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conditional nazirite vow and a drunk woman's case
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conditional nazirite vow and a drunk woman's case
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one says 'I am a nazirite from this cup' and becomes a nazirite. It then recounts a story of a drunk woman who said the same, and the Sages ruled she only meant to dedicate the wine as a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if one is handed a cup and says 'I am a nazirite from this,' he becomes a nazirite.
The Mishnah recounts a story of a drunk woman who said the same, and the Sages ruled she only meant to dedicate the wine as a sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution of the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution of the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah brings a story that seems to contradict the first ruling, suggesting the text is missing a clause. It explains that the Mishnah actually teaches: if one is sober, the vow takes effect; if drunk, it is not a nazirite vow but merely a declaration of dedication. The story illustrates the drunk case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the story contradicts the first ruling, implying that only this specific wine is forbidden but other wine is permitted.
The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's structure: the story seems to contradict the first ruling, implying that only wine from that cup is forbidden, while other wine is permitted.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it should state that a drunk person who says this is not a nazirite, and the story is merely an illustration.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it actually teaches that a sober person's vow takes effect, but a drunk's vow is not a nazirite vow but merely a declaration of dedication; the story illustrates the drunk case.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional nazirite vows and Rabbi Shimon's disputes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional nazirite vows and Rabbi Shimon's disputes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who says 'I am a nazirite on condition that I drink wine' is a nazirite and forbidden from all. It then presents cases of ignorance: one unaware of the prohibition is forbidden (Rabbi Shimon permits), while one who thought the Sages would permit due to need is permitted (Rabbi Shimon forbids).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I am a nazirite on condition that I drink wine and become impure from the dead' is a nazirite and forbidden in all.
The Mishnah states that one who says 'I am a nazirite on condition that I drink wine' is a nazirite and forbidden from all.
The Mishnah presents the case of one who knows about naziriteship but not the prohibition of wine: he is forbidden, but Rabbi Shimon permits.
The Mishnah rules that one unaware of the prohibition is forbidden, with Rabbi Shimon permitting.
The Mishnah presents the case of one who knows the prohibition but thought he was exempt due to necessity: he is permitted, but Rabbi Shimon forbids.
The Mishnah rules that one who thought the Sages would permit due to need is permitted, with Rabbi Shimon forbidding.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Shimon's position in the first case
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Shimon's position in the first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon did not dispute the first case. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says he did dispute it. Ravina argues he did not, because a condition contradicting Torah law is void, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi considers such a condition as an exception.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon did not also dispute the first case in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers that Rabbi Shimon did in fact dispute the first case.
Ravina objects that Rabbi Shimon did not dispute the first case, because a condition contradicting Torah law (מתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה) is void.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that the phrase 'על מנת' (on condition) is treated like an exception (כחוץ דמי), so the condition is not void but rather removes the person from the category of nazir entirely.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Ravina's view
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Ravina's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Ravina: one who says 'I am a nazirite on condition that I drink wine' is a nazirite and forbidden, because any condition against Torah law is void.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's second case
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's second case
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a textual issue: the Mishnah says 'I know the nazirite is forbidden to wine' but then rules 'forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon permits'. It suggests either reading 'forbidden' as 'permitted' or explains that the case is different because the person acknowledges the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording, noting that it previously said Rabbi Shimon permits, but now the text seems to say he forbids.
The Gemara resolves by suggesting the text should be read as 'he is forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon permits,' or alternatively, the text is not reversed and the distinction lies elsewhere.
The Gemara offers an alternative: do not emend the text; rather, the case is different because the person acknowledges the prohibition, so the Mishnah's ruling stands.

items.text: Resolution of the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Resolution of the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's case: the first clause deals with one who vowed from one type of produce, where according to the Rabbis he is a nazirite and prohibited, but according to Rabbi Shimon he is permitted unless he vowed from all. The latter clause deals with one who vowed from all and then sought absolution from one, where the Rabbis permit him but Rabbi Shimon prohibits until he is absolved from all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's first clause: one who vowed from one type of produce is a nazirite according to the Rabbis but permitted according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara explains the second clause: one who vowed from all produce and sought absolution from one type is permitted according to the Rabbis but prohibited by Rabbi Shimon until absolved from all.
The Gemara concludes that this is why the Mishnah states 'and Rabbi Shimon prohibits'.

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute about coerced vows
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute about coerced vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about coerced vows (נדרי אונסין), based on the disagreement between Shmuel and Rav Asi. The Rabbis follow Shmuel who says these vows do not require a sage's dissolution, while Rabbi Shimon follows Rav Asi who says they do require it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about coerced vows (נדרי אונסין), citing the Mishnah of four types of vows that the Sages permit.

sub.text: Citation of Rav Yehuda quoting Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Citation of Rav Yehuda quoting Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav Asi that these four types of vows require a formal inquiry (שאלה) before a Sage.
Shmuel objects to Rav Asi's statement, arguing that the Mishnah says 'the Sages permitted' (היתירו), not that they require inquiry.
The Gemara aligns the Rabbis with Shmuel's view (vows are permitted outright) and Rabbi Shimon with Rav Asi's view (vows require inquiry).

items.text: Mishnah: "I am a nazirite and I take upon myself to shave a nazirite"
items.text_en: Mishnah: "I am a nazirite and I take upon myself to shave a nazirite"
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one says "I am a nazirite and I take upon myself to shave a nazirite," and his friend responds "And I take upon myself to shave a nazirite." If they are clever, they shave each other; otherwise, other nazirites shave them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: one says 'I am a nazirite and I take upon myself to shave a nazirite,' and his friend responds 'and I take upon myself to shave a nazirite'; if they are clever they shave each other, otherwise others shave them.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: what does "and I" mean?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: what does "and I" mean?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when the friend says "and I," does he accept the entire statement or only part of it? If only part, does he accept the first part (being a nazirite) or the latter part (shaving a nazirite)? The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that "and I" refers to part of the statement, specifically the beginning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when a friend says 'וַאֲנִי' (and I), does it mean he accepts the entire statement or only part of it?
If 'וַאֲנִי' refers to part of the statement, the Gemara asks whether it refers to the beginning (being a nazirite) or the end (shaving a nazirite).
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that 'וַאֲנִי' refers to part of the statement, since the friend adds 'וְעָלַי לְגַלֵּחַ' (and upon me to shave).
The Gemara concludes that 'וַאֲנִי' refers to the beginning of the statement (being a nazirite), because the friend explicitly adds 'וְעָלַי לְגַלֵּחַ' for the shaving part.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua challenges Rava: perhaps "and I" refers to the entire statement, and "upon me" refers only to the latter part. Rava responds that if the first clause were necessary, the latter clause would be unnecessary, but here both are stated, proving the interpretation.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects to Rava's proof: perhaps 'and I' refers to the entire statement, and 'upon me' refers only to the latter part, as in the parallel case of half a nazirite.
Rava rejects the objection: if the first clause were necessary, the latter clause would be unnecessary, but here both are stated, proving the interpretation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about an agent
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about an agent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan regarding one who says to his agent... (the text is cut off, beginning a new topic).

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan beginning a new statement about one who says to his agent.

items.text: Opening statement: the case of a general agency
items.text_en: Opening statement: the case of a general agency
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one says to an agent 'go and betroth a woman for me' without specifying which woman, the agent is forbidden to marry any woman in the world, because the agent is presumed to fulfill his mission and since the principal did not specify, the agent does not know which woman was intended.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a general agency to betroth a woman forbids the agent from marrying any woman, because the agent is presumed to fulfill his mission and does not know which woman was intended.

items.text: Resh Lakish's objection from a bird-offering case
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's objection from a bird-offering case
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing a mishna about an unspecified bird-offering (קן סתומה) where one fledgling flew away or died: the owner may pair the remaining one with another bird. But if the offering was specified (קן מפורשת), there is no remedy. Resh Lakish asks: why is the unspecified case fixable? Shouldn't we say each bird might be the one that flew?

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish cites a mishna about a קן סתומה (unspecified bird-offering) where one fledgling flew away or died: the owner may pair the remaining one with another bird.
Resh Lakish contrasts with a קן מפורשת (specified offering), which has no remedy.
Resh Lakish asks: why is the unspecified case fixable? Shouldn't we say each bird might be the one that flew?

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: distinction between fixed and mobile items
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: distinction between fixed and mobile items
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan responds: I am discussing a woman who is not mobile (i.e., she stays in one place), while you are citing a case of a mobile bird. Even if you argue that here too the woman might be mobile (e.g., found in the market), in the bird case the bird does not return to its original place, whereas a woman does.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer to Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer to Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a woman who is not mobile (does not move from place to place) and the bird case Resh Lakish cited, which involves a mobile bird.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's further response to a potential objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's further response to a potential objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan addresses the potential objection that the woman might also be mobile (e.g., found in the market), arguing that a woman returns to her place, unlike a bird that does not return.

items.text: Rava's addition: Rabbi Yochanan concedes in a case of no relatives
items.text_en: Rava's addition: Rabbi Yochanan concedes in a case of no relatives
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Yochanan concedes in the case of a woman who has no daughter, granddaughter, mother, grandmother, or sister. Even if she later had a sister who was divorced, that sister is permitted. The reason: at the time of the agency, those women were married to other men, and one only appoints an agent for a matter that is currently available, not for one that is not.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Yochanan concedes in the case of a woman with no female relatives, and even if a sister later becomes divorced, that sister is permitted.
Rava explains the reason: at the time of the agency, those women were married to other men, and one only appoints an agent for a matter that is currently available, not for one that is not.

items.text: Gemara's question from a Nazirite vow case
items.text_en: Gemara's question from a Nazirite vow case
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna: if one says 'I am a nazirite and I am responsible for shaving a nazirite,' and another says 'I too, and I am responsible for shaving a nazirite,' if they are clever they shave each other, otherwise others shave them. The Gemara asks: the second one has the first before him, but the first — does he have the second before him? (implying a problem of uncertainty).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about two nazirites who each vow to shave the other, and questions how the first can shave the second if the second's vow was not yet made when the first spoke.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the earlier case: the husband meant that if he finds his wife is a nazirite, he will shave her; similarly, the man meant that if you find she is divorced, then betroth me.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the earlier statement: the husband meant that if he finds his wife is a nazirite, he will shave her; similarly, the man said to his friend: if you find she is divorced, then betroth me.

items.text: Principle: agent only for immediate actions
items.text_en: Principle: agent only for immediate actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: one only appoints an agent for a matter that can be done now, not for something that cannot be done at present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a principle: a person only appoints an agent for a matter that he himself can currently perform, not for something he cannot currently do.

items.text: Challenge from the case of an agent for annulment
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of an agent for annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle with a baraita: one can appoint an agent to annul his wife's vows, even though the husband himself cannot annul them now (since they haven't been made). Rabbi Yoshiya limits this, but Rabbi Yonatan says the agent is like himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a baraita: a man told his guardian to annul his wife's vows, and Rabbi Yoshiya says the annulment is invalid because the verse says 'her husband shall confirm it and her husband shall annul it', while Rabbi Yonatan says a person's agent is like himself.

The baraita presents Rabbi Yoshiya's position that the agent cannot annul, based on the verse 'אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ', and Rabbi Yonatan's opposing view that the agent is like the husband himself.

items.text: Distinction between agent and direct statement
items.text_en: Distinction between agent and direct statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's limitation is only because of the verse; otherwise an agent could annul. But regarding the husband himself, a conditional annulment is disputed between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yoshiya, only the verse prevents the guardian from annulling, and contrasts this with a case where a husband tells his wife her vows are upheld or annulled, where Rabbi Eliezer says it is annulled and the Sages say it is not.

The Gemara contrasts the agent case with the husband himself, citing a baraita where a conditional annulment by the husband is disputed: Rabbi Eliezer holds it is annulled, while the Sages hold it is not annulled.

items.text: Resolving the challenge: which opinion does Rabbi Yoshiya follow?
items.text_en: Resolving the challenge: which opinion does Rabbi Yoshiya follow?
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yoshiya follows the Sages who say the husband cannot annul conditionally, so the agent would annul. But it suggests he might follow Rabbi Eliezer, who allows conditional annulment; then why appoint an agent? Because the husband might forget, get angry, or be distracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yoshiya follows the Sages who say the husband cannot annul conditionally, so the agent would annul.
The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yoshiya might follow Rabbi Eliezer, who allows conditional annulment.
The Gemara answers that even if conditional annulment is possible, the husband appoints an agent because he might forget, get angry, or be distracted.

items.text: Mishnah: partial nazirite vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: partial nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if one says 'I take upon myself to shave half a nazirite' and another says 'and I', Rabbi Meir says each must bring a full nazirite offering, while the Sages say each brings only half.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: one says 'I take upon myself to shave half a nazirite' and another says 'and I', Rabbi Meir says each shaves a full nazirite, and the Sages say each shaves half a nazirite.
Rabbi Meir rules that each person must shave a full nazirite offering.
The Sages rule that each person shaves only half a nazirite.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that all agree on the distinction between 'half the offerings of a nazirite' (brings half) and 'offerings of half a nazirite' (brings full). The dispute is about the language of the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir holds that 'upon me' obligates the full offering, while the Sages view it as a vow with a built-in opening.

sub.desc_en: Rava establishes that all agree on the distinction between 'half the offerings of a nazirite' (brings half) and 'offerings of half a nazirite' (brings full), because naziriteship cannot be split.
Rava explains that the dispute is about the language of the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir holds that 'עלי' (upon me) obligates the full offering, while the Sages view it as a vow with a built-in opening (פתח).

items.text: Mishnah: conditional nazirite vow for a child
items.text_en: Mishnah: conditional nazirite vow for a child
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who says 'I am a nazirite when I have a son': if a son is born, he is a nazirite; if a daughter, tumtum, or androgyne, he is not. But if he said 'when I have a child', any offspring makes him a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one says 'I am a nazirite when I have a son' and a son is born, he is a nazirite; if a daughter, tumtum, or androgynous is born, he is not a nazirite; but if he said 'when I have a child', even a daughter, tumtum, or androgynous makes him a nazirite.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: miscarriage and subsequent birth
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: miscarriage and subsequent birth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man says he will be a nazir when his wife gives birth. If she miscarries, he is not a nazir. Rabbi Shimon allows him to stipulate that if the fetus was viable, the nazirite vow is obligatory, otherwise it is voluntary. If she later gives birth, he becomes a nazir; Rabbi Shimon again allows a conditional statement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic case: if a man vowed to be a nazir when his wife gives birth, and she miscarries, he is not a nazir.
Rabbi Shimon allows the man to stipulate that if the fetus was viable, the nazirite vow is obligatory (חובה), otherwise it is voluntary (נדבה).
The Mishnah continues: if she later gives birth, he becomes a nazir.
Rabbi Shimon again allows a conditional statement to determine which birth triggers the obligatory nazirite vow.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state certain cases, explaining that it teaches that a tumtum or androgynous child does not count as a 'child' for the vow, and that the phrase 'when I have a child' refers to any viable offspring, not just a son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that one who vows to be a nazirite when a son is born is a nazirite, suggesting it is obvious.

The Gemara answers that the ruling is stated due to the latter clause, which teaches that a daughter, tumtum, or androgynous child does not fulfill the vow, and that one might think the vow meant 'when I am built up' by any child.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that if one says 'when I have a child' the vow applies to any child, including a daughter, tumtum, or androgynous child.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that one might think only a child considered significant by people is meant, but the Mishnah clarifies that any viable offspring counts.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the first clause of the Mishnah (miscarriage does not make him a nazir) follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that doubtful nazirite vows are treated leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the mishna's ruling that a miscarriage does not make him a nazirite follows Rabbi Yehuda, who treats doubtful nazirite vows leniently.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's inquiry about a separated offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's inquiry about a separated offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna about a case where a man vowed to be a nazir when his son is born, his wife miscarried, he separated a korban, and then she gave birth. The Gemara clarifies that the question is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who is lenient: is the korban sanctified or not? The practical difference is whether the animal can be shorn or worked. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna about a case where a man vowed to be a nazir when his son is born, his wife miscarried, he separated a korban, and then she gave birth.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who is lenient regarding ספק נזירות (doubtful nazirite status), and asks whether the separated korban is sanctified or not.
The Gemara states the practical difference is whether the animal can be shorn or worked, and concludes the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Ben Rechumi's inquiry about a friend joining the vow
items.text_en: Ben Rechumi's inquiry about a friend joining the vow
items.desc_en: Ben Rechumi asks Abaye about a case where a man says he will be a nazir when he has a son, and a friend says 'and upon me' — does the friend's vow depend on the speaker's words or on the event itself? Then, if the friend says 'and I', does he mean he himself becomes a nazir or that he loves the speaker like himself?

sub.desc_en: Ben Rechumi asks Abaye whether a friend who says 'ועלי' (and upon me) after hearing a nazirite vow conditioned on having a son is bound by the speaker's words (אדיבורא) or by the event itself (אגופא).

Ben Rechumi then asks, if the friend is bound by the event, what about a friend who says 'ואני' (and I) — does he mean he himself becomes a nazir (אנפשיה קאמר) or does he mean 'I love you as myself' (רחימנא לך כוותיך), leaving each to his own vow?

items.text: Opening question about contingent naziriteship
items.text_en: Opening question about contingent naziriteship
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a person who says 'I am a nazir when so-and-so has a son' and his friend says 'and I' intends to accept naziriteship on himself or to join the original vow. The question is left unresolved (תיבְּעֵי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question about a person who says 'I am a nazir when so-and-so has a son' and his friend responds 'and I' — whether the friend intends to accept naziriteship on himself or to join the original vow.

items.text: Mishnah: Two formulations of naziriteship with a son
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two formulations of naziriteship with a son
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: if one says 'I am a nazir and a nazir when I have a son', he completes his own term first; if he says 'I am a nazir when I have a son and a nazir', he interrupts his own term to observe the son's term first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'I am a nazir, and a nazir when I have a son' — he begins counting his own term, and if a son is born later, he completes his own term first and then counts the son's term.

The Mishnah presents the reverse case: one who says 'I am a nazir when I have a son, and a nazir' — if a son is born after he began counting, he interrupts his own term, counts the son's term, and then completes his own.

items.text: Rava's query about sequential nazirite periods
items.text_en: Rava's query about sequential nazirite periods
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one says 'I am a nazir for twenty days from now, and for one hundred days starting now', do the hundred days not take effect because they overlap with the twenty, or do they take effect because there is eventual hair growth? The Gemara notes that this implies a prior question about a shorter nazirite period, and that Rava's query is derived from that.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if one says 'I am a nazir for twenty days from now, and for one hundred days starting now', do the hundred days not take effect because they overlap with the twenty, or do they take effect because there is eventual hair growth?
The Gemara notes that this implies a prior question about a shorter nazirite period, and that Rava's query is derived from that.

items.text: Three unresolved hypotheticals about sequential nezirut
items.text_en: Three unresolved hypotheticals about sequential nezirut
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three unresolved questions: (1) If one vows a short nezirut after a long one, do the extra days of the long one count toward the short? (2) If one says 'I am a nazir after 20 days and now a permanent nazir,' does the permanent vow take effect? (3) If one says 'I am a Shimshon nazir after 20 days and now a standard nazir,' does the Shimshon vow take effect, given it cannot be dissolved? The Gemara also asks about a vow 'like Moshe on the 7th of Adar.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the first unresolved question: if one vows a short nezirut after a long one, do the extra days of the long one count toward the short?
The Gemara raises the second unresolved question: if one says 'I am a nazir after 20 days and now a permanent nazir,' does the permanent vow take effect?
The Gemara raises the third unresolved question: if one says 'I am a Shimshon nazir after 20 days and now a standard nazir,' does the Shimshon vow take effect given it cannot be dissolved?
The Gemara raises a fourth unresolved question: if one vows 'like Moshe on the 7th of Adar,' what is the halacha?

items.text: Resolution of the first hypothetical
items.text_en: Resolution of the first hypothetical
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the first question: If one says 'I am a nazir after 20 days and now for 100 days,' he counts 20 days, then 30, then 80 to complete the first nezirut. This implies that the later period does count toward the earlier vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the first hypothetical: one who says 'I am a nazir after 20 days and now for 100 days' counts 20 days, then 30, then 80 to complete the first nezirut, implying the later period counts toward the earlier vow.

items.text: Dispute about impurity during the intervening period
items.text_en: Dispute about impurity during the intervening period
items.desc_en: If the nazir becomes impure during the days between the two nezirut periods, Rabbi Yochanan holds that he must restart the entire sequence, viewing it as one long nezirut. Reish Lakish holds that he does not restart, because each period is independent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute: if a nazir becomes impure during the intervening days between two nezirut periods, Rabbi Yochanan says he must restart the entire sequence, while Reish Lakish says he does not restart.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his position: the two periods are viewed as one long nezirut, so impurity in the intervening days requires restarting the entire count.
Reish Lakish explains his position: each nezirut period is independent, so impurity in the intervening days does not affect the other period.

items.text: Dispute on impurity during leprosy period
items.text_en: Dispute on impurity during leprosy period
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue whether a nazirite who becomes impure during his leprosy period must restart (סותר) his nazirite count. Rabbi Yochanan says he must, because he is still in naziriteship; Reish Lakish says he does not, because leprosy and naziriteship are separate.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a nazirite who becomes impure during his leprosy period must restart (סותר) his count, while Reish Lakish rules he does not.
The gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds he is still in naziriteship, while Reish Lakish holds that leprosy and naziriteship are separate domains.
The gemara notes that both disputes are necessary, as each case might otherwise have led to agreement in the other.

items.text: Need for both disputes
items.text_en: Need for both disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both disputes (the earlier one about impurity during naziriteship and this one about leprosy) are necessary. If only the first were stated, one might think Rabbi Yochanan only disagrees there because it's one naziriteship, but here he might agree with Reish Lakish; and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both disputes are necessary, because each case has a unique factor that would prevent the other's ruling from being inferred.

items.text: Dispute on impurity during hair-growing day
items.text_en: Dispute on impurity during hair-growing day
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about a nazirite who becomes impure on the day of hair growth (after completing his naziriteship but before bringing offerings). Rav says he does not restart, even according to Rabbi Yochanan, because hair growth is completion of naziriteship. Shmuel says he does restart, even according to Reish Lakish, because here it is one naziriteship.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a new dispute: Rav rules that impurity on the day of hair growth does not restart the count, even according to Rabbi Yochanan, because hair growth is completion of naziriteship.
Shmuel rules that impurity on the day of hair growth does restart the count, even according to Reish Lakish, because here there is only one naziriteship.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement on consecrated hair
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement on consecrated hair
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if a nazirite consecrated his hair with blood (i.e., brought the offering), there is no remedy. The Gemara questions this: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that shaving is essential, why wouldn't he restart? It concludes that the statement is according to the Rabbis, and 'no remedy' means no remedy for the mitzvah of shaving.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree: if a nazirite sanctified his hair with blood (i.e., brought the sacrifice), there is no remedy.
The gemara asks: according to which authority does Rav Chisda speak? If according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that shaving is essential, why would impurity not restart the count?
The gemara resolves: Rav Chisda speaks according to the Rabbis, and 'no remedy' means no remedy for the mitzvah of shaving.
The Gemara objects: if according to the Rabbis, who hold that shaving does not impede, why would there be no remedy?
The Gemara resolves: the statement is according to the Rabbis, and 'no remedy' means no remedy for the mitzvah of shaving.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on post-completion violations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on post-completion violations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says that a nazirite whose days have ended is liable for impurity but not for shaving or wine. The Gemara challenges this, noting that the verses for shaving and wine also say 'all the days of his naziriteship,' which should include post-completion days.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina rules: a nazirite whose days have ended is liable for impurity but not for shaving or wine, citing the verse 'כׇּל יְמֵי הַזִּירוֹ לַה׳' to include post-completion days.
The gemara objects: if so, one should also be liable for shaving and wine, since the same inclusive logic applies to the verses about shaving and wine.
The Gemara objects: if so, shaving should also be punishable, since the verse 'all the days of his nazirite vow no razor shall pass over his head' includes days after completion.
The Gemara further objects: similarly, the verse 'all the days of his naziriteship from anything made from the grapevine' should include days after completion, so why is wine not punishable?

items.text: Gemara's objection to Rav's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a nazirite whose days are completed is still prohibited from shaving, drinking wine, and contracting impurity; if he does so, he receives lashes. This is a refutation of Rav's implied leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a nazirite whose days are completed is still prohibited from shaving, drinking wine, and contracting impurity; if he does so, he receives lashes, refuting Rav's implied leniency.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one says 'I am a nazirite when I have a son' and 'I am a nazirite for 100 days', and a son is born within 70 days, he loses nothing; if after 70 days, he loses 70 days, because no haircut is less than 30 days apart.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one says 'I am a nazirite when I have a son' and 'I am a nazirite for one hundred days', and a son is born within seventy days, he loses nothing; after seventy days, he loses seventy days, because no shaving period is less than thirty days.

items.text: Rav's statement and Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rav's statement and Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav says: Day 70 counts for both the original vow and the son's vow. The Gemara challenges: If so, the Mishnah's phrase 'within 70 days' would imply gain, not just no loss. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah uses '70' in the first clause to parallel the second clause.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the seventieth day counts for both the son-related naziriteship and the hundred-day naziriteship.
The Gemara questions Rav: if the seventieth day counts for both, why does the Mishnah say 'until seventy' he loses nothing — that would imply he gains, not just loses nothing.
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah should not have said 'until seventy' at all, but because the latter clause says 'after seventy', the former clause also uses 'seventy' for symmetry.

items.text: Analysis of 'after 70' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Analysis of 'after 70' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's phrase 'after 70'. It suggests that 'after' might mean 'after the end of 70', i.e., day 71, in which case Rav's position is supported. But if 'after' means literally after 70, then even after 70 he does not lose anything, contradicting the Mishnah. The Gemara concludes that 'after' means literally after 70, and the Mishnah supports Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'after 70' and asks whether 'after' means 'after the end of 70' (day 71) or literally 'after 70' (i.e., on day 70 itself).
The Gemara objects: if 'after' means literally after 70 (i.e., on day 70), then even after 70 he does not lose anything, contradicting the Mishnah's ruling that after 70 he loses 70 days.
The Gemara resolves: 'after' means literally after 70 (i.e., on day 70), and the Mishnah supports Rav's position that day 70 counts for both terms.

items.text: Comparison to Abba Shaul's ruling
items.text_en: Comparison to Abba Shaul's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With whom does Rav align? It suggests Abba Shaul, who rules that if one buries his dead three days before a festival, the seven-day mourning period is annulled; if eight days before, the thirty-day period is annulled, and he may shave on the eve of the festival. This parallels Rav's idea that a partial period can count for both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks with whom Rav's ruling aligns, suggesting it might be Abba Shaul.
The Gemara cites Abba Shaul's ruling that burying a dead three days before a festival annuls the seven-day mourning period.
The Gemara continues citing Abba Shaul's ruling that burying eight days before the festival annuls the thirty-day mourning period, allowing shaving on the eve of the festival.

items.text: Abba Shaul's ruling on haircutting before a festival
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's ruling on haircutting before a festival
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul states that even if one did not cut their hair before the festival, they may cut it after the festival, because just as the commandment of three days overrides the decree of seven, so too the commandment of seven overrides the decree of thirty.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul rules that one who did not cut his hair before the festival may cut it after, because the commandment of seven days overrides the decree of thirty, just as the commandment of three days overrides the decree of seven.

items.text: Gemara's question about Abba Shaul's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Abba Shaul's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Abba Shaul's reasoning, suggesting it might be because he holds that the seventh day counts for both the seven and the thirty days of mourning. It then raises a doubt: perhaps Abba Shaul only said this regarding rabbinic mourning, but not regarding nazirite impurity which is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Abba Shaul's reasoning is, suggesting it might be because he holds that the seventh day counts for both the seven-day and thirty-day mourning periods.
The Gemara objects that Abba Shaul's leniency might apply only to rabbinic mourning, not to the Torah-based nazirite prohibition.

items.text: Rav's opinion aligned with Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rav's opinion aligned with Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav holds like Rabbi Yosei, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yosei says that a woman who observes a day for a day, if they slaughtered and sprinkled the Passover offering on her second day and she subsequently saw blood, she may not eat of it but is exempt from bringing a second Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a woman who observed a day for a day and then saw blood after the sacrifice is exempt from the second Passover.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, suggesting it is because he holds that part of the day is like the whole. It then raises a doubt: perhaps it is because he holds that impurity only applies from that point forward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is the principle of מקצת היום ככולו (part of the day counts as the whole) or that impurity only applies from now onward.
The Gemara raises a doubt: perhaps Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is because he holds that impurity only applies from that point forward (מכאן ולהבא הוא מטמא), not retroactively.

items.text: Challenge from another baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from another baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yosei actually holds that view, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says that a zav with two sightings or a woman observing a day for a day, if they saw after slaughter and sprinkling, they are exempt from a second Passover even though they retroactively defile. The Gemara explains that the retroactive impurity is rabbinic, and suggests that if it were biblical they would not be exempt. It then offers an alternative: even if it is biblical, the depths of the zav's impurity were permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yosei actually holds the view attributed to him.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that a zav with two sightings or a woman observing a day for a day, who saw after slaughter and sprinkling, are exempt from a second Passover despite retroactive impurity.
The Gemara explains that the retroactive impurity is rabbinic, and argues that if it were biblical they would not be exempt.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: even if the impurity is biblical, the depths of the zav's impurity were permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya says that a zav who sees on his seventh day negates the preceding days, but Rabbi Yochanan says he only negates that day. The Gemara questions this: if he negates, he should negate all; if not, he should negate nothing. It concludes that Rabbi Yochanan means he negates neither the preceding days nor that day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Oshaya holds that a zav who sees on his seventh day negates the preceding days retroactively by rabbinic decree, while Rabbi Yochanan says he negates only that day.

The Gemara challenges the logic: if a sighting on the seventh day is considered significant enough to negate, it should negate all preceding days; if it is not significant, it should negate nothing, not even that day.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan actually means the zav negates neither the preceding days nor that day itself.

items.text: Conclusion of Rabbi Yosei's dispute
items.text_en: Conclusion of Rabbi Yosei's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in Rabbi Yosei's position: although he holds that a zavah counts only from the future, his retroactive impurity is only rabbinic. It then addresses how a complete zavah can ever bring a sacrifice given his view that part of a day counts as a full day, offering two answers: she sees three consecutive days, or she sees near sunset so there is no time for counting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosei can agree with the view that a zavah is impure only from the future, given that he elsewhere holds retroactive impurity.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei's retroactive impurity is only rabbinic, not biblical.
The Gemara asks how a complete zavah can ever bring a sacrifice according to Rabbi Yosei, given his principle that part of a day counts as a full day.
The first answer suggests that she sees three consecutive days, leaving no counting time between them.
The second answer proposes that she sees near sunset, so there is no time for counting a full day.

items.text: Transition: Hadran on the previous chapter
items.text_en: Transition: Hadran on the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך הריני נזיר' (we return to you, 'Behold I am a nazirite').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך הריני נזיר' (we return to you, 'Behold I am a nazirite').

items.text: Mishnah: Nazirite haircut and impurity rules
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazirite haircut and impurity rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of a nazirite's haircut: one who says 'I am a nazirite' shaves on day 31, but if he shaved on day 30 it is valid; for a 30-day nazirite, shaving on day 30 is invalid. It then discusses a nazirite who took two naziriteships, and a testimony of Rabbi Pappiyas about counting days. Finally, it addresses impurity: if a nazirite becomes impure on day 30, he starts over (Rabbi Eliezer says only 7 days); for a 100-day nazirite, impurity on day 100 starts over (Rabbi Eliezer says 30 days), and impurity on day 101 requires 30 days (Rabbi Eliezer says 7).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that an unspecified nazirite shaves on day 31, and if he shaved on day 30 it is valid, but for a specified 30-day nazirite, shaving on day 30 is invalid.
The Mishnah rules that one who took two naziriteships shaves the first on day 31 and the second on day 61, with allowances for earlier shaving.
Rabbi Pappiyas testifies that for a double nazirite, shaving the first on day 30 allows the second to be shaved on day 60, and day 30 counts toward the count.

The Mishnah concludes with impurity rules: for an unspecified nazirite, impurity on day 30 cancels everything (Rabbi Eliezer says only 7 days); for a 100-day nazirite, impurity on day 100 cancels everything (Rabbi Eliezer says 30 days), and on day 101 cancels 30 days (Rabbi Eliezer says 7).

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins its analysis by quoting the Mishnah's first case: one who says 'I am a nazirite' and becomes impure on day 30 starts over, while Rabbi Eliezer says only 7 days. This sets up the ensuing discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins its discussion by restating the Mishnah's first case about an unspecified nazirite who becomes impure on day 30.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view on partial nullification
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view on partial nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's position that if a nazirite vow of 100 days is interrupted on day 100, only 30 days are nullified, not the entire term, contrasting with a 30-day vow where the whole term is nullified. This sets up the background for the main discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states Rabbi Eliezer's principle that after seven days of impurity, partial days count, and in a 30-day nazirite vow interrupted on day 30, he agrees the entire term is nullified.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's distinction
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's distinction
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for a 100-day nazirite vow interrupted on day 100, Rabbi Eliezer rules only 30 days are nullified, and the entire discussion follows the positions of Bar Pada and Rav Mattana.

items.text: Mishnah: Nazirite in a cemetery
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazirite in a cemetery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who takes a nazirite vow while in a cemetery does not count days of naziriteship and does not bring a purification offering. Rabbi Eliezer adds that the first days are void unless there are 'first days' to fall away, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first opinion: one who takes a nazirite vow while in a cemetery does not count those days toward the term and does not bring a טומאה (impurity) offering, but if he leaves and re-enters, the days count and he brings the offering.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that the day of leaving does not count, citing the verse 'והימים הראשונים יפלו' (the first days shall fall) to require that he have prior valid days.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that naziriteship takes effect even in a cemetery because purification is possible, while Reish Lakish argues it does not take effect unless the person later reaffirms the vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says the nazirite vow takes effect even while in the cemetery, while Reish Lakish says it does not take effect.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his view: the vow is suspended and contingent, and since purification is possible, it takes effect.
Reish Lakish explains his view: the vow does not take effect now, but if he later repeats the vow after leaving, it takes effect; otherwise it does not.

items.text: First objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah: since it says one does not bring a purification offering, implying the vow does take effect. Reish Lakish deflects by saying the person is not subject to impurity or offering laws at all.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah: since it says he does not bring a טומאה (impurity) offering, implying the vow does take effect.
Reish Lakish responds that the Mishnah means he is not subject to the laws of טומאה (impurity) or offering at all.

items.text: Second objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Second objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan brings a baraita stating that a person who was impure and then took a nazirite vow is liable for lashes if he violates the prohibitions. This supports the view that the vow takes effect, otherwise lashes would not apply. The argument is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan raises another objection from a baraita: if one was impure and took a nazirite vow, he is liable for lashes for violations, which would only make sense if the vow took effect.
The Gemara poses a rhetorical question: if the vow does not take effect, why would the person be liable for lashes?

items.text: Gemara's framing question
items.text_en: Gemara's framing question
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case under discussion is that of a nazirite who goes in and out of a cemetery (יוצא ונכנס).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case under discussion is that of a nazirite who goes in and out of a cemetery (יוצא ונכנס).

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between a person who was impure when he vowed and a pure nazirite who became impure: the former's seventh day counts toward his term, implying the vow took effect, contradicting the assumption that it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between a person who was impure when he vowed and a pure nazirite who became impure: the former's seventh day counts toward his term, implying the vow took effect, contradicting the assumption that it does not.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that everyone agrees the vow takes effect (חיילא); the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is only about whether one is liable for lashes.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves that all agree the vow takes effect (חיילא), and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is only about whether one is liable for lashes.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a mishnah about one who vowed while in a cemetery: he does not bring a guilt-offering for impurity, implying he is lashed. The Gemara explains that the mishnah only mentions the offering because it wants to contrast with the case of יוצא ונכנס.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish by citing a mishnah that implies one who vowed while in a cemetery is lashed, even though he does not bring a guilt-offering.

The Gemara explains that the mishnah deliberately omits 'he does not get lashes' in the first clause, because it only mentions the guilt-offering in order to set up the contrast with the case of יוצא ונכנס (one who went out and re-entered).

items.text: Further objection from the baraita
items.text_en: Further objection from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another objection from the baraita that says the only difference between the two cases is the counting of the seventh day, implying they are equal regarding lashes. Reish Lakish deflects by saying it refers to shaving, not lashes, and the Gemara notes the baraita does not discuss lashes because it deals with the remedy, not the penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states the only difference between the two cases is the counting of the seventh day, implying they are equal regarding lashes.
Reish Lakish deflects by saying the baraita refers to shaving, not lashes.
The Gemara asks: if the baraita only discusses shaving, why does it not mention lashes explicitly?
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with the remedy (תקנתיה) of shaving, not the penalty (קלקוליה) of lashes.

items.text: Conclusive refutation from a baraita
items.text_en: Conclusive refutation from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who was impure when he vowed and then shaved, drank wine, or became impure receives lashes, providing a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one who was impure when he vowed and then shaved, drank wine, or became impure receives lashes, providing a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish's position.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about warning
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about warning
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a nazirite in a cemetery requires a waiting period (שהייה) for lashes, and the Gemara clarifies that if he was warned, no waiting period is needed, just as with a regular nazirite.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a nazirite who is already in a cemetery requires a waiting period (שהייה) before being liable for lashes.
The Gemara clarifies that if the nazirite was warned not to take a nazirite vow, no waiting period is needed, just as with a regular nazirite who is warned.

items.text: Unresolved query about entering a container into a cemetery
items.text_en: Unresolved query about entering a container into a cemetery
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a case where one enters a cemetery inside a chest, box, or cabinet, and a friend removes the covering. The doubt is whether the laws of 'waiting' (שהייה) apply only in the Temple or also outside. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a case where one enters a cemetery inside a chest, box, or cabinet, and a friend removes the covering, questioning whether the laws of שהייה (waiting) apply only in the Temple or also outside.
The Gemara states that the law of שהייה (waiting) is only learned for the Temple, but outside it may not apply; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Ashi's query: nazirite who was in a cemetery when he vowed
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query: nazirite who was in a cemetery when he vowed
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a person who was already in a cemetery when he took the nazirite vow requires shaving upon leaving. The doubt is whether shaving applies only to a pure nazirite who became impure, but not to one who was already impure at the time of the vow. The question is left open.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a nazirite who was already in a cemetery when he vowed requires shaving upon leaving, or whether shaving applies only to a pure nazirite who became impure.

items.text: First attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: First attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who vowed while in a cemetery for 30 days does not have those days count, and does not bring a sin-offering. The Gemara infers that he does require shaving, but the baraita is reinterpreted: it means he does not require shaving, hence no sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as a proof: one who vowed while in a cemetery does not have those days count and does not bring a sin-offering.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that although he does not bring a sin-offering, he does require shaving.
The Gemara rejects the inference by reinterpreting the baraita: it means he does not require shaving, and therefore does not bring a sin-offering.

items.text: Second attempted proof from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between an impure nazirite and a pure one who became impure only regarding the seventh day counting. The Gemara initially thinks this implies they are equal regarding shaving, but rejects this: the Mishnah refers to lashes, not shaving. The Gemara then challenges that if shaving differs, it should have been stated, but the Tanna included all details in 'seventh day and all matters'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between an impure nazirite and a pure one who became impure only regarding the seventh day counting, and infers that they are equal regarding shaving.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the Mishnah's equality refers to lashes, not shaving.
The Gemara objects that if shaving differs, the Mishnah should have stated it explicitly.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna included all details in the phrase 'his seventh day and all matters'.

items.text: Discussion of days of leprosy and impurity regarding counting
items.text_en: Discussion of days of leprosy and impurity regarding counting
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines whether days of leprosy (ימי חלוטו) count toward the nazirite term, using a kal vachomer from impurity days. It is argued that impurity days cancel previous days, so they don't count, but leprosy days do not cancel, so they might count. A further argument from a nazirite in a grave (whose hair is fit for shaving) suggests leprosy days (where hair is not fit) should certainly not count. The Gemara clarifies that the shaving referred to is pure shaving, not impurity shaving, and concludes that this is logical.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that uses a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) to argue that days of leprosy (ימי חלוטו) should not count toward the nazirite term, just as days of impurity do not count.
The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed: impurity days cancel previous days, so they do not count, but leprosy days do not cancel, so they might count.

The Gemara raises a second objection: a nazirite in a grave, whose hair is fit for shaving, does not have those days count, so leprosy days, where hair is not fit for shaving, certainly should not count.
The Gemara resolves that the shaving referred to in the objection is shaving of purity (תגלחת טהרה), not impurity shaving, and concludes that this is logical.

items.text: Gemara's initial rejection of the alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Gemara's initial rejection of the alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the mishnah meant the shaving of impurity, then the days of sealing (leprosy) would also require shaving, which is not the case. Therefore, the mishnah must be referring to the shaving of naziriteship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the mishnah refers to shaving of impurity, because then days of sealing would also require shaving, and concludes it must refer to shaving of naziriteship.

items.text: Proof from the verse 'and he defiled his nazirite head'
items.text_en: Proof from the verse 'and he defiled his nazirite head'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the verse 'and he defiled his nazirite head' as referring to a pure nazirite who became impure, requiring hair removal and bird offerings, and exempting a nazirite who was already impure at the start (nazir be-kever). A kal va-chomer argument is refuted by the verse, concluding that the mishnah's distinction stands.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited interpreting the verse 'וְטִמֵּא רֹאשׁ נִזְרוֹ' (and he defiled his nazirite head) as speaking of a pure nazirite who became impure, requiring hair removal and bird offerings, and exempting a nazirite who was already impure at a grave, concluding with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument and a scriptural limitation.

The baraita raises a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) argument: if a pure nazirite who became impure requires hair removal and bird offerings, then one who was impure from the start should certainly require them.

The baraita concludes with a 'תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר' (the verse teaches) that the verse specifically speaks of one who was pure and became impure, thereby exempting the nazir be-kever, and the Gemara affirms: 'שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ' (learn from it).

items.text: Question about the Tanna of the baraita
items.text_en: Question about the Tanna of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that states the only difference between a nazirite who was impure from the start and one who became impure is that the seventh day counts for the former but not the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that distinguishes between a nazirite who was impure from the start and a pure nazirite who became impure, regarding whether the seventh day counts toward his naziriteship.

items.text: Rav Chisda's identification: Rabbi
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's identification: Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi, who holds that pure naziriteship does not take effect until the eighth day. If it were Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, he would hold that it takes effect from the seventh day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the baraita follows Rabbi's opinion, who holds that pure naziriteship only takes effect from the eighth day, unlike Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda who holds it takes effect from the seventh.

items.text: Source of the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Source of the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita where Rabbi interprets 'and he shall consecrate his head on that day' as the day of bringing his offerings, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it is the day of his shaving.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited explaining the dispute: Rabbi interprets 'וְקִדַּשׁ אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ' (and he shall consecrate his head) as the day of bringing his offerings, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it is the day of his shaving.

The baraita cites the verse 'and he shall consecrate his head on that day' and records Rabbi's interpretation as the day of bringing offerings and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's as the day of shaving.

items.text: Application to a nazirite who contracted multiple impurities
items.text_en: Application to a nazirite who contracted multiple impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mishnah that a nazirite who contracted many impurities brings only one offering. Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that pure naziriteship takes effect from the seventh day. The case is when he was impure on the seventh day and again on the seventh day, so no hour suitable for bringing an offering passed. If it were Rabbi, impurity on the seventh day is a single extended impurity, and on the eighth day an hour suitable for an offering has passed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah that a nazirite who contracted many impurities brings only one offering.
The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of this mishnah.
Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that pure naziriteship takes effect from the seventh day.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's explanation of the case
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation of the case
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the case is when he was impure on the seventh day and again on the seventh day, so no hour suitable for bringing an offering passed, and he is liable for only one offering.

The Gemara objects that if the Tanna were Rabbi, impurity on the seventh day is a single extended impurity, and on the eighth day an hour suitable for an offering has passed, which would require multiple offerings.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi's reasoning from the verse 'and he shall atone for him for that which he sinned regarding the soul' and then 'and he shall consecrate his head'. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda argues that if so, the verse should have said 'and he shall consecrate his head' immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda: Rabbi derives from the verse order that consecration follows atonement, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda argues that the verse should have simply said 'וְקִדַּשׁ אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ' (and he shall consecrate his head) if that were the case.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda objects that if the verse intended to teach that consecration follows atonement, it should have said 'וְקִדַּשׁ אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ' (and he shall consecrate his head) immediately after the atonement verse, without the intervening phrase.

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse "on that day"
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse "on that day"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says "on that day" regarding the nazirite's consecration, and explains that if it does not apply to the eighth day, apply it to the seventh. It then notes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi interprets the phrase to mean even if he did not bring his offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says 'בְּיוֹם הַהוּא' (on that day) regarding the nazirite's consecration, and explains that if it does not apply to the eighth day, apply it to the seventh; it then notes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi interprets the phrase to mean even if he did not bring his offerings.

items.text: Rav Chisda's difficulty and the implication about night
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's difficulty and the implication about night
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Chisda was forced to interpret the mishnah according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, suggesting he could have interpreted it according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in a case of impurity on the night of the eighth. The Gemara infers that Rav Chisda holds that night is not considered a missing time (מחסור זמן).
