sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Chisda was forced to interpret the mishnah according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, suggesting he could have interpreted it according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in a case of impurity on the night of the eighth.
The Gemara infers that Rav Chisda holds that night is not considered a missing time (מחסור זמן).

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the status of night as a missing time is interdependent with when the nazirite becomes fit for offerings: if night is missing time, naziritehood only takes effect at morning; if not, it takes effect from the previous night.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the issue of night being a time deficiency is interdependent with the timing of the nazirite's purity: if night is a deficiency, the nazirite's consecration only takes effect in the morning; if not, it takes effect from the night.

items.text: Mishnah: impurity on the seventh and eighth days
items.text_en: Mishnah: impurity on the seventh and eighth days
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a nazirite became impure on the seventh day and again on the seventh, he brings only one offering; if on the eighth and again on the eighth, he brings an offering for each. Rabbi Eliezer says he begins counting immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah: if a nazirite became impure on the seventh day and again on the seventh, he brings only one offering; if on the eighth and again on the eighth, he brings an offering for each; Rabbi Eliezer says he begins counting immediately.
The mishnah states the contrasting rule for impurity on the eighth day.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that the nazirite begins counting immediately after purification.

items.text: Sages' opinion and the role of the sin-offering
items.text_en: Sages' opinion and the role of the sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Sages say he brings one offering for all until he brings his sin-offering; once he brings it and becomes impure again, he brings an offering for each. If he brought his sin-offering but not his guilt-offering, he begins counting.

sub.desc_en: The Sages say: one offering covers all until he brings his sin-offering; if he brought his sin-offering and became impure again, he brings an offering for each; if he brought his sin-offering but not his guilt-offering, he counts.
Once he brings his sin-offering and becomes impure again, he brings an offering for each impurity.
If he brought his sin-offering but not his guilt-offering, he begins counting his nazirite period.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's opinion on the guilt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's opinion on the guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says that just as the sin-offering delays him, so too the guilt-offering delays him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says: just as his sin-offering delayed him, so too his guilt-offering delays him.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verses for each opinion
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verses for each opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis: for Rabbi Eliezer, "on that day" means even without offerings; for the Sages, it means even without the guilt-offering; for Rabbi Yishmael, it means even without the burnt-offering, which the Sages say needs no exclusion since it is merely a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Eliezer, the verse 'בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא' (on that day) teaches that the nazirite begins counting even without bringing his offerings.
The Gemara explains that for the Sages, the same verse teaches that the nazirite begins counting even without bringing his guilt-offering.
The Gemara asks what purpose the verse 'הַהוּא' serves for Rabbi Yishmael, since he already has a different interpretation.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that the verse teaches that the nazirite begins counting even without bringing his burnt-offering.
The Gemara resolves that the Sages do not need an exclusion for the burnt-offering, since it is merely a gift (דּוֹרוֹן) and does not delay the counting.

items.text: Source for the Sages' position
items.text_en: Source for the Sages' position
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse "and he shall bring a year-old lamb as a guilt-offering" that all other guilt-offerings delay, but this one might not; the baraita is cut off, implying a continuation.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the Sages' reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the Sages' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Sages, and cites a baraita: the verse 'וְהֵבִיא כֶּבֶשׂ בֶּן שְׁנָתוֹ לְאָשָׁם' (and he shall bring a year-old lamb for a guilt-offering) teaches that although all other guilt-offerings in the Torah delay, one might think this one also delays.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהִזִּיר לַה׳ אֶת יְמֵי נִזְרוֹ וְהֵבִיא כֶּבֶשׂ בֶּן שְׁנָתוֹ לְאָשָׁם' (and he shall consecrate to the Lord the days of his naziriteship and bring a year-old lamb as a guilt-offering) that all other guilt-offerings in the Torah delay (מעכבין), but this one might not delay — the baraita is cut off, implying a continuation.

items.text: Dispute on the necessity of bringing a sacrifice for nezirut to take effect
items.text_en: Dispute on the necessity of bringing a sacrifice for nezirut to take effect
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse 'וְהִזִּיר ... וְהֵבִיא' that even if one did not bring the sacrifice, the nezirut is effective. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, argues that the nezirut only takes effect when the sacrifice is brought.

sub.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse 'וְהִזִּיר ... וְהֵבִיא' that even if one did not bring the sacrifice, the nezirut is effective.
Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, argues that the nezirut only takes effect when the sacrifice is brought.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita about a woman whose husband annulled her vow
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita about a woman whose husband annulled her vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that states a woman who vowed to be a nazirite, became impure, and then her husband annulled her vow, brings a bird sin-offering but not a burnt-offering. Rav Chisda identifies this as the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita about a woman whose husband annulled her nazirite vow after she became impure, where she brings a bird sin-offering but not a burnt-offering.
Rav Chisda answers that the baraita follows the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Analysis of Rav Chisda's identification and resolution
items.text_en: Analysis of Rav Chisda's identification and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Chisda's identification: if the husband's annulment is retroactive (עקר), she should not bring any offering; if it is from that point forward (גז), she should bring both. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who considers a nazirite a sinner, so she brings a sin-offering even though the nezirut is retroactively annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Chisda's identification: if the husband's annulment is retroactive (עקר), she should not bring any offering; if it is from that point forward (גז), she should bring both.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda holds the husband's annulment is retroactive, and Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Elazar HaKappar who considers a nazirite a sinner, so she brings a sin-offering even though the nezirut is retroactively annulled.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view that a nazirite is a sinner
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view that a nazirite is a sinner
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar HaKappar who derives from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו מֵאֲשֶׁר חָטָא עַל הַנָּפֶשׁ' that a nazirite who abstains from wine is called a sinner, and by a fortiori argument, one who abstains from everything is even more so. The Gemara questions why this is stated regarding a impure nazirite, and answers that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar holds even a pure nazirite is a sinner, but the verse is written about an impure nazirite because he sinned twice.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar HaKappar who derives from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו מֵאֲשֶׁר חָטָא עַל הַנָּפֶשׁ' that a nazirite who abstains from wine is called a sinner, and by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument, one who abstains from everything is even more so.
The Gemara objects that the verse is written about an impure nazirite, yet the baraita applies it to a pure nazirite.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar holds even a pure nazirite is a sinner, but the verse is written about an impure nazirite because he sinned twice.

items.text: The case of a nazirite who left and re-entered the camp
items.text_en: The case of a nazirite who left and re-entered the camp
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a nazirite left the camp and re-entered, the days count. The Gemara questions this: does leaving impose nezirut? Shmuel explains it refers to one who left, sprinkled, waited, and immersed. The Gemara then clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'even if he re-entered' is not exclusive; it means that even re-entry counts, and certainly leaving counts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a nazirite left the camp and re-entered, the days count toward his term.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah implies that leaving the camp imposes a new period of nezirut (נזירות) on the nazirite.
Shmuel explains that the case is one where the nazirite left, sprinkled the purification water, waited, and immersed, so the days count only after full purification.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's phrasing implies only re-entry counts, but not leaving, which seems contradictory.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah uses a 'not only' formulation: not only leaving counts, but even re-entry counts.

items.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav about not explaining
items.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav about not explaining
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav why he did not explain these matters to them. Rav responds that he thought they did not need it.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav why he did not explain these matters to them.
Rav responds that he thought they did not need the explanation.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view on cancellation of days by impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view on cancellation of days by impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that impurity does not cancel previous days unless there are at least thirty days of purity beforehand, based on the verse 'וְהַיָּמִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים יִפְּלוּ'. Ulla explains that Rabbi Eliezer only applies this to an impure nazirite who vowed, but for a pure nazirite who becomes impure, even one day cancels all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that impurity does not cancel previous days unless there are at least thirty days of purity beforehand, citing the verse 'וְהַיָּמִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים יִפְּלוּ' to require 'first days'.
Ulla clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer's rule applies only to an impure nazirite who vowed, but for a pure nazirite who becomes impure, even one day cancels all.

items.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'for his naziriteship became impure' that the impurity is effective because he was already impure when he took the vow.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse 'כי טמא נזרו' (for his naziriteship became impure) implies that the impurity is effective because he was already impure when he took the vow.

items.text: Abaye's challenge from the baraita on a 100-day nazirite
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from the baraita on a 100-day nazirite
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita that discusses a nazirite who vowed to be a nazirite for 100 days and became impure at the beginning, end, or one day before the end. The baraita concludes that only when there are both 'first days' and 'last days' does impurity cause the first days to fall. Abaye argues that this contradicts Rava's position, since the baraita implies that impurity at the start of the term does not cause the days to fall, even if the person was impure when he took the vow.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about a nazirite who vowed 100 days and became impure at the beginning, showing that impurity at the start does not cause the days to fall because there are no 'first days'.

The baraita continues: impurity at the end does not cause the days to fall because there are no 'last days', but impurity one day before the end does cause the days to fall because there are both first and last days.

Abaye concludes that the baraita refutes Rava's position, since it implies that a person who was impure when he took the vow does not have 'first days' and thus impurity does not cause the days to fall.

items.text: Clarification of the minimum days for 'the first days shall fall'
items.text_en: Clarification of the minimum days for 'the first days shall fall'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether the 'days' referred to in the baraita mean one day out and two beginning, or two days out and three beginning. Abaye did not know, so he asked Rava, who answered that the verse says 'shall fall' (יִפְּלוּ), implying at least two days. The Gemara then explains that both 'days' and 'shall fall' are necessary: 'days' excludes a single day, and 'shall fall' excludes the possibility of two days out and three beginning, requiring that two days have passed and three begin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether the 'days' in the baraita mean one day out and two beginning, or two days out and three beginning.
Abaye did not know, so he asked Rava, who answered that the verse says 'יִפְּלוּ' (shall fall), implying at least two days.

The Gemara explains that both 'יָמִים' (days) and 'יִפְּלוּ' (shall fall) are necessary: 'יָמִים' excludes a single day, and 'יִפְּלוּ' excludes the possibility of two days out and three beginning, requiring that two days have passed and three begin.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a nazirite returning from abroad
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a nazirite returning from abroad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if someone took many nazirite vows and completed them abroad, then came to the Land of Israel, Beit Shammai says he must be a nazirite for 30 days, while Beit Hillel says he must begin anew as a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the case of one who took many nazirite vows and completed them abroad.
Beit Shammai rules that upon entering the Land, the person must observe a 30-day nazirite period.
Beit Hillel rules that the person must begin a completely new nazirite term.

items.text: Story of Queen Helene as a precedent
items.text_en: Story of Queen Helene as a precedent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that Queen Helene vowed to be a nazirite for seven years if her son returned safely from war. She fulfilled the vow, then came to the Land of Israel, and Beit Hillel ruled that she must be a nazirite for another seven years. After those seven years, she became impure, resulting in a total of 21 years of naziriteship. Rabbi Yehuda disputes this, saying it was only 14 years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts the precedent of Queen Helene, who vowed to be a nazirite for seven years if her son returned safely, fulfilled it, came to the Land of Israel, and was ruled by Beit Hillel to be a nazirite for another seven years; after impurity, her total was 21 years, but Rabbi Yehuda disputes it was only 14.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, suggesting that they disagree about whether the impurity of the Land of the Nations (ארץ העמים) is decreed due to its clods of earth (גושה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a nazirite who completed many nezirut vows abroad and then came to the Land of Israel.
The Gemara proposes that the dispute is based on whether the impurity of the Land of the Nations (ארץ העמים) was decreed due to its clods of earth (גושה).

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both schools agree that the decree was due to the grave (gusha), not the air (aveira). Beit Shammai holds that the woman accepted naziriteship in a general sense, while Beit Hillel holds that she accepted it only at the beginning of her naziriteship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Hillel holds that the decree was due to the airspace (aveira) of the grave.
The Gemara answers that both schools agree the decree was due to the grave itself (gusha), not the airspace.
Beit Shammai holds that the woman accepted naziriteship in a general sense (bistam nezirut).
Beit Hillel holds that the woman accepted naziriteship only at the beginning of her term (bitchilat nezirut).

items.text: Question about the case of Queen Helena
items.text_en: Question about the case of Queen Helena
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: Did the case of Queen Helena involve her becoming impure, according to Beit Shammai, or did it involve her not becoming impure, according to Beit Hillel?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the story of Queen Helene: whether the case involved her becoming impure (according to Beit Shammai) or not becoming impure (according to Beit Hillel).

items.text: Resolution from the baraita
items.text_en: Resolution from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from the baraita: Queen Helena went up to the Land of Israel and Beit Hillel instructed her to be a nazirite for another seven years. If she had become impure according to Beit Shammai, Rabbi Yehuda should have said fourteen years and thirty days, not just fourteen years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: Queen Helene went up to the Land and Beit Hillel ruled she should be a nazirite for another seven years, and then challenges that if the case was about impurity according to Beit Shammai, Rabbi Yehuda should have said fourteen years and thirty days.
The Gemara objects that if the case involved impurity, Rabbi Yehuda should have required fourteen years and thirty days, not just fourteen years.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that the verse 'This is the law of the nazirite' teaches that if one becomes impure on the day of completion, he is given the full law of a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that the verse 'זאת תורת הנזיר' teaches that if a nazirite becomes impure on the day of completion, he must observe the full nazirite laws again.

items.text: Mishnah: Conflicting witness testimony
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conflicting witness testimony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where two sets of witnesses testify about a person's nazirite vow: one says he vowed for two terms, the other says five. Beit Shammai says the testimony is divided and there is no naziriteship; Beit Hillel says five includes two, so he is a nazirite for two terms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: two sets of witnesses testify about a person, one set says he vowed to be a nazirite for two terms, the other says five terms.
Beit Shammai rules that the testimony is divided and there is no naziriteship at all.
Beit Hillel rules that five includes two, so he becomes a nazirite for two terms.

items.text: Gemara: The Mishnah is not like this tanna
items.text_en: Gemara: The Mishnah is not like this tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not align with the view of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who says that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree in the case of two sets of witnesses, and only disagree when there is one set with conflicting testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah does not align with the following Tanna.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka teaches that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree in the case of two sets of witnesses that five includes two.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that the dispute is only about a single set of witnesses where one says two and the other says five.
Beit Shammai rules that their testimony is divided.
Beit Hillel rules that five includes two.

items.text: Rav's statement about a counter
items.text_en: Rav's statement about a counter
items.desc_en: Rav says that everyone agrees in the case of a counter. Rav Chama asks Rav Chisda what this means: if one says five and not two, and another says two and not five, they contradict each other. Rather, it means one says one and two, and the other says three, four, five.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that everyone agrees in the case of a 'counter' (moneh).

sub.text: Rav Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama asks Rav Chisda: What does Rav mean?
Rav Chama objects: If one says five and not two, and the other says two and not five, they contradict each other.
Rav Chama clarifies: Rather, one says one and two, and the other says three, four, five.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rav's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav's statement about a lenient case is needed, since he already stated a stricter case. The answer from the West is that there is no refutation in counting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav's lenient case is needed, given that he already stated a stricter case.
The answer from the West is that there is no refutation in counting, so both cases are necessary.

items.text: Mishnah: Nazirite vows and responses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazirite vows and responses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where one person says 'I am a nazirite' and others respond 'And I', making them all nazirites. It also discusses cases involving a husband and wife, and the husband's ability to annul his wife's vow.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who says 'I am a nazirite' and others respond 'And I', establishing that all become nazirites, with rules for release of the first and last.

The Mishnah presents cases involving a husband and wife, stating that a husband can annul his wife's nazirite vow but not his own, and that when the husband says 'Amen' to his wife's vow he cannot annul it.

items.text: Reish Lakish's teaching about the time frame
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's teaching about the time frame
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish teaches that the rule applies only if all responded within 'within the time of speech', which is defined as the time it takes to greet a teacher.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish, seated before Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah, states that the Mishnah's rule applies only if they all pledged (התפיסו) within a single span of speech (תוך כדי דיבור).
Reish Lakish defines 'תוך כדי דיבור' (within the span of speech) as the time required for a student to greet his teacher.

Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah objects that by defining the interval so narrowly, Reish Lakish leaves the student no 'space' (ריווח) — i.e., the greeting itself takes time, leaving no gap for the גמר of the greeting.

items.text: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah objects that Reish Lakish leaves no room for the student to respond to the greeting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah objects that Reish Lakish's definition of תוך כדי דיבור (within the interval of speech) leaves no room for the student to respond to the greeting.

items.text: Baraita supporting the rule of kdei dibur
items.text_en: Baraita supporting the rule of kdei dibur
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the earlier ruling: one who says 'I am a nazir' and his friend, after waiting the time for a greeting, says 'and I'—the first is forbidden, the second is permitted. The measure of kdei dibur is defined as the time for a student to greet his rabbi.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the earlier ruling: one who says 'I am a nazir' and his friend, after waiting the time for a greeting, says 'and I'—the first is forbidden, the second is permitted, and the measure of kdei dibur is defined as the time for a student to greet his rabbi.

items.text: Gemara's question about the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita only mentions 'and I' twice, implying no more than three people. It suggests that the tanna should have listed more like a peddler. The answer is that the baraita needs to teach the case of a middle person, so it mentions 'and I' twice.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks whether the baraita supports the position that only the first person is bound, since the baraita only lists two 'and I' statements and no more.

The gemara answers that the baraita mentions two 'and I' statements because the later clause about the first being released or the last being released implies there is a middle person, so the baraita must include at least three people.

items.text: The inquiry: does each attach to the previous or to the first?
items.text_en: The inquiry: does each attach to the previous or to the first?
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised: does each subsequent nazir attach to the one immediately before him, or do they all attach to the first? The practical difference is whether they can continue indefinitely or only within kdei dibur of the first.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an inquiry: does each subsequent person become bound by the previous one (חד בחבריה מיתפיס) or by the first person (בקמא מיתפסי), and what is the practical difference?

items.text: First attempt to prove: they attach to the first
items.text_en: First attempt to prove: they attach to the first
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the baraita that they attach to the first, because it only mentions 'and I' twice. If they attached to each other, it should have listed more. The answer is that the baraita needs to teach the case of a middle person, so it only mentions two.

sub.desc_en: The gemara attempts to prove that each person is bound by the first (בקמא מיתפסי) from the baraita that only lists two 'and I' statements, implying no further binding beyond kdei dibur.

The gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita only lists two 'and I' statements because the later clause about the first or last being released implies a middle person, so the baraita must include at least three people.

items.text: Second attempt: from the case of releasing the first
items.text_en: Second attempt: from the case of releasing the first
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the ruling that if the first is released, all are released—but not the middle. This suggests they attach to the first, because the middle is not released with the first.

sub.desc_en: The gemara attempts to prove that each person is bound by the first (בקמא מיתפסי) from the clause 'if the first is released, all are released'—implying that the middle person is not released when the first is released.

items.text: Rejection: they attach to each other, but the baraita focuses on the first
items.text_en: Rejection: they attach to each other, but the baraita focuses on the first
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: even if they attach to each other, the baraita mentions the first because it needs to teach that all are released when the first is released, which would not be true if it mentioned the middle.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the proof, arguing that even if each person is bound by the previous one (חד בחבריה מיתפיס), the baraita mentions the first because it needs to teach the case where all are released.

items.text: Third attempt: from the case of releasing the last
items.text_en: Third attempt: from the case of releasing the last
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the ruling that if the last is released, only the last is permitted, implying that a middle person with someone after him would be permitted. This suggests they attach to each other.

sub.desc_en: The gemara attempts to prove that each person is bound by the previous one (חד בחבריה מיתפיס) from the clause 'if the last is released, the last is released and all are forbidden'—implying that a middle person with someone after him would be released.

items.text: Rejection: 'last' might mean 'middle'
items.text_en: Rejection: 'last' might mean 'middle'
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects: perhaps 'last' in the baraita actually refers to the middle person, and the baraita uses 'last' because it already used 'first'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the proof, arguing that even if each person is bound by the first (בקמא מיתפסי), the term 'last' in the baraita actually refers to the middle person, and the baraita uses 'last' because it previously used 'first'.

items.text: Final proof from an explicit baraita
items.text_en: Final proof from an explicit baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that if the middle is released, those below him are permitted but those above are forbidden. This proves that each attaches to the previous one, because the middle's release only affects those after him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara brings a definitive baraita that explicitly states the case of a middle person being released, proving that each person is bound by the previous one (חד בחבריה מיתפיס), and concludes the inquiry.

items.text: New case: 'my mouth like his mouth'
items.text_en: New case: 'my mouth like his mouth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new case: one who says 'I am a nazir' and his friend says 'my mouth like his mouth and my hair like his hair'—is he a nazir?

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: if one says 'my mouth is like his mouth and my hair is like his hair' after hearing someone declare naziriteship, is he considered a nazir?

items.text: Opening contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Opening contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about hand/foot versus head/liver vows, and resolves it via Rav Yehuda's explanation that the speaker meant to make his mouth like the nazirite's mouth regarding wine and his hair like the nazirite's hair regarding shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: vows of 'my hand is nazirite' or 'my foot is nazirite' are void, but 'my head is nazirite' or 'my liver is nazirite' are valid, with the rule that only a life-dependent limb makes one a nazirite.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the speaker meant to make his mouth like the nazirite's mouth regarding wine and his hair like the nazirite's hair regarding shaving.

items.text: The dilemma: uproot or sever?
items.text_en: The dilemma: uproot or sever?
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dilemma: when a husband says 'I am also' to his wife's nazirite vow, does he uproot the vow entirely or sever it? The practical difference is a case where a second woman says 'I am also' and the first woman's husband annuls her vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dilemma: when a husband says 'I am also' to his wife's nazirite vow, does he uproot the vow entirely or sever it?
The Gemara explains the practical difference: if the husband uproots, both women are freed; if he severs, only his wife is freed and the friend remains bound.

items.text: First proof: husband cannot annul
items.text_en: First proof: husband cannot annul
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita that a husband who says 'I am also' cannot annul, implying he uproots the vow entirely. The argument is that if he only severs, he should be able to annul his wife's part and remain bound himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita that a husband who says 'I am also' cannot annul, implying he uproots the vow entirely, because if he only severs, he should be able to annul his wife's part and remain bound himself.

items.text: Rejection: 'I am also' as ratification
items.text_en: Rejection: 'I am also' as ratification
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the husband cannot annul because saying 'I am also' is like saying 'I ratify your vow,' and he can only annul if he first retracts his ratification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the husband cannot annul because saying 'I am also' is like saying 'I ratify your vow,' and he can only annul if he first retracts his ratification.

items.text: Second proof: animal consecrated after annulment
items.text_en: Second proof: animal consecrated after annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a woman who set aside an animal for her nazirite offering and then her husband annulled: if the animal was his, it goes out to graze; if hers, the sin-offering dies. The Gemara argues that if the husband uproots, the animal should be unconsecrated, so this proves he severs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman who set aside an animal for her nazirite offering and then her husband annulled: if the animal was his, it goes out to graze; if hers, the sin-offering dies.
The Gemara argues that if the husband uproots (עיקר), the animal should be unconsecrated, so this proves he severs (גייז).

items.text: Rejection: sin-offering dies due to owner's death
items.text_en: Rejection: sin-offering dies due to owner's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that even if the husband uproots, the sin-offering must die because the woman no longer needs atonement, analogous to a sin-offering whose owners died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that even if the husband uproots, the sin-offering must die because the woman no longer needs atonement, analogous to a sin-offering whose owners died.

items.text: Third proof: woman who violates after annulment
items.text_en: Third proof: woman who violates after annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that a woman who drank wine and became impure after her husband annulled her vow receives lashes. If the husband uproots, she should not be liable, so this proves he severs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a woman who drank wine and became impure after her husband annulled her vow receives lashes, implying the husband severs the vow.
The Gemara clarifies the case: if the husband did not annul, the baraita is obvious, so it must be after annulment.
The Gemara argues: if the husband uproots the vow, why would she be liable? This proves he severs the vow.

items.text: Rejection: the case is where she did not know
items.text_en: Rejection: the case is where she did not know
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita's case is where the husband annulled but she did not know, so she is liable for violating a vow she thought was still in effect; the proof is from the continuation where she is exempt if she knew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita's case is where the husband annulled but she did not know, so she is liable for violating a vow she thought was still in effect; the proof is from the continuation where she is exempt if she knew.

items.text: Gemara's initial statement
items.text_en: Gemara's initial statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna also taught the first clause (about a sotah who drinks the bitter water) in the same baraita, implying a consistent principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna also taught the first clause (about a sotah who drinks the bitter water) in the same baraita, implying a consistent principle.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: a woman who vowed to be a nazirite, became impure, and then her husband annulled the vow, brings only a bird sin-offering but not a bird burnt-offering. If annulment cuts off the vow (מִיגָּז גָּיֵיז), she should bring the burnt-offering as well, since the impurity occurred while the vow was still in effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that a husband's annulment cuts off the vow retroactively (מִיגָּז גָּיֵיז) by citing a baraita where a woman who became impure and then had her vow annulled brings only a bird sin-offering, not a bird burnt-offering, implying the vow was not retroactively severed.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if annulment uproots the vow entirely (מִיעְקָר עָקַר), she should not bring even the sin-offering. It answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who holds that a nazirite is considered a sinner, so she brings a sin-offering for having taken the vow in the first place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the husband's annulment uproots the vow entirely (מִיעְקָר עָקַר), she should not bring even the sin-offering.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who holds that a nazirite is considered a sinner, so she brings a sin-offering for having taken the vow in the first place.

items.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
items.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says that a nazirite is called a sinner because he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine, and by a fortiori reasoning, one who afflicts himself from all things is even more sinful.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who interprets the verse 'מאשר חטא על הנפש' (from that which he sinned regarding the soul) to teach that a nazirite is called a sinner for afflicting himself from wine, and by קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning), one who afflicts himself from all things is even more sinful.

items.text: Gemara's second challenge from an explicit baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's second challenge from an explicit baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: a woman who vowed to be a nazirite, her friend heard and said 'and I', and the first woman's husband annulled her vow — the first woman is permitted (the vow is annulled) but the friend remains forbidden. This proves that annulment cuts off the vow (מִיגָּז גָּיֵיז), because if it uprooted the vow entirely, the friend's vow would also be uprooted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings an explicit baraita: a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and a friend said 'and I', the first woman's husband annulled her vow — the first is permitted but the friend remains forbidden, proving that annulment cuts off (מִיגָּז גָּיֵיז) rather than uproots.
Rabbi Shimon qualifies: if the friend said 'the same as you', both are permitted, offering an alternative view on the mechanism.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon says: if the friend said 'I am like you', then both are permitted, because the friend's vow was conditional on the first woman's vow remaining in effect.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that if the friend said 'I am like you', both women are permitted, because the friend's vow was conditional on the first woman's vow remaining in effect.

items.text: Mar Zutra's identification with Rami bar Hama's question
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's identification with Rami bar Hama's question
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra identifies the case of a woman who says 'I am a nazirite after you' with Rami bar Hama's question about one who says 'I take upon myself like the flesh of a peace-offering': is the person attaching to the essence of the offering or to its residual coolness?

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra identifies the case of a woman who says 'I am a nazirite after you' with Rami bar Hama's question.
Rami bar Hama asks about one who says 'I take upon myself like the flesh of a peace-offering' — is the person attaching to the essence of the offering or to its residual coolness?
The gemara elaborates the two possibilities: does one attach to the essence (עיקרא) or to the residual coolness (צנינא)?

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the cases are not comparable: in the peace-offering case, the meat is consecrated even after the blood is sprinkled, but here if the husband annulled the wife's vow, the conditional vow would be meaningless. Some say this is indeed Rami bar Hama's question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the cases are not comparable: in the peace-offering case, the meat remains consecrated even after the blood is sprinkled, but here if the husband annulled the wife's vow, the conditional vow would be meaningless.
Some say that this objection is indeed Rami bar Hama's question.

items.text: Question about 'I am a nazirite after you'
items.text_en: Question about 'I am a nazirite after you'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: if a woman says 'I am a nazirite after you', does she mean she is entirely following the other's lead (and thus permitted if the other's vow is annulled), or does she mean she is taking the vow from before the husband annulled it (and thus prohibited)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman who says 'I am a nazirite after you' means she is entirely following the other's lead (and thus permitted if the other's vow is annulled) or means she is taking the vow from before the husband annulled it (and thus prohibited).

items.text: Proof from a baraita about 'And I'
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about 'And I'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a woman vowed to be a nazirite and her husband said 'And I', he cannot annul. If he were attaching to the inception, he could annul her vow and keep his. This proves he attaches to the entire matter, so she is permitted if she says 'after you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a woman vowed to be a nazirite and her husband said 'And I', he cannot annul; if he were attaching to the inception, he could annul her vow and keep his.
The Gemara concludes that the husband attaches to the entire matter, so a woman who says 'after you' is permitted.

items.text: Rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: actually, he attaches to the inception, but saying 'And I' is like saying 'I confirm you', so if he later regrets his confirmation he can annul, otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: actually, the husband attaches to the inception, but saying 'וַאֲנִי' (and I) is like saying 'קַיָּים לִיכִי' (I confirm you), so if he later regrets his confirmation he can annul, otherwise not.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised between two baraitot regarding a man who says 'I am a nazirite and you' and the woman says 'Amen': one says he annuls hers and his stands, another says both are forbidden. Rav Yehuda and Abaye resolve that the latter baraita refers to a case where he ties his vow to hers.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that when a man says 'I am a nazirite and you' and the woman says 'Amen', he annuls her vow and his stands.
The gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says both are forbidden, because he tied his vow to hers.
Rav Yehuda resolves by teaching that the first baraita is authoritative: he annuls hers and his stands.
Abaye says even the second baraita is valid, but it refers to a case where he explicitly tied his vow to hers by saying 'I am a nazirite and you'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and its explanation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and its explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is where a husband annulled his wife's nazirite vow but she did not know, and she continues to drink wine and defile herself to the dead. The Mishnah states she does not receive lashes, but Rabbi Yehuda says she should receive lashes for rebellion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is where a husband said to his wife 'I am a nazirite, and what about you?' — therefore he annuls her vow while his own remains.

The Mishnah states that a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and then drank wine and defiled herself to the dead receives lashes; but if her husband annulled her vow without her knowledge, she does not receive lashes; Rabbi Yehuda says she should receive lashes for rebellion (מכת מרדות).

items.text: Baraita on atonement for an annulled vow
items.text_en: Baraita on atonement for an annulled vow
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that the verse 'Her husband has annulled them, and the Lord will forgive her' speaks of a woman whose husband annulled her vow without her knowledge, showing she needs atonement and forgiveness.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the verse 'Her husband has annulled them, and the Lord will forgive her' refers to a woman whose husband annulled her vow without her knowledge, showing she needs atonement and forgiveness.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on intention and atonement
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on intention and atonement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva wept upon reaching this verse, reasoning that if one who intended to eat pork but ate lamb needs atonement, then one who intended to eat pork and ate pork certainly needs atonement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva weeps upon reaching the verse, reasoning that if one who intended to eat pork but ate lamb needs atonement, then one who intended to eat pork and ate pork certainly needs atonement.

items.text: Further homilies on intention and atonement
items.text_en: Further homilies on intention and atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two similar teachings: one from an anonymous source and one from Isi ben Yehuda, both interpreting the verse 'and he did not know and incurred guilt' to show that one who intended to eat lamb but ate pork needs atonement, all the more so one who intended to eat pork and ate pork.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous teaching introduces a second verse (Leviticus 5:17) to draw a parallel about intention and atonement.
The anonymous teaching argues: if one who intended to eat lamb but ate pork (a case of uncertainty) requires atonement, then one who intended to eat pork and ate pork certainly requires atonement.

Isi ben Yehuda offers a different scenario: two pieces, one forbidden fat and one permitted fat; if one intended to eat lamb but ate pork, the verse says he bears iniquity, and all the more so one who intended to eat pork and ate pork.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: why all three teachings are needed
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: why all three teachings are needed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why all three teachings (the woman, the uncertain piece, and the two pieces) are necessary. Each case teaches a different aspect: the woman had intent for prohibition, the uncertain piece had intent for permission, and the two pieces had a fixed prohibition. Without all three, one might mistakenly think atonement is not needed in some cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara exclaims that those who suffer should suffer, emphasizing the severity of needing atonement.
The Gemara asks why all three teachings are necessary, and answers that without the woman's case one might think the uncertain piece does not require atonement.
The Gemara explains that if only the uncertain piece case were taught, one might think the woman does not require atonement since she was permitted.

The Gemara concludes that without the case of two pieces (one forbidden, one permitted), one might think atonement does not suffice when a prohibition is established; Isi ben Yehuda teaches that it is no different.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's mashal about the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's mashal about the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'For the ways of the Lord are straight; the righteous walk in them, but the wicked stumble in them' with a parable of two people roasting their Paschal lambs—one for the mitzvah, one for gluttony. The one who ate for the mitzvah is righteous, the other is wicked.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan introduces a mashal (parable) of two people roasting their Paschal lambs—one for the mitzvah, one for gluttony—to explain the verse about the righteous walking and the wicked stumbling.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objection and alternative mashal
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection and alternative mashal
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects to calling the glutton a wicked person, since he performed the mitzvah of eating the Paschal lamb. He offers a different mashal: two people with their wife and sister, one encounters his wife (permitted) and the other his sister (forbidden). The Gemara then objects that this involves two different paths, not one, and offers a mashal of Lot and his daughters.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects to calling the glutton a wicked person, since he performed the mitzvah of eating the Paschal lamb.
Reish Lakish offers a different mashal: two people with their wife and sister, one encounters his wife (permitted) and the other his sister (forbidden).
The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish's mashal involves two different paths, not one.
The Gemara offers a mashal of Lot and his daughters: they intended for a mitzvah, he intended for a transgression, yet all followed the same path.

items.text: Discussion of Lot's intentions and actions
items.text_en: Discussion of Lot's intentions and actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Lot also intended for a mitzvah, and Rabbi Yochanan says the entire verse about Lot was said in the context of sin. The Gemara then analyzes Lot's actions, noting that he was coerced, but a teaching from Rabbi Yosei bar Rav Choni shows that Lot knew what happened when his older daughter arose. The Gemara concludes that he should not have drunk wine afterwards.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Lot also intended his actions for the sake of a mitzvah.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the entire verse about Lot was stated in the context of sin, implying Lot intended to sin.
Rabbi Yochanan supports his claim by interpreting each phrase in the verse about Lot as allusions to licentiousness, citing parallels from other biblical verses.
The Gemara objects that Lot was forced into the act, as he was asleep.

sub.text: Teaching in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rav Choni
sub.text_en: Teaching in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rav Choni
sub.desc_en: A teaching in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rav Choni explains that a dot on the word 'וּבְקוּמָהּ' indicates that Lot knew what happened when his older daughter arose, showing he was not entirely coerced.
The Gemara asks what Lot could have done about the past event.
The Gemara answers that although the past cannot be changed, Lot should not have drunk wine on the following night, showing his desire for the outcome.

items.text: Rava's homily on a verse
items.text_en: Rava's homily on a verse
items.desc_en: Rava begins a homily on the verse 'A brother who offends is stronger than a city of strength', but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a homily on the verse 'A brother who offends is stronger than a city of strength', but the text cuts off.

items.text: Lot's sin and its public exposure
items.text_en: Lot's sin and its public exposure
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets verses about Lot, showing that his separation from Abraham led to conflict, and his shame was publicized in synagogues and study halls through the prohibition of Ammonites and Moabites.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about Lot as one who separated from Abraham and caused strife like bars and a fortress, leading to the prohibition of Ammonites and Moabites.
Rava (or Rabbi Yitzchak) teaches that Lot's shame was publicized in synagogues and study halls, as the Mishnah states that Ammonites and Moabites are permanently forbidden.

items.text: Tamar and Zimri: contrasting outcomes of sin
items.text_en: Tamar and Zimri: contrasting outcomes of sin
items.desc_en: Ulla contrasts Tamar's sin, which produced kings and prophets, with Zimri's sin, which caused tens of thousands of Israelites to fall.

sub.desc_en: Ulla opens by juxtaposing Tamar's act of זנות (illicit sexual relations) with Zimri's act of זנות.
Ulla resolves the contrast: Tamar's sin produced kings and prophets, while Zimri's sin caused tens of thousands of Israelites to fall.

items.text: Sin for its own sake vs. mitzvah not for its own sake
items.text_en: Sin for its own sake vs. mitzvah not for its own sake
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak initially claims that a sin done for a good purpose is greater than a mitzvah not done for its own sake, but the Gemara objects with Rav's principle that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as it leads to doing them for their own sake. The Gemara then amends the statement to say that such a sin is like a mitzvah not for its own sake, citing Yael's blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that a sin done for its own sake (לשמה) is greater than a mitzvah not done for its own sake (שלא לשמה).

The Gemara objects by citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav: a person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, because from not for their own sake they come to do them for their own sake.
The Gemara amends the statement: a sin for its own sake is like (not greater than) a mitzvah not for its own sake, citing Yael's blessing as proof.

items.text: Yael's encounter with Sisera and the nature of the wicked's good
items.text_en: Yael's encounter with Sisera and the nature of the wicked's good
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes Sisera's seven illicit acts with Yael, and questions whether Yael benefited from the act. He answers that all good of the wicked is actually evil for the righteous, proving this from the verse about Laban's offer to Jacob.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Sisera performed seven illicit acts with Yael, citing the verse that describes his repeated falling between her legs.
The Gemara questions whether Yael derived benefit from the illicit act, which would be problematic for a righteous woman.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that all good of the wicked is actually evil for the righteous, proving this from the verse where Laban was forbidden from speaking even good to Jacob.

items.text: Balak's reward and Ruth's lineage
items.text_en: Balak's reward and Ruth's lineage
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as it leads to doing them for their own sake, citing Balak's forty-two sacrifices which merited Ruth. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that Ruth was the granddaughter of Eglon king of Moab.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as it leads to doing them for their own sake, citing Balak's forty-two sacrifices which merited Ruth.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that Ruth was the granddaughter of Eglon king of Moab, linking Balak's merit to Ruth's lineage.

items.text: Reward for a proper speech: Moab vs. Ammon
items.text_en: Reward for a proper speech: Moab vs. Ammon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan shows that God rewards even a proper speech: because the elder daughter named her son Moab, Israel was commanded not to war with Moab but could harass them, while the younger daughter named her son Ben-Ammi, and Israel was commanded not to harass them at all.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan demonstrates that God does not withhold reward even for a proper speech, citing that because the elder daughter named her son Moab, Israel was commanded not to war with Moab but could harass them.
The gemara contrasts the younger daughter who named her son Ben-Ammi, for whom Israel was commanded not to harass them at all, completing the proof of reward for proper speech.

items.text: The reward for precedence in mitzvot
items.text_en: The reward for precedence in mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that one should always hasten to perform a mitzvah, as the elder daughter's one night of precedence over the younger daughter earned her the privilege of having kings and prophets descend from her line.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that one should always hasten to perform a mitzvah, because the elder daughter's one night of precedence over the younger daughter earned her the privilege of having kings and prophets descend from her line.

items.text: Opening statement
items.text_en: Opening statement
items.desc_en: A brief statement about four generations preceding the monarchy in Israel, serving as a lead-in to the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a statement that four generations preceded the monarchy in Israel.

items.text: Mishnah: Nazirite woman whose husband annulled her vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nazirite woman whose husband annulled her vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and set aside animals for her offerings, but her husband later annulled her vow. It distinguishes between animals that belonged to the husband (which go out to graze) and those that belonged to the wife (with specific rules for each type of offering). It also addresses the status of unspecified and designated funds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and set aside animals, and her husband later annulled her vow; if the animal belonged to the husband, it goes out to graze.

The Mishnah rules that if the animal belonged to the wife, the חטאת (sin-offering) dies, the עולה (burnt-offering) is offered, and the שלמים (peace-offerings) are offered and eaten for one day without bread.
The Mishnah rules that unspecified funds go to a free-will offering, while designated funds for a חטאת (sin-offering) are cast into the Dead Sea, with no benefit or misuse liability.

The Mishnah concludes that funds designated for a עולה (burnt-offering) are used for a burnt-offering with misuse liability, and funds for שלמים (peace-offerings) are used for peace-offerings eaten for one day without bread.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Who is the Tanna?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Who is the Tanna?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that a husband is not financially liable for his wife's vow offerings. Rav Chisda answers that it is the Rabbis (Rabbanan), not Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that a husband is liable for his wife's offerings, as stated in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that a husband is not financially liable for his wife's vow offerings.
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis (Rabbanan), not Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Chisda argues that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Yehuda, the animal would not go out to pasture because the husband is liable.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a husband brings a rich man's offering for his wife, because he wrote in her marriage contract that he assumes all her prior obligations.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah could be consistent because Rabbi Yehuda's liability only applies to matters necessary for the wife, not to matters unnecessary for her (like the nazirite vow after annulment).

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah's ruling that the animal goes out to graze is consistent, because Rabbi Yehuda's lien only applies to matters necessary for the wife, not to matters unnecessary for her like the nazirite vow after annulment.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the discussion states that Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda, who only holds the husband liable for necessary matters. The Gemara clarifies that the husband's liability applies only when he explicitly undertook responsibility for her offerings.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version opens by asking which Tanna is the subject, and Rav Chisda answers that it is Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yehuda only holds the husband liable for necessary matters, not for unnecessary ones.
The Gemara supports this by noting that the Rabbis do not hold the husband liable at all.
The Gemara clarifies that the husband's liability applies only when he explicitly undertook responsibility for her offerings, making the animal his own.

items.text: Rava's principle and the case of a married woman's animal
items.text_en: Rava's principle and the case of a married woman's animal
items.desc_en: Rava explains that even according to the Rabbis, a husband only acquires property for his wife's needs, not for things she doesn't need. The Gemara then asks how a woman could have her own animal for a sin-offering if her husband acquires all she owns, and Rav Papa answers that she set aside dough from her own dough, or alternatively, someone else gave it to her on condition that her husband has no rights to it.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that even according to the Rabbis, a husband acquires property for his wife only in matters she needs, not in matters she does not need.
The Gemara asks how a woman could have her own animal for a sin-offering if her husband acquires all she owns.
Rav Papa answers that she set aside dough from her own dough (which her husband does not acquire).
Alternatively, someone else gave it to her on condition that her husband has no rights to it.

items.text: Shmuel's request: the four rams that do not require bread
items.text_en: Shmuel's request: the four rams that do not require bread
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks his father to explain the four types of rams that do not require bread offerings: his (the husband's), hers (the wife's), after death, and after atonement.

sub.text: Shmuel's request to Avuh bar Ihi
sub.text_en: Shmuel's request to Avuh bar Ihi
sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks his father Avuh bar Ihi to explain the four types of rams that do not require bread offerings: his, hers, after death, and after atonement.

items.text: Explanation of 'his' and 'hers'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'his' and 'hers'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'hers' as previously discussed, and 'his' from a mishnah about a father vowing his son as a nazirite. It then cites a baraita about the disposition of unspecified and specified funds for a nazirite's offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies 'hers' as the case already discussed, and 'his' from the mishnah where a father vows his son as a nazirite.
The baraita details the disposition of unspecified and specified funds for a nazirite's offerings, concluding that these four types of rams do not require bread.

items.text: Source for 'after death'
items.text_en: Source for 'after death'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the case of 'after death' from a baraita: if a nazirite dies, unspecified funds go to the donation fund, while specified funds for sin-offering go to the Dead Sea, for burnt-offering are brought as a burnt-offering, and for peace-offerings are brought as peace-offerings without bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the case of 'after death' (that the animal does not require bread)?

The Gemara cites a baraita: one who sets aside money for his naziriteship — the money is not subject to benefit nor to misuse, because it is fit to bring peace-offerings from all of it; if he dies, unspecified funds go to the donation fund, while specified funds for sin-offering go to the Dead Sea, for burnt-offering are brought as a burnt-offering, and for peace-offerings are brought as peace-offerings without bread.

items.text: Reasoning for 'after atonement'
items.text_en: Reasoning for 'after atonement'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'after atonement' is logical: just as after death the animal cannot atone, so too after atonement it cannot atone again.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case of 'after atonement' is logical: just as after death the animal cannot atone, so too after atonement it cannot atone again.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: other cases without bread
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: other cases without bread
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that there are other cases, such as peace-offerings of a nazirite slaughtered not in the proper manner, which are valid but do not require bread. It resolves that the list only counts cases where the offerings were brought in the proper manner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that there is another case — all other peace-offerings of a nazirite slaughtered not in the proper manner — which are valid but do not require bread.
The Gemara resolves that the list only counts cases where the offerings were brought in the proper manner (כמצותן), excluding those not in the proper manner (שלא כמצותן).

items.text: Continuation of the baraita on unspecified funds
items.text_en: Continuation of the baraita on unspecified funds
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the beginning of a baraita about unspecified funds falling to the donation fund.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that unspecified funds from a nazirite's set-aside money fall to the donation fund (נדבה).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that the rule allowing leftover funds to be used for a freewill offering is a halakhic tradition specific to nazirites, while Resh Lakish derives it from the verse 'for all their vows and all their freewill offerings'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But aren't the funds for the sin-offering mixed in with the leftover funds?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is a halakhic tradition specific to nazirites.
Resh Lakish derives the rule from the verse 'for all their vows and all their freewill offerings', saying the Torah stated that leftover vow funds go to a freewill offering.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan, the rule applies only to unspecified funds, but according to Resh Lakish's verse, it should apply even to specified funds, which contradicts the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish: according to Rabbi Yochanan the distinction between unspecified and specified funds is justified by a halachic tradition, but according to Resh Lakish's verse, the rule should apply even to specified funds, contradicting the mishnah.

items.text: Rava's answer citing the baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school
items.text_en: Rava's answer citing the baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school
items.desc_en: Rava answers that specified funds cannot be used for a freewill offering because a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the verse 'Only your holy things which are yours and your vows' refers to offspring of sacrifices and their substitutes, which are not offered but must be brought to the Temple.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that specified funds cannot be used for a freewill offering, citing a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that the verse 'רַק קָדָשֶׁיךָ אֲשֶׁר יִהְיוּ לְךָ וּנְדָרֶיךָ' (Only your holy things which are yours and your vows) speaks of offspring of sacrifices and their substitutes.

items.text: Baraita detailing the law of offspring and substitutes
items.text_en: Baraita detailing the law of offspring and substitutes
items.desc_en: The baraita explains that the verse teaches that offspring of sacrifices and their substitutes must be brought to the Temple and treated like the original offerings, but not starved to death. Rabbi Yishmael adds that the word 'only' excludes offspring of a sin-offering and substitute of a guilt-offering.

sub.text: Baraita (Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Baraita (Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: The baraita asks what the remedy is for offspring and substitutes, citing the verse that they must be brought to the chosen place, and then clarifies that one may not starve them to death, as the verse says 'you shall make your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood.'

sub.text: Baraita (Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Baraita (Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that one must treat the substitute of a burnt offering like the burnt offering itself, and the offspring of peace offerings like the peace offerings.
Rabbi Yishmael adds that the word 'רַק' (only) excludes the offspring of a sin-offering and the substitute of a guilt-offering from this rule.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that no verse is needed for the exclusion of a guilt-offering substitute, because the verse 'it is a guilt-offering' teaches that it remains in its original status.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that no verse is needed to exclude a guilt-offering substitute, because the verse 'אָשָׁם הוּא' (it is a guilt-offering) teaches that it remains in its original status.

items.text: Gemara's question on the baraita's necessity
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the baraita's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs a verse to teach that one may not starve the offspring of a sin-offering, since it is already known that such offspring must die.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs a verse to teach that one may not starve the offspring of a sin-offering, since it is already known that such offspring must die.

items.text: Opening statement on offspring of consecrated animals
items.text_en: Opening statement on offspring of consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah teaches that offspring of consecrated animals are not offered in the Temple, contrary to what might be assumed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah teaches that offspring of consecrated animals are not offered in the Temple.

items.text: Tanna Kamma's use of the verse 'רק'
items.text_en: Tanna Kamma's use of the verse 'רק'
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma argues that a verse is needed to teach that one who offers a displaced guilt-offering violates a positive commandment, even though the halakha already mandates that such an animal grazes.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma cites a baraita that one might think the displaced offspring of a sin-offering and the substitute of a guilt-offering are also brought, but the verse 'רַק' (only) excludes them.
The Gemara asks why a verse is needed, since the halakhic tradition (הילכתא) already teaches that the offspring of a sin-offering goes to death.
The Gemara answers that the verse comes for the guilt-offering, but the tradition also teaches that anything which would die as a sin-offering grazes as a guilt-offering.

The Gemara resolves that without the verse, one might think the tradition only mandates grazing but imposes no liability for offering it; the verse teaches that one who offers it violates a positive commandment (עשה).

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that no verse is needed because the halakha is already known: anything that would die as a sin-offering grazes as a guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects that no verse is needed because the halakha is already known: anything that would die as a sin-offering grazes as a guilt-offering.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: the verse supports Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: the verse supports Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse comes to support Rav Huna's ruling that a guilt-offering designated for grazing, if slaughtered as a burnt-offering, is valid only if it was first 'detached' from its original status, as the verse 'הוּא' implies it must remain in its original state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse comes to support Rav Huna's ruling about a guilt-offering detached for grazing.
Rav Huna citing Rav rules that a guilt-offering detached for grazing, if slaughtered as a burnt-offering, is valid.
The Gemara infers that only if the offering was detached is it valid; otherwise it is not.
The Gemara cites the verse 'הוּא' (it is) to support that the offering must remain in its original status.

items.text: Transition to other obligated individuals
items.text_en: Transition to other obligated individuals
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's rule applies to a nazirite, and then asks whether there are other cases, citing a baraita about those obligated to bring bird-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's rule is a halacha (binding tradition) specific to a nazirite.
The Gemara asks whether there are no other obligated individuals beyond the nazirite.
The Gemara cites a baraita that lists other individuals obligated to bring bird-offerings (קינין), implying the rule extends beyond the nazirite.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Money for bird offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Money for bird offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a nazirite or one obligated in bird offerings set aside money for their offerings, they may use it to purchase a sin-offering or burnt-offering animal. If they died and the money was unspecified, it goes to the Temple treasury as a freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a nazirite or one obligated in bird offerings may use designated money for animal sin-offerings or burnt-offerings, and if they die with unspecified money, it goes to the Temple treasury as a freewill offering.

items.text: Gemara's distinction: Nazirite vs. other obligated persons
items.text_en: Gemara's distinction: Nazirite vs. other obligated persons
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah specifically refers to a nazirite and those obligated in bird offerings, excluding a case where someone is obligated in a sin-offering and designates money for a burnt-offering. In that case, the money cannot be used for either sacrifice and, if unspecified upon death, must be thrown into the Dead Sea.

sub.desc_en: The baraita distinguishes the nazirite and bird-offering obligants from a person who vowed a burnt-offering while liable for a sin-offering, whose unspecified money goes to the Dead Sea.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah excludes the case of a person obligated in a sin-offering who designates money for a burnt-offering, where the money cannot be used for either sacrifice and, if unspecified upon death, must be thrown into the Dead Sea.

items.text: Rav Ashi's first version: Designation by specifying each offering
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's first version: Designation by specifying each offering
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's ruling on designated money applies even if one said 'these are for my sin-offering, burnt-offering, and peace-offering' in a single statement, not necessarily separately.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that even saying 'these for my sin-offering, burnt-offering, and peace-offering' counts as specified money, not just explicit separate designations.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Ashi's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Ashi's statement
items.desc_en: Another version states that Rav Ashi said even if one merely said 'these are for my obligation,' the money is considered designated, not just when specifying each offering.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Ashi's statement: even saying 'these are for my obligation' renders the money as specified.

items.text: Rava's ruling: Unspecified money with a sin-offering component
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: Unspecified money with a sin-offering component
items.desc_en: Rava states that if unspecified money includes the value of a sin-offering, it is considered designated and does not go to the freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: Rava clarifies that if sin-offering money falls among unspecified funds, those coins are treated as specified.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The baraita presents two cases: one where a nazirite designates money for a chatat and the remainder for other nazirite offerings, and another where money is designated for an olah. In the first case, the chatat money goes to the Dead Sea, and the remainder is split between olah and shelamim; in the second, the olah money is used for an olah, and the remainder falls to a freewill offering. In both cases, me'ilah applies to all the money but not to part of it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the first case: money designated for a sin-offering and the rest for other nazirite obligations; the sin-offering money goes to the Dead Sea, the remainder is split between a burnt-offering and a peace-offering, with me'ilah applying to all but not to part.

The baraita presents the second case: money designated for a burnt-offering and the rest for other nazirite obligations; the burnt-offering money is used for a burnt-offering, the remainder falls to a freewill offering, with me'ilah applying to all but not to part.

items.text: Rav Huna's qualification: only money, not animals
items.text_en: Rav Huna's qualification: only money, not animals
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says in the name of Rav that the baraita's rule applies only to money, but if an animal was designated, it is considered as if it were explicitly designated for a specific offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav that the baraita's rule about unallocated funds applies only to money, but a designated animal is considered explicitly allocated.
