items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the principles of prat u'klal (which includes everything) and mi'ut v'ribuy (which includes everything except what is excluded), noting that the practical difference is that prat u'klal includes even leaves and branches, while mi'ut v'ribuy includes branches but not leaves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the hermeneutical principles of prat u'klal and mi'ut v'ribuy, since both seem to include everything.
The Gemara answers that under prat u'klal even leaves and branches are included, whereas under mi'ut v'ribuy branches are included but leaves are excluded.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle: permitted substance combines with forbidden in nazirite prohibitions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle: permitted substance combines with forbidden in nazirite prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that for all Torah prohibitions, a permitted substance does not combine with a forbidden one to form a prohibited mixture, except for nazirite prohibitions, as the Torah says 'mishrat' (soaking).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu transmits Rabbi Yochanan's principle that for all Torah prohibitions, a permitted substance does not combine with a forbidden one to form a prohibited mixture, except for nazirite prohibitions, as the Torah says 'מִשְׁרַת' (soaking).

items.text: Ze'eiri's statement and its implication
items.text_en: Ze'eiri's statement and its implication
items.desc_en: Ze'eiri states that the prohibition of burning leaven on the altar applies even to a small amount, following Rabbi Elazar's interpretation of the word 'all'. The Gemara clarifies that this also applies to hametz, and that it comes to reject Abaye's view that there is burning of less than an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: Ze'eiri states that the prohibition of burning leaven (שאור) on the altar applies even to a small amount, and the Gemara identifies this as following Rabbi Elazar's interpretation of the word 'all'.
The Gemara asks whether this principle also applies to hametz (חמץ) on Passover.
The Gemara affirms that yes, the same applies to hametz.
The Gemara clarifies that Ze'eiri's statement comes to reject Abaye's view that there is burning (הקטרה) of less than an olive's bulk, teaching that there is no burning of less than an olive's bulk.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita about terumah and hullin
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita about terumah and hullin
items.desc_en: Abaye raises an objection from a baraita about a mixture of terumah and hullin, where a tevul yom invalidates only the place of contact. The Gemara questions why the place of contact is invalid, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that it is because a non-priest is liable for eating an olive's bulk of it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi sits and presents this halachic tradition.
Abaye raises an objection from a baraita about a mixture of תרומה (priestly portion) and חולין (non-sacred food), where a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) invalidates only the place of contact.
The Gemara asks why the place of contact is invalidated.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the reason is because a non-priest (זר) is liable for eating an olive's bulk (כזית) of it.
The Gemara asks what is the reason for Rabbi Yochanan's explanation.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the issue is that 'heter mitztaref le'issur' (permitted food combines with forbidden food). The interlocutor answers that the real issue is whether there is a kezayit within the time of achilat pras.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the issue is that היתר מצטרף לאיסור (permitted food combines with forbidden food).
The interlocutor answers that the real issue is whether there is a כזית (olive's bulk) within the time of אכילת פרס (the time it takes to eat half a loaf).

items.text: Challenge: Is achilat pras biblical?
items.text_en: Challenge: Is achilat pras biblical?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether achilat pras is a biblical concept. The interlocutor affirms it is. The Gemara then asks why the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Elazar regarding Babylonian kutach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether the concept of אכילת פרס (eating an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf) is a biblical (דאורייתא) prohibition.
The interlocutor affirms that אכילת פרס is indeed biblical.
The Gemara objects: if אכילת פרס is biblical, why do the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Elazar regarding Babylonian kutach (כותח הבבלי)?

items.text: Resolution regarding Babylonian kutach
items.text_en: Resolution regarding Babylonian kutach
items.desc_en: The interlocutor explains that Babylonian kutach lacks a kezayit within achilat pras. If one eats it as a solid, his intention is disregarded; if he eats it as a sauce, there is no kezayit within achilat pras.

sub.desc_en: The interlocutor resolves the objection by explaining that Babylonian kutach (כותח הבבלי) either has no kezayit within achilat pras (כזית בכדי אכילת פרס) when eaten as a solid, or if eaten as a sauce, no kezayit is found within achilat pras.

items.text: First baraita challenge: Two mortars and pots
items.text_en: First baraita challenge: Two mortars and pots
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about two mortars and two pots of terumah and hullin that fell into each other, and we assume they fell into their own kind. The Gemara argues that if kezayit bikdei achilat pras is biblical, why rely on such an assumption? The Gemara then suggests that perhaps the issue is 'heter mitztaref le'issur', but that too is challenged. The Gemara resolves that the terumah of untithed produce is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about two mortars and two pots of terumah and hullin that fell into each other, and we assume they fell into their own kind, permitting both.
The Gemara questions: if the measure of a kezayit within the time of אכילת פרס (the time to eat half a loaf) is biblical, why rely on the assumption that they fell into their own kind?
The Gemara objects: even if the issue is היתר מצטרף לאיסור (permitted food joining with forbidden food to form the measure), why rely on the assumption?
The Gemara resolves: set aside this baraita, for the terumah of untithed produce (תרומת תבלין) is rabbinic, not biblical.

items.text: Second baraita challenge: Two baskets and se'ahs
items.text_en: Second baraita challenge: Two baskets and se'ahs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita about two baskets and two se'ahs of terumah and hullin that fell into each other, and we assume they fell into their own kind. The Gemara challenges: if kezayit bikdei achilat pras is forbidden, why rely on such an assumption? The argument is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about two baskets of terumah and hullin and two se'ahs that fell into each other, where we assume they fell into their own kind and both are permitted.

The Gemara challenges: if the principle of כזית בכדי אכילת פרס (an olive's bulk within the time of eating half a loaf) is forbidden by Torah law, why do we rely on the assumption that the mixtures fell into their own kind?

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Dimi's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Dimi's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Dimi's view that the case involves a combination of permitted and forbidden substances, asking why adding more permitted food matters if the issue is about eating a olive's bulk within the time of eating a half-loaf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Dimi's explanation: according to the view that the case involves היתר מצטרף לאיסור (permitted food joining forbidden food), the quantity of permitted food matters, but according to Rav Dimi's view that the issue is eating an olive's bulk within the time of eating a half-loaf, why would adding more permitted food make a difference?

items.text: Rav Dimi's response about terumah
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's response about terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi deflects the question by noting that the case involves terumah in the present day, which is only rabbinic, implying the principle is not fully applicable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi responds: set aside the case of תרומה (priestly portion) in the present era, which is only rabbinic in status.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the shift to 'נותן טעם כעיקר'
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the shift to 'נותן טעם כעיקר'
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the word "מִשְׁרַת" might teach the principle of "נותן טעם כעיקר" (flavor is like the substance) rather than "היתר מצטרף לאיסור". The Gemara notes that Abaye initially had difficulty with Rav Dimi's statement and raised objections, but later accepted the alternative interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions Rav Dimi, suggesting that the word 'מִשְׁרַת' (soaked) might teach the principle of 'נותן טעם כעיקר' (flavor is like the substance) rather than 'היתר מצטרף לאיסור' (permitted combines with forbidden).

The Gemara notes that Abaye initially had difficulty with Rav Dimi's statement and raised objections, but later he turned to the alternative interpretation of 'נותן טעם כעיקר' (flavor is like the substance).
After Rav Dimi resolved Abaye's difficulties, Abaye again suggested that the verse might come to teach the principle of 'נותן טעם כעיקר' (flavor is like the substance).

items.text: Baraita teaching 'נותן טעם כעיקר' from Nazir
items.text_en: Baraita teaching 'נותן טעם כעיקר' from Nazir
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly derives the principle of "נותן טעם כעיקר" from the word "מִשְׁרַת": if grapes were soaked in water and the water has the taste of wine, one is liable. It then applies this principle to all Torah prohibitions through a kal vachomer argument, and notes that the same applies to orlah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the word 'מִשְׁרַת' (soaked) teaches the principle of 'נותן טעם כעיקר' (flavor is like the substance itself), giving the example of grapes soaked in water that taste like wine, and then generalizes to all Torah prohibitions.

The baraita presents a kal vachomer argument: if a nazirite, whose prohibition is less severe (not permanent, not benefit-related, and can be permitted), still has the principle of 'נותן טעם כעיקר', then certainly it applies to כלאי הכרם (diverse kinds in a vineyard), which is more severe.
The baraita adds that the same principle applies to ערלה (orlah) on two of the three counts of severity.

items.text: Identifying which Rabbi Akiva is referenced
items.text_en: Identifying which Rabbi Akiva is referenced
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks about Rabbi Avahu's statement regarding Rabbi Akiva: is it the Rabbi Akiva of the Mishnah who says that even if one soaked bread in wine and there is enough to combine for an olive's bulk, he is liable? The Gemara clarifies that this might be to exclude the first Tanna who required drinking a quarter-log of wine.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks which Rabbi Akiva is referenced by Rabbi Avahu, suggesting it might be the one from the Mishnah who says even if one soaked bread in wine and there is enough to combine for an olive's bulk, he is liable, but questions whether that case involves an actual olive's bulk of wine.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's Rabbi Akiva comes to exclude the first Tanna who requires drinking a quarter-log of wine.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva of the baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the reference is to Rabbi Akiva of a baraita, who explicitly states that a nazir who soaked his bread in wine and ate an olive's bulk from the bread and wine is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rather, it is the Rabbi Akiva of the baraita, as it was taught: Rabbi Akiva says a nazirite who soaked his bread in wine and ate an olive's bulk from the bread and the wine is liable.

items.text: Rav Acha's question: source for 'נותן טעם כעיקר' for Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question: source for 'נותן טעם כעיקר' for Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi: since Rabbi Akiva uses the verse for "היתר מצטרף לאיסור", where does he derive "נותן טעם כעיקר"? The answer is from meat in milk, where mere flavor is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya asks Rav Ashi: according to Rabbi Akiva, who interprets 'וכל משרת' for היתר מצטרף לאיסור (permitted joining forbidden), from where does he derive נותן טעם כעיקר (flavor as substance)? He learns it from בשר בחלב (meat in milk): isn't it just flavor and it is forbidden? Here too it is no different.

items.text: Rabbis' objection: meat in milk is a novelty
items.text_en: Rabbis' objection: meat in milk is a novelty
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that one cannot learn from meat in milk because it is a novelty (חידוש). The Gemara explores what the novelty is: not that they are permitted separately and forbidden together (since kilayim is similar), but that if one roasts meat in milk all day it is permitted, but if one cooks it in milk it is forbidden. The Gemara then questions whether Rabbi Akiva also considers meat in milk a novelty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Rabbis do not learn the principle of טעם כעיקר (taste as the substance) from meat in milk, because meat in milk is a חידוש (novelty).
The Gemara asks what the novelty of meat in milk is, and rejects the suggestion that it is simply that each is permitted alone but forbidden together, since kilayim (mixed seeds) has the same rule.
The Gemara explains that the novelty is that if one roasts meat in milk all day it is permitted, but if one cooks it in milk it is forbidden, which is unlike other prohibitions.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva also considers meat in milk a novelty, implying that he might derive the principle from it differently.

items.text: Deriving the prohibition from pagan libation wine
items.text_en: Deriving the prohibition from pagan libation wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the prohibition of forbidden mixtures can be derived from the law of pagan libation wine (גיעולי גוים), where even a mere taste is forbidden. The same logic should apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the prohibition of forbidden mixtures from the law of pagan libation wine (גיעולי גוים), where mere taste is forbidden, and applies the same logic here.

items.text: Rejection: Pagan libation is a novelty
items.text_en: Rejection: Pagan libation is a novelty
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that pagan libation wine is a novelty (חידוש) because in the entire Torah, a forbidden taste that is spoiled (נותן טעם לפגם) is permitted, but with pagan libation it is forbidden. Therefore, it cannot serve as a precedent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy to pagan libation wine, explaining that it is a חידוש (novelty) because in the entire Torah a spoiled taste (נותן טעם לפגם) is permitted, but with pagan libation it is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's distinction and the Rabbis' counter
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's distinction and the Rabbis' counter
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya explains that Rabbi Akiva limits the novelty to a pot used on the same day (קדירה בת יומא), where the taste is not spoiled. The Rabbis counter that even a pot used on the same day has some slight spoilage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya explains that Rabbi Akiva limits the Torah's prohibition to a pot used on the same day (קדירה בת יומא), which is not a case of נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a spoiled taste).
The Rabbis counter that even a pot used on the same day (קדירה בת יומא) inevitably imparts some slight spoilage (פגם פורתא), so Rabbi Akiva's distinction is not absolute.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge: Why not derive from Mishrat?
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge: Why not derive from Mishrat?
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya challenges Rav Ashi: Just as the Rabbis derive from the word 'משרת' that taste is like the main substance for all prohibitions, Rabbi Akiva, who uses 'משרת' for 'permitted joins with forbidden', should also derive a general principle from it.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya challenges Rav Ashi: Just as the Rabbis derive from 'משרת' that taste is like the main substance for all prohibitions, Rabbi Akiva, who uses 'משרת' for 'permitted joins with forbidden', should also derive a general principle from it.

items.text: Answer: Nazir and Chatat are two verses that come as one
items.text_en: Answer: Nazir and Chatat are two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that Nazir and Chatat are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), which cannot teach a general principle. The Gemara explains the derivation from Chatat (segments 7-8), why the Rabbis need both verses (9-10), Rabbi Akiva's reasoning (11-12), and the final conclusion that both verses are needed for 'permitted joins with forbidden', making them two verses that come as one (13-14).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the cases of Nazir and Chatat are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), which cannot teach a general principle, and asks what the derivation from Chatat is.
A baraita is cited to show that from the verse about Chatat (חטאת), the principle that a permitted substance joins with a forbidden substance is derived.
The Rabbis explain that both verses are necessary because neither case could be derived from the other, so they are not two verses that come as one.
Rabbi Akiva objects that the case of Chatat could be derived from Nazir, since all prohibitions are derived from Nazir, so both verses are not necessary.
The Rabbis reject Rabbi Akiva's objection, arguing that Chatat teaches the specific principle of permitted joining with forbidden, and non-sacred items cannot be derived from consecrated items.
The Rabbis conclude that the term 'משרת' (soaked) teaches the principle that flavor is like the substance, and from here one derives for all prohibitions of the Torah.

The Gemara resolves that according to Rabbi Akiva, both verses teach the same principle of permitted joining with forbidden, making them two verses that come as one, which do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question about combining prohibitions
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question about combining prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: According to Rabbi Akiva, if 'permitted joins with forbidden' is derived, then certainly 'forbidden joins with forbidden' should be derived from the verse 'מכל אשר יעשה מגפן היין'? Rav Kahana answers that the verse teaches that forbidden substances combine even when eaten one after the other, not just simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: According to Rabbi Akiva, if 'permitted joins with forbidden' is derived, then certainly 'forbidden joins with forbidden' should be derived from the verse 'מכל אשר יעשה מגפן היין'?
Rav Kahana answers that the verse teaches that forbidden substances combine even when eaten one after the other, not just simultaneously.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's view (fragment)
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's view (fragment)
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the beginning of Rabbi Shimon's opinion, which is cut off. This likely introduces a new argument or distinction.

sub.desc_en: The daf begins to present Rabbi Shimon's opinion, but the text is cut off, likely introducing a new argument or distinction.

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse 'mikol asher yei'aseh'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse 'mikol asher yei'aseh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that there is no combination (tziruf) for a nazirite, derives from the phrase 'mikol asher yei'aseh'. It answers that he requires it to teach that one is not a nazirite unless he abstains from all of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that there is no combination (צירוף) for a nazirite, derives from the verse 'מכל אשר יעשה'.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan requires the verse to teach that one is not a nazirite unless he abstains from all of them.

items.text: Rabbi Abahu citing Rabbi Elazar on the exception of the nazirite's revi'it
items.text_en: Rabbi Abahu citing Rabbi Elazar on the exception of the nazirite's revi'it
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that in all Torah cases, permitted liquid does not combine with forbidden liquid, except for the revi'it of wine for a nazirite, because the Torah said 'mishrat'. The Gemara then notes the difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: Rabbi Yochanan includes even solid foods, while Rabbi Elazar limits it to liquids.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that in all Torah cases, permitted liquid does not combine with forbidden liquid, except for the nazirite's revi'it of wine, because the Torah said 'משרת' (soaking).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yochanan's and Rabbi Elazar's positions.
The Gemara answers that the difference is that Rabbi Yochanan includes even solid foods in the combination, while Rabbi Elazar limits it to liquids only.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's list of ten revi'iyot: five red and five white
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's list of ten revi'iyot: five red and five white
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states there are ten revi'iyot in the Torah, and Rav Kahana held five red and five white. The red ones are: the nazirite's revi'it of wine, the Passover revi'it, the revi'it for a judge who drank wine, the revi'it for entering the Temple after drinking, and the revi'it of blood from two corpses. The white ones are: the revi'it of oil for challah, the nazirite's revi'it of oil, the leper's revi'it of water, the revi'it for invalidating a body, and the revi'it for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states there are ten revi'iyot in the Torah, and Rav Kahana held five red and five white.

The red revi'iyot are enumerated: the nazirite's revi'it of wine, the Passover revi'it (as per Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel), the revi'it for a judge who drank wine, and the revi'it for entering the Temple after drinking.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for red revi'it of blood
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for red revi'it of blood
sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from a verse that a revi'it of blood from two corpses imparts טומאה (ritual impurity) in a tent.
The white revi'iyot are enumerated: the revi'it of oil for challah, the nazirite's revi'it of oil, the leper's revi'it of water, and the revi'it for invalidating a body.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for white revi'it of Shabbat
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for white revi'it of Shabbat
sub.desc_en: A baraita states that other liquids invalidate the body in a revi'it, and other poured liquids also in a revi'it.

items.text: Gemara's challenges and exclusion of disputed revi'iyot
items.text_en: Gemara's challenges and exclusion of disputed revi'iyot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there are additional revi'iyot, such as the revi'it for netilat yadayim, the revi'it for the laver, and the revi'it for a mikveh. It answers that the list excludes disputed cases (pelugta) and that the mikveh revi'it was nullified by the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the list of ten revi'iyot by asking whether the revi'it for netilat yadayim (hand-washing) is missing.
The Gemara answers that the list excludes disputed cases (פלוגתא), and the revi'it for hand-washing is disputed.
The Gemara asks about the revi'it for the laver (כיור), where Rabbi Yehuda requires a revi'it.
The Gemara again answers that the list excludes disputed cases, as the laver measure is disputed between the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks about the revi'it for a mikveh, where Rabbi Zakkai requires a revi'it.
The Gemara answers that this too is a disputed case and thus excluded.
The Gemara asks about the revi'it for a mikveh (immersion pool), which is not disputed.
The Gemara resolves that the mikveh revi'it is excluded because the Sages nullified it (ביטלו רבנן), removing it from the list.

items.text: Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi Akiva on the measure for nazirite prohibitions
items.text_en: Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi Akiva on the measure for nazirite prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma does not compare all nazirite prohibitions to drinking, while Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse that all prohibitions require a kezayit, just like eating.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nazirite is only liable when he eats a kezayit (olive's bulk) of grapes.

The Gemara explains that the Tanna Kamma does not compare all nazirite prohibitions to drinking, while Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'וַעֲנָבִים לַחִים וִיבֵשִׁים לֹא יֹאכֵל' (and fresh and dried grapes he shall not eat) that just as eating requires a kezayit, so too all prohibitions require a kezayit.

items.text: Baraita: liability for each distinct name within one species
items.text_en: Baraita: liability for each distinct name within one species
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse that one is liable separately for fresh grapes and dried grapes, and applies this principle to all Torah prohibitions where one species has two names.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וַעֲנָבִים לַחִים וִיבֵשִׁים לֹא יֹאכֵל' (fresh and dried grapes he shall not eat) and derives that one is liable separately for each distinct name within one species.
The gemara explains that the baraita's principle comes to include new wine and grapes as separate categories.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute lashes for חרצן and זג
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute lashes for חרצן and זג
items.desc_en: Abaye holds that eating חרצן or זג incurs two lashes each, and three for both; Rava argues one only, because the prohibition is included in a general negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that eating חרצן (grape seed) alone incurs two lashes, eating זג (grape skin) alone incurs two lashes, and eating both incurs three lashes.
Rava argues that one incurs only one lash, because the prohibition is included in a general negative commandment (לאו שבכללות).

items.text: Rav Pappa challenges Rava from a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava from a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer lists five lashes for various grape products, implying multiple distinct prohibitions, contradicting Rava. The Gemara questions why not six, including the prohibition of 'מכל אשר יעשה'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a nazirite who consumes various grape products in one day is liable to five lashes, implying multiple distinct prohibitions, which contradicts Rava's position.
The Gemara objects that according to the baraita's logic, the nazirite should be liable to six lashes, including one for the prohibition of 'מכל אשר יעשה' (from anything made from grapes).

items.text: Gemara resolves: the baraita omitted 'לא יחל דברו'
items.text_en: Gemara resolves: the baraita omitted 'לא יחל דברו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the baraita omitted the prohibition of 'לא יחל דברו', but rejects this because that prohibition appears elsewhere (in Nedarim).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita omitted, and answers that it omitted the prohibition of 'לא יחל דברו' (he shall not profane his word).
The Gemara objects that this is not a true omission, because the prohibition of 'לא יחל דברו' appears elsewhere in Nedarim.

items.text: Ravina and Rav Ashi: the baraita omitted 'בין הביניים'
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Ashi: the baraita omitted 'בין הביניים'
items.desc_en: Ravina from Parzikya suggests the baraita omitted the prohibition of drinking wine between the intervals (בין הביניים). Rav Pappa then concludes that the baraita does not actually teach five lashes.

sub.text: Ravina from Parzikya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Ravina from Parzikya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Ravina from Parzikya objects to Rav Ashi that the baraita omitted the prohibition of drinking wine between the intervals (בין הביניים).
Rav Pappa concludes that the baraita does not actually teach five lashes, resolving the objection.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rav Pappa's retraction
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rav Pappa's retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Pappa initially thought the Mishnah did not teach 'five' and then retracted, and Rav Pappa explains that he thought it was not a tradition but then realized it was.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa initially cited a tradition of 'five' if the Mishnah does not teach 'five', and what caused him to retract.
Rav Pappa explains that he initially thought the tradition was not a reliable גמרא (received tradition) in his possession, but then realized it was, so he did not retract.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's statement and Rav Yosef's interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's statement and Rav Yosef's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the Aramaic translation of a phrase in the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosi's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that the Targumic translation of 'from Purtsnin to Itzurin' follows the opinion of Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef states that the Aramaic translation of the phrase 'מפורצנין ועד עיצורין' follows Rabbi Yosi's opinion.

items.text: Mishnah: Standard nazirite period and shaving rules
items.text_en: Mishnah: Standard nazirite period and shaving rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that standard naziriteship is 30 days, and if a nazirite shaves or is shaved by bandits, he must restart 30 days. It also rules that a nazirite who shaves with scissors or a razor, or plucks any hair, is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that unspecified nezirut lasts 30 days, that shaving or being shaved by bandits resets the count, and that a nazir who shaves with scissors or a razor or plucks any hair is liable.
The Mishnah rules that if a nazirite shaves or is shaved by bandits, he must restart 30 days.
The Mishnah rules that a nazirite who shaves with scissors or a razor, or plucks any hair, is liable.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Does hair grow from below or above?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Does hair grow from below or above?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether hair grows from below (the root) or from above (the tip), and explains the practical difference for a nazirite shaved by bandits who left enough hair to bend the tip to the root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether hair grows from below (the root) or from above (the tip), and explains the practical difference for a nazirite shaved by bandits who left enough hair to bend the tip to the root.
The Gemara presents the first answer: if hair grows from below, the nazirite's hair has been removed; if from above, the consecrated hair remains.

items.text: Proof from a living date palm branch
items.text_en: Proof from a living date palm branch
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that hair grows from below by citing a living date palm branch, which has its fruit at the base, but concludes that the fruit descends due to its vitality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence from a live palm branch where the fruit sits at the base of the branch, suggesting growth from below, but deflects that the fruit descends due to its vitality.
The Gemara resolves that hair indeed grows from below, but the fruit descends due to the vitality of the living branch.

items.text: Proof from a dead date palm branch
items.text_en: Proof from a dead date palm branch
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that hair grows from above by citing a dead date palm branch, which has its fruit at the tip, but concludes that the fruit climbs due to lack of vitality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence from a dead palm branch where the fruit sits at the top, suggesting growth from above, but deflects that the fruit climbs due to lack of vitality.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that in a dead branch the fruit climbs upward because the branch lacks vitality, so the analogy to hair growth is invalid.

items.text: Proof from the hair of Cushites
items.text_en: Proof from the hair of Cushites
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that hair grows from below by citing Cushites' hair, which loosens from below after growing, but concludes that it is due to lying down.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence from Cushite hair that loosens from below after growing, but deflects that the loosening is due to the weight of the hair.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the loosening is due to lying down, not growth from below.

items.text: Proof from a carding comb and elders' beards
items.text_en: Proof from a carding comb and elders' beards
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that hair grows from below by citing a carding comb where wool loosens from below, and then mentions that when elders dye their beards white, the roots grow white first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence from wool carding where the wool loosens from below, and adds that when elders dye their beards white, the roots grow white first, supporting growth from below.

items.text: Inference about hair growth from below the root
items.text_en: Inference about hair growth from below the root
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that hair growth from below the root (מלתחת רבי) is considered significant, concluding 'שמע מינה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that hair growth from below the root (מלתחת רבי) is considered significant, concluding 'שמע מינה'.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita about nazir shaved by bandits
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita about nazir shaved by bandits
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference with a baraita where a nazir shaved by bandits after the completion of his term does not reset his count, and explains that this follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that shaving after completion requires seven days. The Sages hold that within seven days enough hair grows to bend the tip to the root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous inference by citing a baraita where a nazir shaved by bandits after his term does not reset his count, arguing that if hair growth from below were significant, it should reset.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to a case where the bandits shaved the nazir after the completion of his term, and it follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the shaving of purification and the shaving of impurity, both requiring seven days.
The Gemara concludes that the Sages hold that within seven days enough hair grows to bend the tip to the root, so the shaving does not reset the count.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan on liability for non-scissors removal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan on liability for non-scissors removal
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a nazir who shaves with a razor or scissors, or who plucks any amount, is liable. Rabbi Yoshiya derives this from the verse 'קדוש יהיה', while Rabbi Yonatan exempts for plucking or tweezing, arguing that the verse only imposes a positive and negative commandment for razor shaving.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a nazir who shaves with a razor or scissors, or who plucks any amount, is liable.
Rabbi Yoshiya derives liability for plucking, tweezing, or scraping from the verse 'קָדוֹשׁ יִהְיֶה' (he shall be holy).
Rabbi Yonatan exempts for plucking, tweezing, or scraping any amount, limiting liability to razor shaving alone.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yonatan: does not the verse 'קָדוֹשׁ יִהְיֶה' (he shall be holy) imply liability for any removal?
Rabbi Yonatan explains that the verse only imposes a positive and negative commandment for razor shaving, not for other methods.

items.text: Alternative derivation from 'לא יעבור' and the need for a razor for the final shaving
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from 'לא יעבור' and the need for a razor for the final shaving
items.desc_en: Another baraita derives liability for any hair removal from 'לא יעבור על ראשו', and questions why the Torah specifies 'תער'. The answer is that we need to learn that the final shaving (after the nazirite period) must be done with a razor, which cannot be derived from the leper.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives liability for any hair removal from the verse 'לֹא יַעֲבוֹר עַל רֹאשׁוֹ' (a razor shall not pass over his head), expanding beyond a razor alone.
The gemara asks: since the baraita already includes all methods of hair removal from 'לֹא יַעֲבוֹר', why does the Torah specifically mention 'תַּעַר' (razor)?
The answer: the word 'תַּעַר' teaches that the final shaving (after the nazirite period) must be done with a razor, a detail that cannot be derived from the leper's shaving.

items.text: Rabbi's derivation that shaving must be with a razor
items.text_en: Rabbi's derivation that shaving must be with a razor
items.desc_en: Rabbi argues that the verse 'a razor shall not pass over his head until the days are fulfilled' implies that after fulfillment, shaving must be with a razor. The Gemara objects that the verse already prohibits a razor, and explains that the repetition creates two negative commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that one cannot derive a stricter ruling from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) to impose stringency.
Rabbi argues that the verse 'תער לא יעבור על ראשו עד מלאת' (a razor shall not pass over his head until the days are fulfilled) implies that after fulfillment, shaving must be with a razor.
The Gemara objects that the verse already explicitly prohibits a razor, so why is a separate derivation needed?
The Gemara explains that the repetition of the prohibition creates two negative commandments (לאוין), one for the period of nezirut and one for after fulfillment.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling and the requirement of 'like a razor'
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling and the requirement of 'like a razor'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that for lashes one violation suffices, for impediment two are needed, and for resetting the count only a majority of hair with a razor resets. The Gemara questions whether only a razor works, citing a baraita that includes all removers, and concludes that it must be 'like a razor'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that for lashes one violation suffices, for delay two violations are needed, and shaving only resets the count if done with a razor on most of the head.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah includes all types of hair removers, not just a razor.
The Gemara resolves that the requirement is for something similar to a razor (כעין תער), meaning a tool that cuts hair like a razor.

items.text: Baraita on resetting with a razor and majority
items.text_en: Baraita on resetting with a razor and majority
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a nazir who plucks, pulls, or cuts any amount does not reset unless he shaves the majority of his head with a razor. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says that just as two hairs impede, so two hairs reset.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Chisda: a nazir who plucks, pulls, or cuts any amount does not reset the count unless done with a razor on most of the head.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon adds that just as two hairs delay the count, two hairs also reset it.

items.text: Mishnah: Three who shave as a mitzvah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three who shave as a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three people shave as a mitzvah: nazir, metzora, and Levites. If they shaved without a razor or left two hairs, they have done nothing. The Gemara explains that this teaches that it is not merely for hair removal, but a specific requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three people shave as a mitzvah: nazir, metzora, and Levites; if they shaved without a razor or left two hairs, they have done nothing.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement is not obvious; it teaches that shaving is not merely for hair removal but a specific requirement, countering the possibility that any removal method would suffice.

items.text: Derivation that a metzora must shave with a razor
items.text_en: Derivation that a metzora must shave with a razor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for a metzora's razor requirement. It attempts to derive from Levites but is refuted, then from nazir but is refuted. It then derives from the common element of both, concluding that all who require shaving must use a razor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah requires a razor for all three shavers, and asks: for a metzora (מצורע), from where do we derive that his shaving must be with a razor?
The Gemara proposes deriving the metzora's razor requirement from the Levites (לויים), but refutes it because Levites require waving (תנופה) of their own bodies, which the metzora does not.
The Gemara proposes deriving the metzora's razor requirement from the nazir (נזיר), but refutes it because the nazir's offering requires bread (לחם), which the metzora's does not.
The Gemara concludes that since neither alone suffices, it derives from both the Levites and the nazir together, using a combined argument (צד השוה).
The Gemara formalizes the combined derivation: the common element (צד השוה) of both Levites and nazir is that they require shaving and their shaving is with a razor, so the metzora is also included.

items.text: Rava's objection to the common element
items.text_en: Rava's objection to the common element
items.desc_en: Rava from Barnish asks Rav Ashi whether one can refute the common element because both Levites and nazir have additional stringencies not shared by a metzora.

sub.text: Rava from Barnish's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava from Barnish's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava from Barnish objects to Rav Ashi that the common element itself has a flaw: both nazir and Levites have additional requirements (bread offering and wave-offering) that the metzora (leper) lacks, so the derivation is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Tanna's logic
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Tanna's logic
items.desc_en: Rava bar Mesharshya questions Rava about the Tanna's reasoning: initially he says one cannot learn from a leper because a lenient case cannot teach a stricter one, but then he suggests learning from a kal vachomer. The question is why the Tanna contradicts himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna's logic: initially he says one cannot learn from a leper because a lenient case cannot teach a stricter one, but then he suggests learning from a kal vachomer, contradicting himself.

Rava bar Mesharshya asks Rava about the contradiction, and Rava answers that the first statement is according to the Rabbis and the second according to Rabbi Eliezer, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable even for plucking hair with tweezers.

items.text: Rava's answer: two different opinions
items.text_en: Rava's answer: two different opinions
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Tanna's statements align with different authorities: the first part follows the Rabbis, the second follows Rabbi Eliezer. He cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable even for removing hair with tweezers or a plane.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the Tanna's first statement follows the Rabbis and the second follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Rava cites a Mishnah where the Rabbis require a razor for liability, while Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable even with tweezers or a plane.

items.text: Rabbis' reasoning from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbis' reasoning from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' view through a baraita: the word 'his beard' excludes a leper from the prohibition, and the phrase 'do not destroy' limits liability to shaving with a razor, not scissors. The baraita concludes that the only form of shaving that involves destruction is with a razor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis (who hold that a nazir is liable only for shaving with a razor).
The baraita cites the verse 'his beard' (זקנו) to exclude a leper from the prohibition of shaving the corners of the beard.

The baraita derives that liability is only for a razor: the phrase 'do not destroy' (לא תשחית) limits liability to shaving that involves destruction, which is specifically with a razor, not scissors or tweezers.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the baraita means that even with tweezers one fulfills a mitzvah, and it teaches that even with a razor one is not liable? The Gemara answers: if tweezers were valid, the verse would be silent, and we would infer from the nazirite that even for a mitzvah one is liable; thus the verse must exclude tweezers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the baraita means that even with tweezers one fulfills a mitzvah, and it teaches that even with a razor one is not liable.
The Gemara answers: if tweezers were valid, the verse would be silent, and we would infer from the nazirite that even for a mitzvah one is liable; thus the verse must exclude tweezers.

items.text: Reish Lakish's principle of aseh docheh lo ta'aseh
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's principle of aseh docheh lo ta'aseh
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Reish Lakish's principle that when a positive commandment and a negative commandment conflict, if both can be fulfilled that is preferable, but if not, the positive commandment overrides the negative one. This is applied to the case of a leprous nazirite who shaves with a depilatory or a plane, which is a positive commandment and thus overrides the prohibition of shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one assumes that shaving with a depilatory or a plane fulfills a positive commandment, then the positive commandment overrides the prohibition.
The Gemara cites Reish Lakish's principle that wherever a positive commandment and a negative commandment conflict, if both cannot be fulfilled, the positive commandment overrides the negative one.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation from "rosho"
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation from "rosho"
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: he derives from the word "rosho" (his head) that a leprous nazirite is permitted to shave with a razor, even though a regular nazirite is prohibited. The baraita teaches that without "rosho", one might think a leprous nazirite is also prohibited, but the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is for permitting a leprous nazirite to shave with a razor.
A baraita is cited to show that the word "rosho" (his head) teaches that a leprous nazirite is permitted to shave with a razor, unlike a regular nazirite.

The Gemara objects that perhaps the baraita only permits shaving with a razor, but even removing hair with tweezers or a plane is still a מצוה (commandment), and the verse teaches that even with a razor it is permitted.

items.text: Reish Lakish's principle applied again
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's principle applied again
items.desc_en: The Gemara reiterates that if one assumes shaving with a depilatory or a plane is a commandment, then since the Torah did not write "ta'ar" (razor) in the context of the leprous nazirite, Reish Lakish's principle applies: the positive commandment overrides the negative prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if shaving with a depilatory or plane were considered a commandment, then since the Torah did not write 'תער' (razor) in the leprous nazirite context, Reish Lakish's principle applies: the positive commandment overrides the negative prohibition.

items.text: Rabbis' interpretation of "rosho" for the prohibition of hakafah
items.text_en: Rabbis' interpretation of "rosho" for the prohibition of hakafah
items.desc_en: The Rabbis (Sages) interpret the word "rosho" to teach that the prohibition of shaving the corners of the head (hakafah) does not apply to a leprous nazirite. A baraita states that without "rosho", one might think a leprous nazirite is also prohibited from shaving his head corners, but the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the word 'rosho' (his head) in the context of the nazirite.
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis need the word to exclude the leprous nazirite from the prohibition of hakafah (shaving the corners of the head).
A baraita is cited: the verse 'Do not round the corners of your head' might include a leprous nazirite, but the word 'rosho' teaches otherwise.

items.text: Need for both "rosho" and "zekano"
items.text_en: Need for both "rosho" and "zekano"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why both "rosho" and "zekano" (his beard) are written, since the same derivation could be made from "zekano" alone. It explains that both are necessary: if only "zekano" were written, one might think that shaving the entire head is not considered hakafah, so "rosho" is needed to teach that it is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote 'rosho' (his head) in the context of the leprous nazirite, since the same exclusion could be derived from 'zekano' (his beard).
A baraita is cited that derives from 'zekano' that the leprous nazirite is permitted to shave his beard, despite the general prohibition of shaving the corners of the beard.

The Gemara answers that both terms are necessary: if only 'zekano' were written, one might think that shaving the entire head is not considered hakafah (rounding the corners), so the Torah wrote 'rosho' to teach that it is.

items.text: Explanation of the dual terms 'his head' and 'his beard'
items.text_en: Explanation of the dual terms 'his head' and 'his beard'
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the Torah had only written 'his head' and not 'his beard', one might have thought that the positive commandment overrides the negative prohibition and that the entire head is considered a single unit for the prohibition of rounding. It then asks how we would know that a razor is prohibited, so the Torah wrote 'his beard' to teach this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara posits that if the Torah had written only 'his head' without 'his beard', one might have mistakenly inferred both that the positive commandment overrides the negative prohibition and that rounding the entire head constitutes a single act of rounding.
The Gemara asks how we would know that a razor is prohibited for shaving the head, given only the term 'his head'.
The Gemara resolves that the Torah therefore wrote 'his beard' to teach that a razor is prohibited for shaving the beard, and by extension for the head.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's source for positive overriding negative
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's source for positive overriding negative
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives the principle that a positive commandment overrides a negative one, and answers that he learns it from the law of fringes (gedilim), citing a baraita about the prohibition of wearing wool and linen together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Eliezer derives the principle that a positive commandment overrides a negative one.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer learns it from the law of fringes (גדילים).
The Gemara cites a baraita that begins with the prohibition of wearing wool and linen together (שעטנז), which serves as the basis for the derivation.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah: רובו ככולו is Torah law
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah: רובו ככולו is Torah law
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's ruling that if a nazirite shaved without a razor or left two hairs, it is invalid, that the principle of 'majority is like the whole' (רובו ככולו) is Torah law. This is derived from the verse regarding a nazirite's shaving on the seventh day, implying that only when the entire head is shaved is it valid, but elsewhere majority suffices.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the Mishnah's ruling that if a nazirite shaved without a razor or left two hairs, it is invalid.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's inference
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's inference
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika infers from the Mishnah that the principle of 'majority is like the whole' (רובו ככולו) is Torah law.
The Gemara proves the inference from the verse regarding a nazirite's shaving on the seventh day, which implies that only when the entire head is shaved is it valid, but elsewhere majority suffices.

items.text: Objection by Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina and resolution
items.text_en: Objection by Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina objects that the verse cited is about a defiled nazirite, not a pure one. The Gemara in the West resolves this by noting that the law of shaving with a razor for a defiled nazirite is derived from a pure nazirite, so the same logic applies in reverse: just as leaving two hairs invalidates a defiled nazirite's shaving, so too for a pure nazirite.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina objects that the verse cited (regarding shaving with a razor) is written about a defiled nazirite, not a pure one.

The Gemara in the West resolves that since the law of shaving with a razor for a defiled nazirite is derived from a pure nazirite, the same logic applies in reverse: just as leaving two hairs invalidates a defiled nazirite's shaving, so too for a pure nazirite.

items.text: Abaye's query: regrowth and re-shaving of leftover hairs
items.text_en: Abaye's query: regrowth and re-shaving of leftover hairs
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: if a nazirite shaved but left two hairs, then his hair grew back and he shaved those two hairs again, does the original leftover hair still invalidate the shaving? The question is whether the regrowth and re-shaving remove the impediment.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether leftover hairs that grew back and were re-shaved still invalidate the original shaving.

items.text: Rava's query and discussion: one hair shaved, one fell out
items.text_en: Rava's query and discussion: one hair shaved, one fell out
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if a nazirite shaved and left two hairs, then shaved one and the other fell out, what is the law? Rav Acha from Difti clarifies that Rava's question is about the case where one fell out first and then he shaved the other. The answer is that there is no shaving here (since only one hair was shaved) and no hair (since the other fell out), so the mitzvah of shaving is not fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if a nazirite shaved and left two hairs, then shaved one and the other fell out, what is the law? Rav Acha from Difti clarifies that Rava's question is about shaving one hair at a time.
Rav Acha rephrases the case: one fell out first and then he shaved the other, and concludes that there is no shaving here and no hair, so the mitzvah of shaving is not fulfilled.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on washing and combing for a nazirite
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on washing and combing for a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nazirite may wash and rub his hair but not comb it. The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi Shimon's view, who permits an unintended act, while the prohibition of combing aligns with the Rabbis. Rabba resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, since combing is always intended to remove loose hairs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nazirite may wash and rub his hair but may not comb it.
The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, and answers that the first clause permitting washing and rubbing follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits an unintended act.
The Gemara objects that the second clause prohibiting combing follows the Rabbis, who forbid an unintended act that inevitably causes hair removal.
Rabba resolves the contradiction by explaining that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, since combing is always intended to remove loose hairs.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on using earth for washing
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on using earth for washing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael rules that a nazirite should not wash with earth because it loosens hair. The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrase is 'because it loosens hair' or 'because of the loosener', and the practical difference is whether any earth that does not loosen hair is permitted. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that a nazirite should not wash with earth because it loosens hair.
The Gemara raises a question: was the Mishnah's phrase 'because it loosens hair' or 'because of the loosener', and what is the practical difference?

The Gemara explains the practical difference: if the phrase is 'because it loosens', earth that does not loosen hair is permitted; if 'because of the loosener', all earth is forbidden. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: multiple violations of nazirite prohibitions
items.text_en: Mishnah: multiple violations of nazirite prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a nazirite drinks wine all day, he is liable only once, but if warned 'do not drink' each time, he is liable for each. The same applies to shaving and becoming impure from corpses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nazirite who drinks wine all day is liable only once.
If witnesses warned him each time, he is liable for each drinking act.
Similarly, a nazirite who shaves all day is liable only once.
If warned each time, he is liable for each shaving act.
A nazirite who contracts impurity from corpses all day is liable only once.
If warned each time, he is liable for each act of contracting impurity.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding multiple tumah prohibitions
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding multiple tumah prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rabbah, citing Rav Huna, argues that the verse 'lo yitama' prohibits tumah and 'lo yavo' prohibits bi'ah, but multiple tumah violations are not separately prohibited. Rav Yosef counters that Rav Huna actually holds even multiple tumah violations are prohibited, citing a case of a nazir already standing in a cemetery who touches another corpse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah, citing Rav Huna, states that the verse 'לֹא יִטַּמָּא' (he shall not become impure) is a complete verse, and 'לֹא יָבֹא' (he shall not enter) warns separately about tumah (impurity) and bi'ah (entering the Temple), but multiple tumah violations are not separately prohibited.
Rav Yosef objects, swearing that Rav Huna actually holds even multiple tumah violations are prohibited, citing a case of a nazir standing in a cemetery who touches another corpse and is liable.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita about a priest
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita about a priest
items.desc_en: Abaye objects with a baraita: a priest already carrying a corpse on his shoulder who touches another corpse is exempt because he is already 'mechulal' (profaned). This suggests that one already impure is not liable for additional tumah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects with a baraita: a priest already carrying a corpse on his shoulder who touches another corpse is exempt because he is already 'mechulal' (profaned), suggesting that one already impure is not liable for additional tumah.

items.text: Rav Yosef's counter-objection from a mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's counter-objection from a mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef responds by citing a mishnah where a nazir who is repeatedly warned 'al titamei' is liable for each warning, even though he is already impure. This contradicts the baraita, creating a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing a mishnah where a nazir who is repeatedly warned 'אל תיטמא' is liable for each warning, even though he is already impure, creating a contradiction with the baraita.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between connected and unconnected tumah
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between connected and unconnected tumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita deals with tumah through attachments (chiburim), while the mishnah deals with tumah without attachments. Thus, one is liable for multiple prohibitions only when not already connected to the source of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between tumah through attachments (chiburim) and tumah without attachments.

items.text: Question about the validity of tumah through attachments for a nazir
items.text_en: Question about the validity of tumah through attachments for a nazir
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether tumah through attachments is a Torah concept for a nazir, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef that it applies only to terumah and kodashim, not to nazir and the paschal offering. The Gemara distinguishes between attachments of a person to a person and attachments of a person to a corpse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether טומאה בחיבורין (impurity through attachments) is a Torah concept for a nazir, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's statement that it applies only to תרומה (priestly portion) and קדשים (sacred offerings), not to a nazir or the paschal offering, and asks why the distinction.

The Gemara resolves the question by distinguishing between attachments of a person to a person (which is not a Torah concept for a nazir) and attachments of a person to a corpse (which is a Torah concept for a nazir).

items.text: Rejection of multiple tumah violations
items.text_en: Rejection of multiple tumah violations
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that multiple tumah violations are not separately prohibited because the person is already impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that multiple tumah violations are not separately prohibited because the person is already impure.

items.text: Distinction between tumah and bi'ah in a house vs. a field
items.text_en: Distinction between tumah and bi'ah in a house vs. a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if one is already impure, why is he liable for bi'ah (entering the Temple)? Rabbi Yochanan answers: the case of bi'ah is in a house (the Temple), while the case of tumah is in a field (where impurity is not from entering).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if one is already impure, why should he be liable for bi'ah (entering the Temple) as well, since he is already standing in impurity?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: the case of bi'ah (entering) is in a house (the Temple), while the case of tumah (impurity) is in a field (where impurity is not from entering).

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction between impurity and entry
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction between impurity and entry
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects earlier attempts to explain how a nazir can enter a tent with a corpse without becoming impure immediately. Rava, Rav Pappa, and Mar bar Rav Ashi offer scenarios where impurity and entry occur simultaneously, such as entering via a box or while dying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that when entering a tent, as soon as one inserts a hand, impurity enters before the body, so entry and impurity cannot be simultaneous.
Rabbi Elazar proposes that one first inserts only the hand (impurity without entry), then the body simultaneously, but the Gemara objects that the nose enters first.
Rava suggests inserting the hand first, then the body, but the Gemara objects that the toes enter first.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Mar bar Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Mar bar Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Mar bar Rav Ashi resolve the contradiction by proposing scenarios where impurity and entry occur exactly simultaneously: entering via a sealed container or while dying.

items.text: Baraita on the source for impurity until death
items.text_en: Baraita on the source for impurity until death
items.desc_en: A baraita cites two verses: "lehachallo" (to defile himself) until death, and Rabbi's verse "bemotam" (in their death) until death. This sets up the debate on whether a goses is considered dead for impurity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites two verses — 'lehachallo' (to defile himself) and 'bemotam' (in their death) — both interpreted to mean impurity applies only until death, not to a goses.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on the difference
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on the difference
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the difference is in the exegesis of the verses, while Resh Lakish says it is whether a goses transmits impurity. According to the one who learns from "lehachallo", even a goses is included; according to "bemotam", only after actual death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two verses.
Rabbi Yochanan says the difference lies in the exegetical method of interpreting the verses.

Resh Lakish says the difference is whether a goses (a dying person) transmits impurity: according to the one who learns from "להחלו" even a goses is included, while according to "במותם" only after actual death.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: reconciling the verses for each opinion
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: reconciling the verses for each opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the one who learns from "lehachallo" explains the verse "bemotam", and answers that it is needed for Rabbi's derivation that a nazir does not become impure from negaim or zivim. Conversely, for the one who learns from "bemotam", the word "bemotam" implies two things: impurity at death and exclusion of goses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who learns from "lehachallo", what does he do with the verse "bemotam"?
The Gemara answers that it is needed for Rabbi's derivation that a nazir does not become impure from negaim or zivim.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi says that from "bemotam" he derives that a nazir becomes impure only from death, not from negaim or zivim.
The Gemara asks: for the one who learns from "bemotam", doesn't he need the word for his own derivation?
The Gemara answers that if the verse had said "bemot" (singular), it would imply one thing; the plural "bemotam" implies two things: impurity at death and exclusion of goses.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: the word "lehachallo" for the other opinion
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: the word "lehachallo" for the other opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the one who learns from "bemotam" explains "lehachallo", and answers that it excludes a nazir who is already desecrated (e.g., by being a leper). For the one who learns from "lehachallo", the word "lehachallo" implies two things: impurity until death and exclusion of the already desecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who derives the law from 'bemotam', what does he do with the word 'lehachallo'?
The Gemara answers that 'lehachallo' excludes a nazir who is already desecrated (e.g., a leper), and the plural form teaches two things: impurity until death and exclusion of the already desecrated.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about goses
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about goses
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a person does not transmit impurity until his soul departs, even if cut up or dying. The Gemara objects: for the one who learns from "lehachallo", this baraita says a goses does not transmit impurity! The answer: the baraita refers to impurity (tum'ah), but for desecration (chillul), a goses is already desecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that a person does not transmit impurity until his soul departs, even if cut up or dying, challenging the view that a goses is already desecrated.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: for impurity (טומאה), the baraita applies until death, but for desecration (חילול), a goses is already desecrated.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on a missing limb
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on a missing limb
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says in the name of Rav that if the father's head was severed, the nazir may not become impure for him, based on the verse requiring the father to be whole.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules in the name of Rav that if the father's head was severed, the nazir may not become impure for him, based on the verse requiring the father to be whole.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Chisda with a case where the father is killed by bandits, suggesting the nazir should still be obligated. Rav Chisda responds that this is a met mitzvah, and the Gemara clarifies that the father is considered without buriers since his son is traveling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Chisda with a hypothetical case where bandits decapitate the father, arguing that the nazir should still be obligated to become impure for him.
Rav Chisda responds that the father is a met mitzvah (a corpse with no one to bury it), and if one is obligated to bury any such corpse, certainly one is obligated for his own father.
The Gemara objects that the father is not a met mitzvah, citing a baraita that defines a met mitzvah as one who has no buriers, but here the son exists.
The Gemara resolves that since the son is traveling, he is considered as having no buriers, making the father a met mitzvah.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about limbs
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says a nazir may not become impure for a limb from his living father, but may gather a bone the size of a barley grain. The Gemara asks if this implies that if the father is missing even a small part, the nazir may become impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that limits impurity for a limb from a living father, implying that if the father is missing even a small part, the nazir may become impure.

items.text: Rejection: the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one may become impure for a limb from a dead father but not from a living one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection by asserting that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits impurity for a limb from a dead father but not from a living one.

items.text: Additional baraita and scriptural expansion
items.text_en: Additional baraita and scriptural expansion
items.desc_en: Another baraita from Rav Kahana bar Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov excludes certain impurities like an olive's bulk from a corpse, but the verse adds impurity for the spine, skull, and majority of the body's structure or count.

sub.text: Baraita of Rav Kahana bar Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rav Kahana bar Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita from Rav Kahana bar Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that a nazirite may become impure for his father's corpse but not for detached limbs, excluding an olive's bulk from a corpse, an olive's bulk of congealed corpse-liquid, and a full tarvad of decay.

The baraita then notes that one might think the nazirite is not impure for the spine, skull, or majority of the body's structure or count, but the verse 'וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵיהֶם' adds another impurity, teaching that these do convey impurity.

items.text: Continuation of the baraita on impurity to relatives
items.text_en: Continuation of the baraita on impurity to relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier baraita (about impurity to a spinal column and skull) follows Rabbi Yehuda's view. It then cites a story about Rabbi Yitzchak's father who died abroad, and the sages ruled that one may become impure only for a complete corpse, not a deficient one.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites a possible exclusion from impurity for a spinal column, skull, and majority of structure or count of others, then derives from the sister that one becomes impure for any relative whose body depends on him.
The Gemara identifies that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda's view, and notes that Rav aligns with a Tanna who cites a story about Rabbi Yitzchak's father dying abroad.
Rabbi Yitzchak asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Eliezer and four elders, who ruled that one may become impure for a father only when the corpse is complete, not when it is deficient.

items.text: Mishnah: Three prohibitions of a nazir and their stringencies
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three prohibitions of a nazir and their stringencies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the three prohibitions for a nazir: impurity, shaving, and grape products. It then compares them: impurity and shaving cancel the nazirite period, while grape products do not; grape products were never permitted in any context, while impurity and shaving were permitted for a mitzvah; impurity cancels everything and requires a sacrifice, while shaving only cancels thirty days and requires no sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the three prohibitions for a nazir (טומאה, תגלחת, and grape products) and states that impurity and shaving cancel the nazirite period, while grape products do not.

The Mishnah notes a stringency of grape products over impurity and shaving: grape products were never permitted in any context, while impurity and shaving were permitted for a mitzvah (תגלחת מצוה and מת מצוה).
The Mishnah concludes by stating that impurity is more stringent than shaving: impurity cancels everything and requires a sacrifice, while shaving only cancels thirty days and requires no sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara: Impurity permitted for a mitzvah via kal vachomer from wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Impurity permitted for a mitzvah via kal vachomer from wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should impurity not be permitted in any context? A kal vachomer from wine suggests that since wine (which does not cancel) was never permitted, impurity (which cancels) should certainly not be permitted. However, a verse teaches that impurity is permitted for a met mitzvah (a corpse with no one to bury it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a kal vachomer argument: since wine, which does not cancel the nazirite count, was never permitted in any context, impurity, which does cancel, should certainly never be permitted in any context.

The Gemara resolves the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'לְאָבִיו וּלְאִמּוֹ לֹא יִטַּמָּא' (to his father and mother he shall not become impure), which implies that he may become impure for a met mitzvah (a corpse with no one to bury it), thus permitting impurity in that specific context.

items.text: Gemara: Wine not permitted via kal vachomer from impurity
items.text_en: Gemara: Wine not permitted via kal vachomer from impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should wine be permitted in some contexts? A kal vachomer from impurity argues that since impurity (which cancels) was permitted for a mitzvah, wine (which does not cancel) should certainly be permitted. But a verse prohibits even mitzvah wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that wine should be permitted for a mitzvah, since impurity, which is more severe, was permitted.
The Gemara cites a verse to reject the kal vachomer, teaching that wine of a mitzvah is forbidden like ordinary wine.

items.text: Gemara: Wine does not cancel the entire nazirite period
items.text_en: Gemara: Wine does not cancel the entire nazirite period
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should wine cancel the entire nazirite period? A kal vachomer from impurity argues that since impurity (which was permitted for a mitzvah) cancels everything, wine (which was never permitted) should certainly cancel. But a verse limits cancellation to impurity alone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if impurity, which was permitted for a mitzvah, cancels everything, then wine, which was never permitted, should certainly cancel everything.
The verse limits cancellation to impurity alone, teaching that impurity cancels but wine does not.

items.text: Gemara: Shaving does not cancel the entire period
items.text_en: Gemara: Shaving does not cancel the entire period
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should shaving cancel the entire nazirite period? A kal vachomer from impurity argues that since impurity (where the one who impurifies is not treated like the impurified) cancels everything, shaving (where the one who shaves is treated like the one shaved) should certainly cancel. But a verse limits cancellation to impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) argument: if impurity, where the one who impurifies is not treated like the impurified, cancels everything, then shaving, where the one who shaves is treated like the one shaved, should certainly cancel everything.
The verse limits cancellation to impurity only, teaching that shaving does not cancel the entire nazirite period.

items.text: Gemara: Impurity treats the impurifier like the impurified
items.text_en: Gemara: Impurity treats the impurifier like the impurified
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should impurity treat the one who causes impurity like the one who becomes impure? A kal vachomer from shaving argues that since shaving (which only cancels thirty days) treats the shaver like the shaved, impurity (which cancels everything) should certainly do so. But a verse teaches that impurity applies only to the nazir himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) from shaving to argue that impurity should treat the one who causes impurity like the one who becomes impure.

The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'וְטִמֵּא רֹאשׁ נִזְרוֹ' (and he shall defile his consecrated head), which teaches that impurity applies only to the nazir himself, not to others.

items.text: Gemara: Shaving does not treat the shaver like the shaved
items.text_en: Gemara: Shaving does not treat the shaver like the shaved
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should shaving not treat the shaver like the shaved? A kal vachomer from impurity argues that since impurity (which cancels everything) does not treat the impurifier like the impurified, shaving (which only cancels thirty days) should certainly not. But a verse teaches that the nazir himself may not pass a razor, and also may not have another pass it over him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from impurity: since impurity, which cancels everything, does not treat the impurifier like the impurified, shaving, which only cancels thirty days, should certainly not treat the shaver like the shaved.
