The Gemara answers with a verse: 'תַּעַר לֹא יַעֲבוֹר עַל רֹאשׁוֹ' (a razor shall not pass over his head), which is interpreted to mean that the nazir himself may not pass a razor, and also may not have another pass it over him, thereby treating the shaver like the shaved.

items.text: Gemara: Shaving not permitted via kal vachomer from wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Shaving not permitted via kal vachomer from wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should shaving not be permitted in any context? A kal vachomer from wine argues that since wine (which does not cancel) was never permitted, shaving (which cancels) should certainly not be permitted. But the Merciful One permits shaving for a nazir's head and beard (for a mitzvah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks a kal vachomer: since wine, which does not cancel the nazirite period, was never permitted from its general prohibition, shaving, which does cancel, should certainly not be permitted from its general prohibition.
The Gemara resolves that the Merciful One explicitly permits shaving for a nazir's head and beard (for a mitzvah), overriding the kal vachomer.

items.text: Gemara: Shaving does not cancel at all via kal vachomer from wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Shaving does not cancel at all via kal vachomer from wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should shaving not cancel at all? A kal vachomer from wine argues that since wine (which was never permitted) does not cancel, shaving (which was permitted for a mitzvah) should certainly not cancel. But the Gemara answers that shaving requires hair growth, and here there is none (since the nazir shaved at the end of his term).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should shaving not cancel at all, via a kal vachomer from wine?
The Gemara answers: shaving requires hair growth, and here there is none (since the nazir shaved at the end of his term).

items.text: Gemara: Wine does not cancel thirty days via kal vachomer from shaving
items.text_en: Gemara: Wine does not cancel thirty days via kal vachomer from shaving
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should wine cancel thirty days? A kal vachomer from shaving argues that since shaving (which was permitted for a mitzvah) cancels, wine (which was never permitted) should certainly cancel. But the Gemara answers that the reason shaving cancels is due to hair growth, and regarding wine, his hair remains (so no cancellation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether wine should cancel thirty days of the nazirite term, using a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from shaving: since shaving, which was permitted for a mitzvah, cancels thirty days, wine, which was never permitted, should certainly cancel.
The Gemara answers that the reason shaving cancels is due to the need for hair growth, but regarding wine, his hair remains (so there is no cancellation).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the procedure for a nazirite's purification after impurity: sprinkling on the third and seventh days, shaving on the seventh, and bringing offerings on the eighth. Rabbi Akiva allows shaving on the eighth and bringing offerings that same day, while Rabbi Tarfon questions the difference between a nazirite and a leper. Rabbi Akiva explains that a nazirite's purification depends on days, while a leper's depends on shaving, and offerings require sunset.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the procedure for a nazirite's purification after impurity, presenting Rabbi Akiva's position that shaving on the eighth allows bringing offerings that same day.
Rabbi Tarfon questions the difference between a nazirite and a leper regarding the timing of offerings.
Rabbi Akiva explains that a nazirite's purification depends on days, while a leper's depends on shaving, and offerings require sunset.

items.text: Gemara's question: Did Rabbi Tarfon accept Rabbi Akiva's answer?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Did Rabbi Tarfon accept Rabbi Akiva's answer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Tarfon accepted Rabbi Akiva's reasoning. It cites a baraita from Hillel stating that if a nazirite shaved on the eighth day, he brings offerings on the ninth, implying that Rabbi Tarfon did not accept Rabbi Akiva's view, since otherwise offerings could be brought on the eighth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Tarfon accepted Rabbi Akiva's answer, and cites a baraita from Hillel stating that if a nazirite shaved on the eighth day, he brings offerings on the ninth, implying that Rabbi Tarfon did not accept Rabbi Akiva's view, since otherwise offerings could be brought on the eighth.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Distinction based on immersion
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Distinction based on immersion
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two cases: if the nazirite immersed on the seventh day, he may bring offerings on the eighth; if he did not immerse on the seventh, he must wait until the ninth.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction: the baraita refers to a case where he did not immerse on the seventh day, while Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies when he did immerse on the seventh.

items.text: Abaye's teaching: The requirement of sunset for a zav
items.text_en: Abaye's teaching: The requirement of sunset for a zav
items.desc_en: Abaye reports that he found colleagues discussing a verse about a zav bringing an offering only after immersion and sunset, indicating that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) is still considered impure like the zav himself.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reports that he found Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya's colleagues citing a verse to prove that a זב (zav) may only bring his offering after immersion and sunset, implying that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) is still impure.
Abaye concludes that the colleagues hold that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) of a זב (zav) is considered like the זב himself, still impure.

items.text: Abaye's inference: Same rule applies to a nazirite
items.text_en: Abaye's inference: Same rule applies to a nazirite
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the same principle applies to a nazirite who became impure: he may only bring his offering after immersion and sunset, as indicated by the verse about bringing offerings to the Tent of Meeting.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to the colleagues: the same verse applies to a nazirite who became impure, requiring immersion and sunset before bringing offerings, which would contradict Rabbi Akiva's leniency.

items.text: Location of Nicanor's gates and exclusion of those lacking atonement
items.text_en: Location of Nicanor's gates and exclusion of those lacking atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Nicanor's gates stand in the Levite camp, but cites a baraita allowing a corpse to enter that camp. Abaye resolves this by explaining that a zav's tevul yom is like a zav, yet still excluded because lacking atonement. The Gemara then deduces that the Levite camp also excludes those lacking atonement, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Nicanor's gates stand, and answers that they stand in the Levite camp.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that a corpse-impure person may enter the Levite camp, even a corpse itself, as Moses brought Joseph's bones with him.
Abaye resolves that a zav's tevul yom is like a zav, yet because he lacks atonement (מחוסר כפרה), he does not enter.

The Gemara questions why the verse calls it 'Ohel Moed' if it stands in the Levite camp, and deduces that just as there one lacking atonement does not enter, so too in the Levite camp one lacking atonement does not enter.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'טָמֵא יִהְיֶה' to include a tevul yom, and 'עוֹד טוּמְאָתוֹ בּוֹ' to include one lacking atonement.

items.text: Mishnah: The nazirite's purification shaving
items.text_en: Mishnah: The nazirite's purification shaving
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the nazirite's purification shaving: he brings three animals (sin-offering, burnt-offering, peace-offering) and shaves after slaughtering the peace-offering (Rabbi Yehuda) or the sin-offering (Rabbi Elazar). Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel adds that if he brought three unspecified animals, each is offered according to its fitness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure of the purification shaving: the nazir brings three animals and slaughters the peace-offering and shaves upon them, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Elazar says he only shaves upon the sin-offering, because the sin-offering always precedes, but if he shaved upon any of the three, he fulfills his obligation.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if he brought three animals without specifying, each is offered according to its fitness.

items.text: Gemara: The verse 'at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the peace-offering
items.text_en: Gemara: The verse 'at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the peace-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the verse 'the nazirite shall shave at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the peace-offering, as it says 'and he shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting'. It then rejects the possibility that it means the literal entrance, as that would be disrespectful.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the verse 'the nazirite shall shave at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the peace-offering, as it says 'and he shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting'.
The Gemara raises the possibility that the verse might be interpreted literally as the entrance of the Tent of Meeting itself.
The Gemara rejects the literal interpretation, arguing that shaving at the actual entrance would be disrespectful (דרך בזיון).

items.text: Rabbi Yoshiya's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiya's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya argues that the verse is unnecessary: since the Torah says 'do not ascend by steps to My altar', a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument prohibits shaving at the literal entrance, which would be disrespectful.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya argues that the verse is unnecessary because a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from the prohibition of ascending the altar by steps teaches that shaving at the literal entrance would be disrespectful.

items.text: Alternate version of Rabbi Yoshiya's statement
items.text_en: Alternate version of Rabbi Yoshiya's statement
items.desc_en: A variant text (from a midrash) presents Rabbi Yoshiya's argument: the verse speaks of peace-offerings, not the literal entrance, because a kal vachomer from the prohibition of ascending steps teaches that shaving at the literal entrance would be disrespectful.

sub.desc_en: A midrashic variant presents Rabbi Yoshiya's argument that the verse 'וְגִלַּח הַנָּזִיר פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' speaks of peace-offerings, not the literal entrance, because a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the prohibition of ascending steps teaches that shaving at the literal entrance would be disrespectful.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's argument from the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's argument from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak argues that the verse 'and he shall take the hair of his nazirite head and place it on the fire' indicates that the shaving must be at a place requiring only taking and placing, excluding the literal entrance which would require taking, bringing, and placing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak argues that the verse 'וְלָקַח אֶת שְׂעַר רֹאשׁ נִזְרוֹ וְנָתַן עַל הָאֵשׁ' indicates the shaving must be at a place requiring only taking and placing, excluding the literal entrance which would require taking, bringing, and placing.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
items.desc_en: Some say Rabbi Yitzchak explicitly states that the verse speaks of peace-offerings, not the literal entrance, because the verse 'and he shall take the hair of his nazirite head' implies the place where he cooks (the peace-offering) is where he shaves.

sub.text: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rabbi Yitzchak explicitly states the verse speaks of peace-offerings, not the literal entrance, because the verse 'and he shall take the hair of his nazirite head' implies the place where he cooks (the peace-offering) is where he shaves.

items.text: Abba Chanan and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on the timing and location of shaving
items.text_en: Abba Chanan and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on the timing and location of shaving
items.desc_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer says the nazirite shaves only when the entrance of the Tent of Meeting is open. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds that the verse 'and the nazirite shall shave at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the shaving of the nazirite, not the nazirah (female nazirite).

sub.text: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Abba Chanan states in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that the nazirite shaves only when the entrance of the Tent of Meeting is open.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds that the verse 'and the nazirite shall shave at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' refers to the shaving of the nazirite, not the nazirah (female nazirite).

items.text: Opening dispute about suspicion of priestly impropriety
items.text_en: Opening dispute about suspicion of priestly impropriety
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that young priests might become aroused by the nazirite woman. The response counters that the sotah (suspected adulteress) is also brought before the Lord without such concern, and the distinction is that the nazirite woman is adorned with makeup.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that young priests might become aroused by the nazirite woman.
The interlocutor counters that the sotah (suspected adulteress) is also brought before the Lord without such concern.
The Gemara distinguishes that the nazirite woman is adorned with makeup, unlike the sotah.

items.text: Mishnah: Disposal of nazirite's hair
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disposal of nazirite's hair
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the nazirite takes the hair of his naziriteship and places it under the cooking pot. If he shaved in the provinces, he does not place it under the pot. This applies only to the purification shaving, not the impurity shaving. Rabbi Meir says everyone places it under the pot except the impure person who shaved in the provinces.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: the nazirite takes his hair and places it under the cooking pot, but if he shaved in the provinces, he does not place it under the pot.
The Mishnah clarifies that this rule applies only to the purification shaving, not the impurity shaving.
Rabbi Meir says everyone places the hair under the pot except the impure person who shaved in the provinces.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the hair placement law
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the hair placement law
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the nazirite takes the hair and places it under the pot of the peace-offering. If he placed it under the pot of a sin-offering or guilt-offering, it is valid. Rava clarifies that for a pure nazirite there is no guilt-offering, so the baraita refers to an impure nazirite placing hair under the guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the nazirite takes the hair and places it under the pot of the peace-offering, and if placed under the sin-offering or guilt-offering it is valid.
The Gemara questions how a guilt-offering applies to a pure nazirite, since a pure nazirite does not bring a guilt-offering.
Rava resolves that the baraita refers to an impure nazirite who places the hair under the guilt-offering pot, and it is valid.

items.text: Scriptural source and inclusion of other offerings
items.text_en: Scriptural source and inclusion of other offerings
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse 'which is under the peace-offering' that the hair must be under the offering. The Gemara then explains that the word 'zebach' (sacrifice) includes sin-offering and guilt-offering. It rejects the possibility that the entire verse refers only to sin-offering and guilt-offering, concluding that the verse teaches both the primary law and the inclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that the hair must be placed under the pot.
Rava cites the verse 'which is under the peace-offering' to derive that the hair must be under the offering.
The Gemara explains that the word 'זֶבַח' (sacrifice) in the verse includes sin-offering and guilt-offering, and rejects the possibility that it only refers to the broth.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the entire verse refers only to sin-offering and guilt-offering.
The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches both the primary law and the inclusion, since it says 'זֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים' (sacrifice of peace-offering) rather than 'peace-offering and sacrifice'.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute about who sends hair under the pot
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute about who sends hair under the pot
items.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Meir says everyone sends hair except the impure who shaved in the provinces (since his hair is buried). Rabbi Yehuda says pure nazirites always send, impure never send. The Sages say no one sends except the pure nazirite in the Temple, because his act fulfills the commandment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's position: everyone sends hair under the pot except the impure person who shaved in the provinces.
Rabbi Yehuda states that pure nazirites always send hair, while impure ones never send.
The Sages rule that no one sends hair except the pure nazirite in the Temple, because his act fulfills the commandment (מצוה).

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for the nazirite's final offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for the nazirite's final offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that the nazirite cooks or boils the peace-offering. The priest takes the cooked shoulder from the ram, one matzah cake from the basket, and one wafer, places them on the nazirite's hands, waves them, and then the nazirite is permitted to drink wine and become impure from the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the procedure for the nazirite's final offerings: the priest takes the cooked shoulder, matzah, and wafer, places them on the nazirite's hands, waves them, and then the nazirite is permitted to drink wine and become impure from the dead.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that once one of the bloods is sprinkled on the nazirite, he is permitted to drink wine and become impure from the dead.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon rules that once one of the bloods is sprinkled on the nazirite, he is permitted to drink wine and become impure from the dead.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says the nazirite may drink only after all acts (slaughter, sprinkling, shaving, etc.), while the Sages say after a single act. The Gemara explains the Sages' reasoning via a gezerah shavah from shaving, and then questions why the gezerah shavah is needed if both acts might be required.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְאַחַר יִשְׁתֶּה הַנָּזִיר יַיִן' and presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer requires all acts (slaughter, sprinkling, shaving, etc.) before the nazirite may drink, while the Sages require only a single act.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' reasoning: a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse about shaving (אַחַר הִתְגַּלְּחוֹ אֶת נִזְרוֹ) teaches that 'אַחַר' there means after a single act, so here too it means after a single act.
The Gemara objects: why not say both acts (slaughter and shaving) are required? If so, what is the purpose of the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy)?

items.text: Rav's statement about tenufah and its justification
items.text_en: Rav's statement about tenufah and its justification
items.desc_en: Rav says that the waving (tenufah) delays the nazirite's permission. The Gemara questions whether this applies to the Sages (who don't require shaving) or to Rabbi Eliezer (who requires all acts), and concludes that it is necessary for Rabbi Eliezer to teach that tenufah is not merely a leftover mitzvah but a delaying factor.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the waving (תנופה) of the nazirite's offering delays his permission to drink wine.
The Gemara asks according to which authority Rav's statement applies.
The Gemara objects that if Rav's statement is according to the Sages, who already hold that shaving does not delay, it is obvious that waving does not delay either.
The Gemara objects that if Rav's statement is according to Rabbi Eliezer, it is also obvious since Rabbi Eliezer requires all acts after the offerings.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement is necessary to teach that even though waving is a leftover mitzvah (שיירי מצוה) regarding atonement, it still delays the nazirite's permission.

items.text: First version: Rav's statement that waving is indispensable, challenged by a baraita
items.text_en: First version: Rav's statement that waving is indispensable, challenged by a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav states that waving (תנופה) is indispensable for a nazirite. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita that says 'This is the law of the nazirite' applies whether he has hands (for waving) or not, implying waving is not indispensable. The Gemara then compares this to a baraita about a bald nazir, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether he needs to pass a razor over his head. Ravina explains that Beit Shammai says he has no remedy, while Beit Hillel says he does. This is linked to Rabbi Pedat's statement that Beit Shammai and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing, illustrated by Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on a leper missing a thumb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's statement that waving is indispensable by citing a baraita that says 'This is the law of the nazirite' applies whether he has hands or not, implying waving is not indispensable.

The Gemara objects that if waving is not indispensable, then the baraita about a bald nazirite would also imply that shaving is not indispensable, but Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a bald nazirite needs to pass a razor over his head.
Ravina explains that Beit Shammai's statement 'does not need' means he has no remedy, implying that Beit Hillel holds he does have a remedy, so the baraita does not prove that shaving is dispensable.
Rabbi Pedat states that Beit Shammai and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing, linking the dispute to a similar principle.
A baraita illustrates Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: a leper missing a thumb has no purification, while Rabbi Shimon and the Sages offer alternative remedies.

items.text: Second version: Rav's statement reinterpreted, with a different resolution
items.text_en: Second version: Rav's statement reinterpreted, with a different resolution
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav said waving is indispensable. The Gemara questions whether this is according to Rabbi Eliezer (obvious) or the Rabbis (who might not require shaving, so waving is even less likely). The Gemara then challenges from the baraita about hands and hair, and resolves by reinterpreting Beit Hillel's 'needs' as meaning he needs but has no remedy, while Beit Shammai has a remedy, contradicting Rabbi Pedat.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav said waving (תנופה) in the nazirite process is indispensable (מעכבת).

The Gemara questions whether Rav's statement aligns with Rabbi Eliezer (obvious, since he requires all acts) or with the Rabbis, who do not even require shaving (תגלחת), so waving would certainly not be indispensable.

The Gemara challenges from a baraita that says 'זאת תורת הנזיר' applies whether he has hands (כפיים) or not, implying waving is not indispensable; it then asks whether the same would apply to hair, suggesting a contradiction.
A baraita is cited about a bald nazirite (נזיר ממורט): Beit Shammai say he does not need to pass a razor over his head, while Beit Hillel say he does.
Rabbi Avina explains that Beit Hillel's 'needs' means he needs but has no remedy (אין לו תקנה), while Beit Shammai has a remedy, contradicting Rabbi Pedat's earlier statement.

items.text: Mishnah: Shaving on a disqualified or improper sacrifice
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shaving on a disqualified or improper sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a nazirite shaved on a sacrifice that was later found invalid, or on a sin-offering not offered for its own sake, his shaving is invalid and his sacrifices do not count. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: only that sacrifice does not count, but others do. If he shaved on all three and one was valid, his shaving is valid and he brings the remaining sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a nazirite shaved on a sacrifice that was later found invalid, his shaving is invalid and his sacrifices do not count.
The Mishnah adds that shaving on a sin-offering not offered for its own sake also invalidates the shaving and the sacrifices.
The Mishnah further rules that shaving on a burnt-offering or peace-offering not offered for its own sake likewise invalidates the shaving and the sacrifices.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: only that invalid sacrifice does not count, but the other sacrifices do count.
The Mishnah concludes that if he shaved on all three and one was valid, his shaving is valid and he brings the remaining sacrifices.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that a nazirite who shaves on a free-will peace-offering is exempt
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that a nazirite who shaves on a free-will peace-offering is exempt
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that a nazirite who shaved on a free-will peace-offering (not his own) has fulfilled his obligation, because the verse says 'on the fire under the peace-offering' without specifying 'his peace-offering'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava introduces the inference that Rabbi Shimon holds a nazirite who shaved on a free-will peace-offering has fulfilled his obligation.
Rav Adda bar Ahava states the conclusion: a nazirite who shaved on a free-will peace-offering is exempt.
Rav Adda bar Ahava provides the scriptural basis: the verse says 'on the fire under the peace-offering' without specifying 'his peace-offering', implying any peace-offering suffices.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a nazirite who had one blood sprinkled and then became impure must restart all his days, while the Sages say he brings the remaining offerings and becomes pure. They cite a case of Miriam the Tarmodite to support their view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a nazirite who had one blood sprinkled and then became impure must restart all his days, while the Sages say he brings the remaining offerings and becomes pure.

The Sages cite the case of Miriam the Tarmodite, who had one blood sprinkled, was informed her daughter was dangerously ill, went and found her dead, and the Sages ruled she brings the remaining offerings and becomes pure.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Eliezer's ruling, noting he elsewhere says that after the completion of seven days one does not restart. Rav explains that Rabbi Eliezer means he restarts his offerings, not his days. The Gemara supports this from the Sages' response and the case of Miriam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer says 'negates everything' here, when elsewhere he says that after seven days one only negates seven days.
Rav explains that Rabbi Eliezer's 'negates' refers to negating the offerings, not the days of naziriteship.
The Gemara supports this interpretation from the Sages' response that she brings the rest of her offerings, implying the dispute is only about offerings.
The Gemara further supports this from the incident of Miriam of Tarmod, where the Sages ruled she brings the rest of her offerings.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: A brief formulaic statement marking the end of the chapter 'Three Types'.

sub.desc_en: The Stam (anonymous voice) concludes the chapter with the formulaic phrase 'הדרן עלך שלשה מינין' (We return to you, Three Types).

items.text: Mishnah on High Priest and nazirite with met mitzvah
items.text_en: Mishnah on High Priest and nazirite with met mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a High Priest and a nazirite may not become impure for relatives but may for a met mitzvah. If they encounter a met mitzvah, Rabbi Eliezer says the High Priest should become impure, not the nazirite; the Sages say the nazirite should become impure, not the common priest. Each side gives a reason.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a High Priest and a nazirite may not become impure for relatives but may for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse).
Rabbi Eliezer rules that the High Priest should become impure, not the nazirite.
The Sages rule that the nazirite should become impure, not the common priest.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the priest should become impure because he does not bring a sacrifice for his impurity, unlike the nazirite who does.
The Sages argue that the nazirite should become impure because his sanctity is temporary, while the priest's sanctity is permanent.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is about which status is greater: the High Priest or the nazirite. Each side prioritizes the other's impurity based on their view of relative sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: one side considers the High Priest more important, the other considers the nazirite more important.

items.text: Transition to next topic
items.text_en: Transition to next topic
items.desc_en: A brief phrase introducing the next topic: 'Anointed with the anointing oil'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins the next Mishnah with the topic of the priest anointed with the anointing oil.

items.text: Comparison of anointed vs. many-garmented and temporary vs. permanent disqualifications
items.text_en: Comparison of anointed vs. many-garmented and temporary vs. permanent disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the precedence of a High Priest anointed with the anointing oil over one with many garments, and a many-garmented one over a former anointed one. It then compares a priest disqualified due to baldness (temporary) over one disqualified due to a permanent blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a High Priest anointed with the anointing oil (משוח בשמן המשחה) takes precedence over one with many garments (מרובה בגדים), because the anointed one brings the bull for all commandments (פר הבא על כל המצות) while the many-garmented one does not.

The Gemara shifts to compare a former anointed High Priest (משוח שעבר) with a many-garmented one, ruling that the many-garmented one takes precedence because he can perform the service (עבודה) while the former anointed one cannot.

The Gemara shifts to compare a priest disqualified due to baldness (עבר מחמת קירויו) with one disqualified due to a permanent blemish (עבר מחמת מומו), ruling that the bald one takes precedence because he may serve tomorrow (חזי לעבודה למחר) while the blemished one never will.

items.text: Question: War anointed vs. deputy – which is superior?
items.text_en: Question: War anointed vs. deputy – which is superior?
items.desc_en: A question is raised: between the priest anointed for war and the deputy (Segan), which is superior? The war anointed is fit for war, while the deputy is fit for service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: between the priest anointed for war (משוח מלחמה) and the deputy (סגן), which is superior — the war anointed because he is fit for war, or the deputy because he is fit for service?

items.text: Resolution: War anointed precedes in saving life, deputy in impurity
items.text_en: Resolution: War anointed precedes in saving life, deputy in impurity
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited showing that the war anointed becomes impure for a met mitzvah before the deputy, but another baraita says the war anointed precedes. Mar Zutra resolves: for saving life (due to public reliance) the war anointed is superior; for impurity the deputy is superior, as the deputy is designated to replace the High Priest if disqualified.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the only difference between the war anointed and the deputy is that the war anointed becomes impure for a met mitzvah before the deputy.
The gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita that says the war anointed precedes the deputy.
Mar Zutra resolves: for saving life, the war anointed is superior because the public relies on him.
Mar Zutra continues: for impurity, the deputy is superior, as he is designated to replace the High Priest if disqualified, citing Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos.

items.text: High Priest and Nazir: both may become impure for a met mitzvah
items.text_en: High Priest and Nazir: both may become impure for a met mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous dispute only applies when a High Priest and a Nazir walk together; individually, each may become impure for a met mitzvah. A baraita derives from the verse that a High Priest may become impure for a met mitzvah, as the verse speaks of relatives, not a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the earlier dispute about who becomes impure applies only when a High Priest and a Nazir walk together, but individually each may become impure for a met mitzvah.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a High Priest may become impure for a met mitzvah.

The baraita derives from the verse 'עַל כׇּל נַפְשׁוֹת מֵת לֹא יָבֹא' that the prohibition for a High Priest applies only to relatives, not to a met mitzvah, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from an ordinary priest.
The baraita concludes that the verse restricts impurity only for his father (a relative), implying that for a met mitzvah he does become impure.

items.text: Gezeirah Shavah for High Priest from Nazirite
items.text_en: Gezeirah Shavah for High Priest from Nazirite
items.desc_en: Rabbi's teaching that a nazirite may become impure for negaim and zivah but not for death is applied to a High Priest via a gezeirah shavah on the word "imo" (his mother). The Gemara explains that the verse "imo" for the High Priest is superfluous and thus available for this analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) based on Rabbi's teaching, asking how we know the High Priest may become impure for negaim and zivah but not for death.
The Gemara argues that the word 'אִמּוֹ' (his mother) for the High Priest is superfluous, as a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) already proves he cannot become impure for his mother.

The Gemara resolves that the superfluous 'אִמּוֹ' is available for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with the nazirite, teaching that the High Priest may become impure for negaim and zivah but not for death.

items.text: Source for Nazirite's Impurity from Death
items.text_en: Source for Nazirite's Impurity from Death
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the nazirite's impurity from a human corpse. A baraita teaches that the verse "al nefesh met lo yavo" excludes animal carcasses, and Rabbi Yishmael adds that it refers only to impurities that come through entering (i.e., human corpses).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found the source for the High Priest, but from where do we derive the nazirite's impurity from a corpse?
A baraita is cited: the verse 'עַל נֶפֶשׁ מֵת לֹא יָבֹא' excludes animal carcasses, and Rabbi Yishmael adds that it refers only to impurities that come through entering (human corpses).

items.text: Nazirite May Become Impure for Met Mitzvah
items.text_en: Nazirite May Become Impure for Met Mitzvah
items.desc_en: The verse "le'aviv ule'imo" teaches that a nazirite may become impure for a met mitzvah (abandoned corpse). A kal vachomer from the High Priest is refuted because the nazirite brings a sacrifice for impurity, but the verse overrides this to permit impurity for a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse excludes a nazirite from impurity for parents but permits impurity for a met mitzvah (abandoned corpse).

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if the High Priest, whose sanctity is permanent, becomes impure for a met mitzvah, then a nazirite, whose sanctity is temporary, should certainly become impure for a met mitzvah.

The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer: the High Priest does not bring a sacrifice for his impurity, but a nazirite does, so the argument fails; the verse nonetheless overrides this to permit impurity for a met mitzvah.

items.text: Nazirite May Not Become Impure for Other Corpses
items.text_en: Nazirite May Not Become Impure for Other Corpses
items.desc_en: An alternative interpretation that the nazirite may become impure for other relatives is rejected by a kal vachomer from a common priest: since a common priest may not become impure for non-relatives, a nazirite certainly may not.

sub.desc_en: An alternative reading proposes that the nazirite may not become impure for his parents but may become impure for other corpses.

The gemara rejects the alternative with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a common priest, who may become impure for relatives, may not become impure for other corpses, then a nazirite, who may not become impure for relatives, certainly may not become impure for other corpses.

items.text: Initial derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Initial derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by asking what the Torah teaches by specifying 'to his father and to his mother' in the context of a nazir, concluding that it implies he may become impure for a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Torah teaches by specifying 'to his father and to his mother' regarding a nazir, concluding that it implies he may become impure for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse).

items.text: Analogy to the high priest and regular priest
items.text_en: Analogy to the high priest and regular priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes two possible analogies: first, comparing the nazir to the high priest (who may not become impure for his father but may for a met mitzvah), and second, comparing him to a regular priest (who may become impure for his father). The verse is needed to reject the second analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an a fortiori analogy: just as the high priest may not become impure for his father but may for a met mitzvah (abandoned corpse), so too the nazir may not become impure for his father but may for a met mitzvah.
The Gemara offers an alternative analogy: just as a regular priest may become impure for his father, so too the nazir might be permitted to become impure for his father, which the verse must reject.

items.text: Refutation and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Refutation and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the previous derivation, arguing that the verse 'to his father and to his mother' is needed to teach that he may not become impure for them, not to permit impurity for a met mitzvah. It then reinterprets the verse: 'to his father' teaches the prohibition, 'to his brother' implies permission for a met mitzvah, and 'to his mother' is for a gezeirah shavah as per Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'to his father and to his mother' is needed to teach that he may not become impure for them, not to permit impurity for a met mitzvah.
The Gemara reinterprets the verse: 'to his father' teaches the prohibition, 'to his brother' implies permission for a met mitzvah, and 'to his mother' is for a gezeirah shavah as per Rabbi.

items.text: Derivation from 'to his sister'
items.text_en: Derivation from 'to his sister'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the phrase 'to his sister' that a nazir who is on his way to perform a positive commandment (slaughtering his Paschal lamb or circumcising his son) may not become impure for a relative, but may become impure for a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that asks what the verse 'to his sister' teaches regarding a nazir's impurity for a met mitzvah.

The baraita presents a case: a nazir on his way to perform a positive commandment (slaughtering his Paschal lamb or circumcising his son) hears of a relative's death — can he become impure? The answer is no, based on the verse 'he shall not become impure'.

The baraita resolves that one might think he cannot become impure even for a met mitzvah, but the verse 'to his sister' teaches that only for his sister he does not become impure, but for a met mitzvah he does become impure.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse differently: 'souls' refers to distant relatives, 'dead' to close relatives, and 'to his father and to his mother' teaches that he may not become impure for them but may for a met mitzvah. He also derives from 'to his brother' that a nazir who is also a high priest may not become impure for his brother but may for a met mitzvah, and 'to his sister' is as per the baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse: 'souls' refers to distant relatives, 'dead' to close relatives, and 'to his father and to his mother' teaches that a nazir may not become impure for them but may for a met mitzvah.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's derivation from 'to his brother'
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's derivation from 'to his brother'
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from 'to his brother' that a nazir who is also a high priest may not become impure for his brother but may for a met mitzvah.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's reference to the baraita on 'to his sister'
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's reference to the baraita on 'to his sister'
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva references the baraita regarding 'to his sister' that teaches a nazir may become impure for a met mitzvah even when going to perform a מצוה (commandment) punishable by כרת (excision).

items.text: Comparison between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Comparison between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Akiva derives the gezeirah shavah of Rabbi, and explains that since the master taught that a nazir who is also a high priest may not become impure for his brother but may for a met mitzvah, the same applies to a high priest alone. For Rabbi Yishmael, the derivation for a nazir who is also a high priest comes from the fact that the Torah permits one negative commandment for a met mitzvah, so two are also permitted. The verse 'to his sister' is needed to teach that even for positive commandments with karet, one may become impure for a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva derives the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of Rabbi (from the verse 'ולאמו') for a nazir who is also a high priest.

The Gemara answers that since the master taught that a nazir who is also a high priest may not become impure for his brother but may for a met mitzvah, the same applies to a high priest alone, so the גזירה שוה is unnecessary.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yishmael derives the law for a high priest who is also a nazir.
The Gemara answers that since the Torah permits one negative commandment for a met mitzvah, two negative commandments are also permitted.
The Gemara asks why the verse 'לאחותו' is needed for Rabbi Yishmael.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'לאחותו' teaches that even for positive commandments with כרת (karet), such as circumcision and the Paschal lamb, one may become impure for a met mitzvah.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's superfluous verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's superfluous verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since for Rabbi Akiva there is no distinction between a high priest alone and a high priest who is also a nazirite (both are forbidden to defile themselves), the prohibition for relatives is derived from 'to his brother'. Why then is the phrase 'to his father and to his mother' needed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since for Rabbi Akiva there is no distinction between a high priest alone and a high priest who is also a nazirite (both are forbidden to defile themselves), the prohibition for relatives is derived from 'to his brother'. Why then is the phrase 'to his father and to his mother' needed?

The Gemara answers: both terms are necessary; if only 'his father' were written, one might think the reason he does not defile himself is merely a presumption (חזקה) that the father is not his biological father, but for his mother, who is known to have given birth to him, he would be permitted to defile himself.

Conversely, if only 'his mother' were written, one might think the reason is that his lineage does not follow the mother, but for his father, since the verse says 'to their families, to their fathers' house', he would be permitted to defile himself; therefore both terms are needed.
The Gemara asks: why is the additional verse 'and for any dead person he shall not come' needed?

items.text: Gemara's answer: both verses are necessary
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: both verses are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both 'father' and 'mother' are needed. If only 'father' were written, one might think the prohibition is only because paternity is uncertain, but for the mother, who is known, he would be permitted. If only 'mother' were written, one might think the prohibition is because lineage does not follow the mother, but for the father, whose lineage is traced, he would be permitted. Therefore both are stated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: if only 'father' were written, one might think the prohibition applies only because paternity is uncertain, but for the mother, who is known, he would be permitted to become impure for her.

The Gemara continues: if only 'mother' were written, one might think the prohibition is because lineage does not follow the mother, but for the father, whose lineage is traced, he would be permitted — therefore both verses are stated.

items.text: Gemara's question on another verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question on another verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the purpose of the verse 'and over any dead person he shall not come'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'and over any dead person he shall not come' is needed, given that the previous verses already prohibit a nazirite from becoming impure.

items.text: Opening baraita on the verse
items.text_en: Opening baraita on the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the phrase "upon any dead souls" (על כל נפשות מת) to exclude distant relatives, close relatives, and a quarter-log of blood from two corpses, which imparts impurity in a tent.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'עַל כׇּל נַפְשׁוֹת מֵת' (upon any dead souls) to exclude distant relatives, close relatives, and a quarter-log of blood from two corpses from the impurity that imparts impurity in a tent.

items.text: Mishnah: List of impurities for which the nazirite shaves
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of impurities for which the nazirite shaves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the specific sources of corpse impurity (e.g., an olive's bulk of flesh, a ladleful of rot, a spine, a skull, a limb with sufficient flesh, half a kav of bones, half a log of blood) that require the nazirite to shave, bring offerings, and restart his count.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the specific corpse impurities (e.g., an olive's bulk of flesh, a ladleful of rot, a spine, a skull, a limb with sufficient flesh, half a kav of bones, half a log of blood) that require the nazirite to shave.
The Mishnah adds that the nazirite also shaves for contact, carrying, or overshadowing these impurities, and for a barley-grain-sized bone by contact or carrying.

The Mishnah concludes that for these impurities the nazirite shaves, sprinkles on the third and seventh days, cancels previous days, and only begins counting again after purification and bringing offerings.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that after Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda warned his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students enter, as they are contentious. Sumchus entered and reported Rabbi Meir's teaching that the nazirite shaves for an olive's bulk of a corpse, not for a whole corpse. Rabbi Yehuda rebuked him, arguing that if one shaves for an olive's bulk, certainly one shaves for a whole corpse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that after Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda warned his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students enter, as they are contentious and come to challenge him in halachic arguments.
Sumchus forced his way in and reported Rabbi Meir's teaching that the nazirite shaves for a corpse and for an olive's bulk from a corpse.
Rabbi Yehuda rebuked Sumchus, arguing that if one shaves for an olive's bulk from a corpse, certainly one shaves for a whole corpse, so the teaching is redundant and contentious.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's initial statement and the problem of a corpse without an olive's bulk of flesh
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's initial statement and the problem of a corpse without an olive's bulk of flesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei argues that if Rabbi Meir's view is accepted, people will say Meir slept, Judah was angry, and Yosei was silent—what will become of Torah? He then clarifies that his ruling was only needed for a corpse that does not have an olive's bulk of flesh. But one could still argue: if one shaves for a limb from it, all the more so for the entire corpse?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens with a rhetorical warning: if Rabbi Meir's view is accepted, people will say Meir slept, Judah was angry, and Yosei was silent—what will become of Torah?
Rabbi Yosei clarifies that his ruling was only needed for a corpse that does not have an olive's bulk of flesh.
The Gemara objects: if one shaves for a limb from it, all the more so for the entire corpse?

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Yochanan's principle of a fetus whose limbs are not connected by sinews
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Yochanan's principle of a fetus whose limbs are not connected by sinews
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by applying Rabbi Yochanan's statement: the ruling was only needed for a fetus whose limbs were not yet connected by sinews. Here too, it refers to such a fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by applying Rabbi Yochanan's principle: the ruling was only needed for a fetus whose limbs were not yet connected by sinews, and here too it refers to such a fetus.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: majority of the structure and majority of the count
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: majority of the structure and majority of the count
items.desc_en: Rava says the ruling was only needed for a case where there is a majority of the structure and a majority of the count, but without a quarter-log of bones.

sub.desc_en: Rava provides an alternative explanation: the ruling was only necessary for a case where there is a majority of the structure and a majority of the count, but without a quarter-log of bones.

items.text: Definition of נצל (congealed flesh)
items.text_en: Definition of נצל (congealed flesh)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists an olive's bulk of a corpse and an olive's bulk of נצל. The Gemara defines נצל as the flesh of a corpse that has congealed, or the liquid that has boiled (i.e., exuded).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists an olive's bulk of a corpse and an olive's bulk of נצל (congealed flesh), and the Gemara defines נצל as the flesh of a corpse that has congealed, or the liquid that has boiled (i.e., exuded).

items.text: Gemara's question on the definition of נצל
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the definition of נצל
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If we do not know it is from the corpse, what difference does congealing make? If we know it is from the corpse, even without congealing it should be impure!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if we do not know the liquid is from the corpse, congealing proves nothing; if we know it is from the corpse, even without congealing it should be impure — so what is the case of נצל (congealed corpse fluid)?

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: in an ambiguous case
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: in an ambiguous case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya answers: it refers to an ambiguous case. If it congealed, it is considered נצל; if not, it might be spittle or mucus.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya answers: the case is an ambiguous liquid (סתם) — if it congealed it is considered corpse fluid (נצל), if not it is likely spittle or mucus.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry: does נצל apply to animal carcasses?
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry: does נצל apply to animal carcasses?
items.desc_en: Abaye asked Rabbah: is there a concept of נצל for an animal carcass? Do we say that the tradition of נצל applies only to human corpses, but not to animals? Or is it no different?

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah: does the concept of נצל (congealed corpse fluid) apply to animal carcasses, or only to human corpses?

items.text: Discussion of impurity levels and a proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Discussion of impurity levels and a proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the dispute about whether severe impurity extends to a dog or to a convert, and then brings a baraita: if one heated (congealed) it by fire it is impure, by the sun it is pure. The Gemara initially objects, then resolves that the baraita refers to after it decomposed in the sun, becoming dust.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute about whether severe impurity extends to a convert or to a dog works well for the opinion that severe impurity extends to a convert and light impurity to a dog.
The Gemara objects: for the opinion that severe impurity extends to a dog, what can be said?
The Gemara brings a baraita: if one heated (congealed) it by fire it is impure, by the sun it is pure.
The Gemara objects: if you think severe impurity extends to a dog, even heating by the sun should make it impure.
The Gemara resolves: when does he heat it? After it decomposed in the sun, and once it decomposed it becomes dust, so it is no longer subject to impurity.

items.text: Mishnah citation: all that is poured is pure except for certain honey
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: all that is poured is pure except for certain honey
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: all that is poured (from one vessel to another) is pure, except for Ziphian honey and צפיחית (a type of honeycomb).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that all poured liquid is pure except for Ziphian honey and צפיחית (a type of honeycomb).

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai rule that a pot of ground beans or fava beans is considered connected because the mixture congeals backwards.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai rule that a pot of ground beans or fava beans is considered connected because the mixture congeals backwards.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about nitzok for foods
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about nitzok for foods
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the principle of nitzok (connected flow) applies to foods, questioning if it depends on viscosity or on the foods being solid.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the principle of נצוק (connected liquid stream) applies to foods, considering that the Mishnah's ruling might be due to the mixture's congealing rather than the liquid connection.

items.text: Rava's proof and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's proof and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava attempts to prove from the case of melted fat of a corpse that nitzok does not apply to foods, but Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves a column of fire that solidified, making the fat fully connected.

sub.desc_en: Rava attempts to prove from the case of melted corpse fat that nitzok does not apply to foods, arguing that if it did, even a solid lump that melted should be pure.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves a column of fire that solidified at the vessel's mouth, making the fat fully connected, so it does not bear on the nitzok question.

items.text: Ravina's counter-proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ravina's counter-proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the Mishnah of Beit Shammai proves that nitzok applies to foods, but the Gemara distinguishes: there it is because the mixture is solid, here it is because of viscosity.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi to consider the Mishnah itself as proof, but concludes that the Mishnah's ruling is due to the mixture's congealing (סמיכין), not due to נצוק (connected stream).
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that there the mixture is solid (סמיכין), while here the issue is viscosity (רירי).

items.text: Dispute over the measure of mel'o tarvad rakav
items.text_en: Dispute over the measure of mel'o tarvad rakav
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan dispute the measure of a full tarvad of decayed matter: Chizkiyah says a full palm, Rabbi Yochanan says a full handful. The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir and the Sages with similar measures.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the measure of a full ladle of decayed matter, and the Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir (from the base of the fingers upward) and the Sages (a full handful).
The Gemara asks for the measure, and records the positions of Chizkiyah (a full palm) and Rabbi Yochanan (a full handful).
A baraita is cited that defines the measure as from the base of the fingers upward according to Rabbi Meir, and a full handful according to the Sages.
The Mishnah is cited: Rabbi Meir says the measure is from the base of the fingers and upward, while the Sages say it is a full handful.

items.text: Reconciliation of Chizkiyah's view
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Chizkiyah's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Chizkiyah's measure aligns with the Mishnah, and answers that 'full palm' and 'above the knuckles' are the same measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan's position aligns with the Sages, but questions whose view Chizkiyah follows, since it matches neither Rabbi Meir nor the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that a full palm and a full handful from the knuckles upward are actually the same measure.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Adda's objection and teiku
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Adda's objection and teiku
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Adda questions whether 'above the knuckles' means towards the head or below them, which would be a different measure, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Adda objects to Rav Pappa that the phrase 'from the knuckles upward' might refer to the lower part of the hand, which would yield a different measure, and the matter remains unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved, marking it with 'teiku' (let it stand).

items.text: Opening Baraita: Definition of a corpse that produces decay
items.text_en: Opening Baraita: Definition of a corpse that produces decay
items.desc_en: The Sages teach: A corpse buried naked in a marble coffin or on a stone floor produces decay (rakav) that imparts impurity; one buried in shrouds, a wooden coffin, or on a brick floor does not produce such decay.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach the definition of a corpse that produces decay (rakav) and one that does not.

items.text: Ulla's statement on the components of decay and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Ulla's statement on the components of decay and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Ulla states that decay comes only from flesh, sinews, and bones. Rava objects with a baraita that decay from flesh alone is pure, implying decay from bone alone is impure even without flesh. Ulla clarifies that the baraita means decay from flesh is pure unless there is bone in the flesh. The Gemara notes that sinews are always present with flesh and bones.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that decay (רקב) comes only from flesh, sinews, and bones.
Rava objects with a baraita that decay from flesh alone is pure, implying decay from bone alone is impure even without flesh.
Ulla clarifies that the baraita means decay from flesh is pure unless there is bone in the flesh.
The Gemara notes that sinews are always present with flesh and bones, resolving the omission.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on two corpses becoming galgalim for each other
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on two corpses becoming galgalim for each other
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that two corpses buried together become galgalim (a medium that transmits impurity) for each other. Rav Nathan objects with a baraita that decay from two corpses is impure, implying it is not considered galgalim. Rava resolves that the baraita refers to cases where each corpse was buried separately, decayed, and then the decay was combined to a full ladleful.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rav Shmuel bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rav Shmuel bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that two corpses buried together become galgalim (a medium that transmits impurity) for each other.
Rav Nathan objects by citing a baraita that decay from two corpses is impure, implying it is not considered galgalim (which would be pure).
Rava resolves that the baraita refers to cases where each corpse was buried separately, decayed, and then the decay was combined to a full ladleful.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah: Hair cut and buried with the corpse becomes galgalim
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah: Hair cut and buried with the corpse becomes galgalim
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: If one cut his hair and buried it with the corpse, it becomes galgalim. The Gemara cites a mishnah that everything attached to a corpse is impure, except teeth, hair, and nails; but when attached, all are impure.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that hair cut and buried with the corpse becomes galgalim (a source of impurity).
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that everything attached to a corpse is impure, except teeth, hair, and nails when detached, but when attached all are impure.

items.text: Chizkiyah's query: Hair or nail destined to be cut
items.text_en: Chizkiyah's query: Hair or nail destined to be cut
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah asks: What is the status of hair destined to be cut or a nail destined to be clipped? Do we consider them as already cut, or since they are still attached, are they considered connected? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from Rabba bar bar Chanah's statement, but concludes that his statement only applies when cut; when not cut, it remains a question.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah asks whether hair or nail destined to be cut is considered already cut (as if detached) or still attached.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the query from Rabba bar bar Chanah's statement, but concludes that his statement only applies when cut; when not cut, the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeyah's query: Decay from the heel
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah's query: Decay from the heel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah asks: What is the status of decay that comes from the heel? Is it considered decay from the entire corpse, or not? He attempts to resolve this from a baraita of Rabbi Natan bar Oshaya about decay from two corpses, but the Gemara distinguishes: if the entire corpse decayed and the decay came via the heel, it is impure; but if only one limb decayed and came via the heel, the question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah asks whether decay that comes from the heel is considered decay from the entire corpse or not.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Natan bar Oshaya
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Natan bar Oshaya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the query by citing a baraita that decay from two corpses is impure, arguing that if heel-decay were excluded, the baraita would be problematic since decay might come via the heel.
The Gemara distinguishes: if the entire corpse decayed and the decay came via the heel, it is impure; but if only one limb decayed and came via the heel, the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeyah's query: Fetus in the womb as galgalim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah's query: Fetus in the womb as galgalim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah asks: Does a fetus in a woman's womb become galgalim for her? Since the master said a fetus is considered the thigh of its mother, it is part of her body and does not become galgalim; or perhaps since it will eventually emerge, it is considered separate. The Gemara begins to explore this but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah asks whether a fetus in the womb becomes גלגלין (a rolling mass) for the mother, given the principle that a fetus is considered the mother's thigh, or whether it is separate because it will eventually emerge.

items.text: Rav Pappa and others inquire about various substances
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and others inquire about various substances
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether semen in a woman's womb is considered like her own body or external. He then asks about a separated placenta, and Rav Acha and Rav Huna bar Manoach ask about skin, spittle, and mucus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether semen in a woman's womb is considered like her own body or external, since it comes from outside.
Rav Pappa asks whether a separated placenta is considered a living entity or external.
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika asks about the status of skin.
Rav Huna bar Manoach asks about the status of spittle and mucus.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Acha's objection
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha challenges Rav Pappa: if all these are considered limbs, how can one find a case of decay that imparts impurity? He answers by describing a specific scenario involving a drink of palm water, anointing with nasha, and boiling in Tiberias water.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Acha's objection to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha's objection to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Acha objects to Rav Pappa: if all these items are considered limbs (גלגלין), how can one ever find a case of decay (רקב) that imparts impurity?

sub.text: Rav Pappa's answer (via Rav Shmuel bar Acha)
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer (via Rav Shmuel bar Acha)
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers by describing a specific scenario: one gives the person palm water to drink, anoints him with nasha oil, and boils him in Tiberias water, causing decay.

items.text: Abaye's tradition and a query about ground corpse
items.text_en: Abaye's tradition and a query about ground corpse
items.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition: a corpse that was ground has no decay. A dilemma is raised: if it was ground and then decayed, what is the law? The issue is whether the requirement of flesh, sinews, and bones is met, or whether the original form is needed. The case stands unresolved (Teiku).

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition that a ground corpse does not produce decay (רקב).
A dilemma is raised: if the corpse was ground and then decayed, what is the law regarding its impurity?
The gemara considers one side: perhaps the requirement is flesh, sinews, and bones, which are present.
The gemara considers the opposite side: perhaps the original form (כברייתו) is required, and it is lacking.
The dilemma remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Ulla bar Chanina's teaching
items.text_en: Ulla bar Chanina's teaching
items.desc_en: Ulla bar Chanina teaches: a corpse that is missing a part has no decay, no grasping, and no grave vicinity.

sub.desc_en: Ulla bar Chanina teaches that a corpse missing a part does not produce decay (רקב), does not require grasping (תפוסה), and does not create grave vicinity (שכונת קברות).

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that seems to imply a living person has no decay, but a corpse does. The Gemara explains that the baraita refers to a single limb that decayed, and the point is that any corpse has decay, not that a specific corpse has it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that contrasts a corpse, which has decay (רקב), with a living person, who does not, implying that a living person cannot produce decay.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a single limb that decayed, and it teaches a general principle: any corpse has decay, but any living person does not.

items.text: Rava's query about decay during life and death
items.text_en: Rava's query about decay during life and death
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if a person decayed while alive and then died, does the decay count? The Gemara attempts to resolve from the baraita, but concludes that the baraita only teaches that any corpse has decay, not that this specific case is included.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether decay that began while a person was alive counts as decay after death, or only decay that occurred post-mortem.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt to resolve from baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt to resolve from baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve Rava's query by citing the baraita that distinguishes between a corpse (which has decay) and a living person (which does not).

The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita only teaches the general principle that any corpse has decay and any living person does not, without addressing the intermediate case of decay during life followed by death.

items.text: Rava's query about a missing ant
items.text_en: Rava's query about a missing ant
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if an ant is missing a part, does it still impart impurity? The dilemma is whether the measure is based on a fixed size (which is now lacking) or on the creature itself (which still exists).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a missing ant still imparts impurity, framing the dilemma as whether the measure is based on a fixed size (שיעורא) which is now lacking, or on the creature itself (בריה) which still exists.

items.text: Gemara's proof from the verse for the size of a bone fragment
items.text_en: Gemara's proof from the verse for the size of a bone fragment
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta brings a brayta that derives from the verses 'in them' and 'from them' that a bone fragment must be at least the size of a lentil, as that is the beginning of a creature's formation. The Gemara concludes that this size is a tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta introduces a brayta that derives from the verses 'בהם' (in them) and 'מהם' (from them) that a bone fragment must be partial, not whole.

The brayta resolves the contradiction by stating that the bone must touch a portion equivalent to the whole, and the sages set the measure at a lentil (כעדשה), the size of the beginning of a creature's formation.
The Gemara concludes that the lentil-size measure is a received tradition (גמירי).

items.text: Rav Shmaya's distinction regarding a gourd
items.text_en: Rav Shmaya's distinction regarding a gourd
items.desc_en: Rav Shmaya raises a doubt: the lentil-sized measure applies only to a gourd that never had a soul (i.e., never grew a living creature inside), but if it did have a soul, perhaps it is different. This remains a question.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmaya raises a doubt: the lentil-sized measure for a gourd applies only if it never had a soul (i.e., never grew a living creature inside), but if it did have a soul, perhaps it is different; the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Inquiry: 'spine and skull' or 'spine or skull'?
items.text_en: Inquiry: 'spine and skull' or 'spine or skull'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnaic phrase 'the spine and the skull' means both together or either one separately. Rava attempts to prove from a brayta about a spine that had most of its vertebrae scraped off: the brayta states it is pure only because it was scraped, implying that otherwise it would be impure even without a skull. The Gemara rejects this proof, saying the brayta merely teaches that scraping purifies, but the original question remains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: does the mishnaic phrase 'the spine and the skull' mean both together or either one separately?
Rava cites a brayta: a spine whose majority of vertebrae were scraped off is pure, but in a grave even a broken or dismembered spine is impure due to the grave.
The Gemara objects: the brayta implies that without scraping the spine is impure, suggesting the mishna means 'spine or skull' separately.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the brayta merely teaches that scraping purifies, but the original question remains unresolved.

items.text: Proof from the story of the bone box
items.text_en: Proof from the story of the bone box
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story: Rabbi Yehuda lists six items that Rabbi Akiva deemed impure but the Sages deemed pure, and Rabbi Akiva later recanted. In one case, a box of bones was brought to the synagogue of Tarsians, and Todros the doctor and all the doctors said there was no spine from a single corpse. The Gemara infers that if there were either a spine or a skull from a single corpse, a nazir would shave for it, proving that 'or spine or skull' is the correct reading. The Gemara rejects this, saying the doctors meant that there was not even one of them from a single corpse.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehuda's list
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehuda's list
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story: Rabbi Yehuda lists six items where Rabbi Akiva deemed impure and the Sages pure, and a box of bones was brought; Todros the doctor and all the doctors said there was no spine from a single corpse.
The Gemara infers that if there were either a spine or a skull from a single corpse, a nazir would shave for it, proving that 'or spine or skull' is the correct reading.
The Gemara rejects this, saying the doctors meant that there was not even one of them from a single corpse.

items.text: The six items listed in the Mishnah
items.text_en: The six items listed in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that enumerates the six items: a limb from a corpse that came from two corpses, a limb from a living person that came from two people, half a kav of bones from two corpses, a quarter-log of blood from two corpses, a bone the size of a barley grain that was split in two, and 'the spine and the skull'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing the six items regarding which Rabbi Akiva declares ritual impurity and the Sages declare purity.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection: the list would be seven items
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection: the list would be seven items
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the mishnah's list of 'spine or skull' were meant literally, there would be seven items (spine, skull, and five others), but the mishnah lists only six. It then introduces a mnemonic to organize the following answers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the mishnah's list of 'spine or skull' were taken literally, the count of items would be seven, but the mishnah lists only six.
The Gemara introduces a mnemonic (סִימָן) to organize the following answers that will resolve the count discrepancy.

items.text: First answer: the list excludes cases where only an individual disputes
items.text_en: First answer: the list excludes cases where only an individual disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah's list includes only items where multiple Sages dispute the impurity, excluding a bone the size of a barley-corn, which only Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah lists only cases where multiple sages dispute the ruling, excluding the case of a bone the size of a barley grain (עֶצֶם כִּשְׂעוֹרָה) where only a single sage (Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri) disputes.

items.text: Second answer: the list excludes a limb from a living being
items.text_en: Second answer: the list excludes a limb from a living being
items.desc_en: The Gemara alternatively answers that the mishnah's list includes only a limb from a corpse, not a limb from a living person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara alternatively answers that the mishnah lists only cases involving a limb from a corpse (אֵבֶר מִן הַמֵּת), not a limb from a living person (אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי).

items.text: Third answer: the list excludes items for which a nazir does not shave
items.text_en: Third answer: the list excludes items for which a nazir does not shave
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah lists only items for which a nazir shaves due to overshadowing, excluding a bone the size of a barley-corn, which does not cause shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah lists only cases where a nazirite shaves due to the impurity of overshadowing (אֲהִילוֹ), excluding a bone the size of a barley grain which does not cause such shaving.

items.text: Fourth answer: the list excludes items from which Rabbi Akiva retracted
items.text_en: Fourth answer: the list excludes items from which Rabbi Akiva retracted
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah lists only items regarding which Rabbi Akiva retracted his opinion, excluding a quarter-log of blood, from which he did not retract. Rabbi Shimon questions whether Rabbi Akiva retracted after his death, and a baraita notes that Rabbi's teeth blackened from fasting over this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a fourth answer: the mishnah lists only items regarding which Rabbi Akiva retracted, excluding a quarter-log of blood, from which he did not retract, as Rabbi told Bar Kappara not to teach that in the retraction list because Rabbi Akiva's proof remains.
Rabbi Shimon questions whether Rabbi Akiva retracted after his death, expressing uncertainty.
A baraita reports that Rabbi's teeth blackened from his fasts over this matter, supporting the gravity of the dispute.

items.text: Attempted proof from a baraita: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a quarter of bones
