items.text_en: Attempted proof from a baraita: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a quarter of bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the source of a quarter-kav of bones. Rabbi Yehoshua reconciles their views. Shammai adds that even a single bone from the spine or skull suffices. The Gemara initially tries to prove that the Sages require spine and skull, but rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the source of a quarter-kav of bones, and Rabbi Yehoshua reconciles their views.

The baraita elaborates: Beit Shammai specifies two or three bones from the body, Beit Hillel requires a quarter from the corpse's bulk or majority of limbs, and Shammai adds that even a single bone from the spine or skull suffices.
The Gemara initially infers that since Shammai is stringent, the Sages require both spine and skull for a nazirite to shave.
The Gemara rejects the inference: the Sages only dispute Shammai regarding a single bone from the spine or skull, but if the entire spine or skull is present, even one of them suffices.

items.text: Rejection of the proof: Shammai is stringent, Sages dispute only a single bone
items.text_en: Rejection of the proof: Shammai is stringent, Sages dispute only a single bone
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that Shammai is stringent, and the Sages only dispute a single bone from the spine or skull, but agree that an entire spine or skull alone suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shammai is stringent, so perhaps the rabbis require both spine and skull together, not just one.
The Gemara resolves that the rabbis only dispute with Shammai regarding a single bone that comes from the spine or skull, but when the entire spine or skull is intact, even one of them suffices.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's dilemma: a quarter of bones from spine and skull
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's dilemma: a quarter of bones from spine and skull
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a quarter-kav of bones from the spine and skull is treated more stringently than from other limbs. Rava attempts to prove from the mishnah's listing of 'the spine and the skull' that no such distinction exists, but the proof is inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a quarter-kav of bones from the spine and skull is treated more stringently than from other limbs.
Rava attempts to prove from the mishnah's listing of 'the spine and the skull' that no such distinction exists, but the proof is inconclusive.

items.text: Rava's statement about the spine and skull without a quarter-kav of bones
items.text_en: Rava's statement about the spine and skull without a quarter-kav of bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava himself said his ruling was only necessary for a spine and skull that lack a quarter-kav of bones, and that he heard this from Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava himself limited his ruling to a spine and skull lacking a quarter-kav of bones, and that he heard this from Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Shamai's opinion on a single bone from the spine or skull
items.text_en: Shamai's opinion on a single bone from the spine or skull
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a teaching that Shamai says a single bone from the spine or skull conveys impurity, but distinguishes that Shamai is more stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Shammai says a single bone from the spine or skull suffices, but distinguishes Shammai as being particularly stringent.
The Gemara resolves that Shamai is more stringent (מחמיר טפי), so his opinion does not disprove the general rule.

items.text: Attempt to infer that the Rabbis require half-kav of bones
items.text_en: Attempt to infer that the Rabbis require half-kav of bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to infer from Shamai's stringency that the Rabbis require a half-kav of bones for impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one can infer from Shammai's stringency that the Rabbis require a half-kav of bones.

items.text: Rejection: Rabbis only dispute a single bone, but agree on a quarter-kav
items.text_en: Rejection: Rabbis only dispute a single bone, but agree on a quarter-kav
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that the Rabbis only dispute Shamai regarding a single bone, but they would agree that a quarter-kav of bones conveys impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting the Rabbis only disagree with Shammai about a single bone, but would agree regarding a quarter-kav of bones.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's report of earlier elders and the later court's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's report of earlier elders and the later court's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer reports that earlier elders were divided: some said half-kav of bones and half-log of blood apply to all, while a quarter-kav and quarter-log do not; others said even a quarter-kav and quarter-log apply to all. The later court ruled that half-kav and half-log apply to all, but quarter-kav and quarter-log apply only to terumah and sacrifices, not to a nazir or one preparing the Passover offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer reports that some earlier elders said a half-kav of bones and half-log of blood apply to all, but a quarter-kav and quarter-log do not.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer (second group of earlier elders)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer (second group of earlier elders)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer reports that other earlier elders said even a quarter-kav of bones and quarter-log of blood apply to all.
The later court ruled that half-kav and half-log apply to all, but quarter-kav and quarter-log apply only to terumah and sacrifices, not to a nazir or one preparing the Passover offering.

items.text: Question about the third ruling's authority and answer from tradition
items.text_en: Question about the third ruling's authority and answer from tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a third ruling can be decisive, and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi answers that it was received through tradition from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a third ruling cannot decide between two earlier ones, and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi answers that it was based on a tradition from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi answers that this ruling was received through tradition (שמועה) from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, giving it authoritative weight.

items.text: Exclusions from the Mishnah's list: bone the size of a barley grain and the covering stone
items.text_en: Exclusions from the Mishnah's list: bone the size of a barley grain and the covering stone
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'on these' at the beginning excludes a bone the size of a barley grain, which conveys impurity through contact and carrying but not through overshadowing; the phrase at the end excludes the covering stone (אבן הסכוכית).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a half-kav of bones requires shaving, but a quarter-kav does not. The Gemara questions whether this refers to bones with barley-sized fragments, and concludes it refers to ground bone dust.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a half-kav of bones requires the nazirite to shave, but a quarter-kav does not.
The Gemara asks: what kind of bones are being discussed?
The Gemara objects: if the bones contain barley-sized fragments, the nazirite would already be liable due to the rule of a bone the size of a barley grain.
The Gemara resolves: it refers to bones that have been ground into dust.

items.text: Dispute about a limb without proper flesh
items.text_en: Dispute about a limb without proper flesh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions a limb from a corpse or a living person with proper flesh. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish dispute whether a nazir shaves for a limb without proper flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nazir shaves for a limb from a corpse or a living person that has proper flesh on it.
The Gemara asks what the law is if the limb lacks proper flesh.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the nazir does not shave for such a limb.
Resh Lakish rules that the nazir does shave for such a limb.

items.text: Arguments from the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Arguments from the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the Mishnah's opening clause implies that only a limb with an olive's bulk of flesh requires shaving. Resh Lakish counters that the Mishnah does not explicitly state the opposite in its latter clause. Rabbi Yochanan responds that wherever something is implied, the Mishnah does not need to state it explicitly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the Mishnah's first clause implies that only a limb with an olive-bulk of flesh requires shaving, and without it, the nazirite does not shave.
Reish Lakish counters that since the Mishnah does not explicitly state the opposite in its latter clause, a nazirite does shave for a limb without sufficient flesh.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that wherever something is implied from the first clause, the Mishnah does not need to state it explicitly in the latter clause.

items.text: Objection from the half-kav case
items.text_en: Objection from the half-kav case
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: In the case of a half-kav of bones, the Mishnah implies that a quarter-kav does not require shaving, yet it explicitly states the quarter-kav in the latter clause. This contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: In the case of a half-kav of bones, the Mishnah implies that a quarter-kav does not require shaving, yet it explicitly states the quarter-kav in the latter clause. This contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

items.text: Answer: The quarter-kav needed clarification
items.text_en: Answer: The quarter-kav needed clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Without the explicit mention of a quarter-kav, one might have thought that even contact or carrying a quarter-kav does not convey impurity. Therefore, the Mishnah needed to state it explicitly to teach that only overshadowing does not require shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that without the explicit mention of a quarter-kav of bones, one might have thought that even contact or carrying a quarter-kav does not convey impurity, so the Mishnah needed to state it to teach that only overshadowing does not require shaving.

items.text: Objection from the half-log of blood case
items.text_en: Objection from the half-log of blood case
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: In the case of a half-log of blood, the Mishnah implies that a quarter-log does not require shaving, yet it explicitly states the quarter-log. The Gemara answers that this was needed to reject Rabbi Akiva's view that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses conveys impurity in a tent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's mention of a half-log of blood implies a quarter-log does not require shaving, yet the Mishnah explicitly teaches the quarter-log case.
The Gemara answers that the quarter-log case was necessary to reject Rabbi Akiva's view that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses conveys impurity in a tent.

items.text: Analysis of the limb's composition
items.text_en: Analysis of the limb's composition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the dispute: If the limb has a barley-sized bone, why does Rabbi Yochanan say no shaving? If it lacks such a bone, why does Resh Lakish say shaving? Resh Lakish answers that even without a barley-sized bone, the Torah enlarged the limb's impurity. A baraita is cited to explain the verses regarding impurity from a limb, a corpse, and a grave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the nature of the limb: if it has a barley-sized bone, why does Rabbi Yochanan exempt from shaving? If it lacks such a bone, why does Resh Lakish require shaving?
Resh Lakish answers that the limb lacks a barley-sized bone, yet the Torah enlarged its impurity.
A baraita is cited to explain the verses regarding impurity from a limb, a corpse, and a grave, supporting the notion that the Torah enlarged the limb's impurity.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita on tum'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita on tum'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between touching a bone the size of a barley grain, a limb from a living being, a limb from a corpse, and a pre-Sinai grave. It questions the need for a separate category of a limb from a corpse if it already contains a bone the size of a barley grain, and Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse applies to carrying rather than touching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes four categories of טומאה (ritual impurity) from contact: a bone the size of a barley grain, a limb from a living being without healing potential, a limb from a corpse, and a pre-Sinai grave.

The Gemara questions the need for a separate category of a limb from a corpse: if it contains a bone the size of a barley grain, it is already covered by the first category; if not, the Torah would have to expand the rule.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the limb does contain a bone the size of a barley grain, but the verse applies to carrying (משא) rather than touching (מגע), so the category is needed for a separate law.

items.text: Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'and he sprinkles on the third and seventh days and he destroys' as a lead-in to the next question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'and he sprinkles on the third and seventh days and he destroys' as a lead-in to the next question.

items.text: Question about 'until he becomes pure'
items.text_en: Question about 'until he becomes pure'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrase 'until he becomes pure' refers to the seventh day (requiring sunset, according to Rabbi Eliezer) or the eighth day (requiring bringing offerings, according to the Rabbis). It brings a proof from the Mishnah's continuation that the nazirite begins counting immediately, implying the Rabbis' view that purification is on the eighth day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah's phrase 'עד שיטהר' (until he becomes pure): does it refer to the seventh day (requiring sunset, per Rabbi Eliezer) or the eighth day (requiring bringing offerings, per the Rabbis)?

The Gemara resolves the question by citing the Mishnah's continuation that the nazirite begins counting immediately, proving that the phrase refers to the eighth day and aligns with the Rabbis' view that purification (נזירות דטהרה) does not take effect until the eighth day.

items.text: Mishnah: list of items that do not require shaving
items.text_en: Mishnah: list of items that do not require shaving
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various sources of tum'ah (such as overhangs, projections, beit hapras, gentile lands, etc.) for which a nazirite does not shave, and repeats the rule of sprinkling on the third and seventh days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing sources of tum'ah (ritual impurity) for which a nazirite does not shave, starting with overhangs, projections, and beit hapras (a field with scattered bones).
The Mishnah continues listing additional sources of tum'ah: gentile lands, the goller (tombstone), the dofek (side stone), a quarter-log of blood, an ohel (tent), and a quarter-kav of bones.
The Mishnah concludes the list with vessels that touch a corpse, and the days of counting and completion, stating that for these the nazirite does not shave.
The Mishnah repeats the rule that the nazirite sprinkles on the third and seventh days despite not shaving.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that certain days (like those of a zav, zavah, or a metzora's isolation) count toward a nazirite's term and do not invalidate previous days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that certain days of impurity (zav, zavah, metzora's isolation) count toward the nazirite's term and do not invalidate previous days.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's terms
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 's'chachot' refers to a tree that overshadows the ground, and 'pera'ot' refers to branches protruding from a fence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the Mishnah's terms: 's'chachot' are a tree that overshadows the ground, and 'pera'ot' are branches protruding from a fence.

items.text: Gemara's question about the land of the nations
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the land of the nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is the impurity of the land of the nations due to its air (avira) or its soil (gusha)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is the impurity of the land of the nations due to its air (אווירא) or its soil (גושא)?

items.text: Attempted resolution from the baraita
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that requires sprinkling on the third and seventh days for one who enters the land of the nations. If the impurity were due to air, sprinkling would be unnecessary, implying it is due to soil. However, the Gemara deflects: the baraita refers to other impurities (she'ara).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita requiring sprinkling on the third and seventh days for one who enters the land of the nations, arguing that if the impurity were due to air (אַוֵּירָא), sprinkling would be unnecessary.
The Gemara deflects the proof, stating that the baraita refers to other impurities (שְּׁאָרָא), not to the impurity of the land of the nations itself.

items.text: Support for the deflection
items.text_en: Support for the deflection
items.desc_en: The Gemara finds support for its deflection from the baraita's mention of vessels that touch a corpse, which are not subject to sprinkling, proving the baraita deals with other matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the baraita's mention of vessels that touch a corpse, which are not subject to sprinkling, proves that the baraita's ruling about sprinkling applies to other matters (אשארא) and not to the vessels themselves.

items.text: First attempt: framing the debate as airspace (אווירא) vs. mass (גוששא)
items.text_en: First attempt: framing the debate as airspace (אווירא) vs. mass (גוששא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who deems impure) and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda (who deems pure) is about the source of impurity in the Land of the Nations: Rabbi Meir holds it is due to the airspace, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds it is due to the physical earth (mass).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who deems impure) and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda (who deems pure) regarding one who enters the Land of the Nations in a chest, box, or cabinet is about the source of impurity: Rabbi Meir holds it is due to the airspace (אווירא), and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds it is due to the physical earth (גוששא).

items.text: Rejection: both agree on mass, dispute is about the status of a tossed tent
items.text_en: Rejection: both agree on mass, dispute is about the status of a tossed tent
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, arguing that both opinions hold impurity is due to the mass. Rather, they disagree about whether a moving vessel (אוהל זרוק) is legally considered a tent. Rabbi Meir considers it a tent, so the container interposes; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, asserting that both opinions hold impurity is due to the mass (גושא), and the dispute is whether a tossed tent (אוהל זרוק) is legally considered a tent.

items.text: Proof from a baraita and alternative resolution: both agree on airspace, dispute about rabbinic decree
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita and alternative resolution: both agree on airspace, dispute about rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda rules that a box full of vessels thrown over a dead body in a tent is impure, but if stationary it is pure. This contradicts the previous resolution, so the Gemara offers a new answer: both hold impurity is due to airspace, but they dispute whether the rabbis decreed impurity for an unusual case (enclosed containers) in the Land of the Nations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda rules that a box full of vessels thrown over a dead body in a tent is impure, but if stationary it is pure, contradicting the previous resolution.
The Gemara offers a new resolution: both agree impurity is due to airspace, but they dispute whether the rabbis decreed impurity for an unusual case (enclosed containers) in the Land of the Nations.

items.text: Another baraita and a third resolution: concern for protruding head/body
items.text_en: Another baraita and a third resolution: concern for protruding head/body
items.desc_en: Another baraita rules that one entering in a chest, box, or cabinet is pure, but in a wagon, boat, or litter is impure. The Gemara alternatively explains that the disputants argued about the concern that one might stick out his head and most of his body into the land, which would expose him to impurity. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states this condition in a supporting baraita.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one entering the land of the nations in a chest, box, or cabinet is pure, but in a wagon, boat, or litter is impure.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the dispute concerns the concern that one might stick out his head and most of his body into the land, exposing himself to impurity.
A supporting baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states that one entering in a chest, box, or cabinet is pure until he sticks out his head or most of his body.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction on nazirite counting: short vs. long term
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction on nazirite counting: short vs. long term
items.desc_en: Moving to a new topic, Rav Chisda comments on the mishnah's statement that the nazirite 'begins and counts' after becoming defiled. He limits this to a short nazirite term (30 days), but for a long term, the days of impurity count toward the total.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda limits the mishnah's rule that the nazirite 'begins and counts' after defilement to a short nazirite term (30 days).
For a long nazirite term, the days of impurity count toward the total, so the nazirite does not need to restart the count.

items.text: Rav Sherevya's objection: the mishnah implies immediate counting even for short terms
items.text_en: Rav Sherevya's objection: the mishnah implies immediate counting even for short terms
items.desc_en: Rav Sherevya challenges Rav Chisda, citing the mishnah's phrase 'begins and counts immediately, and does not cancel the previous days'. He questions whether this could refer to a short term, since a short-term nazirite would still need hair growth before shaving, implying the new count must start after full shaving.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sherevya objects to Rav Chisda's distinction, citing the mishnah's phrase 'begins and counts immediately' and questioning whether it could apply to a short-term nazirite, since such a nazirite requires hair growth before shaving.

items.text: Gemara's solution to the contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's solution to the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconciles the earlier question by positing a case of extended nezirut (fifty days) where the nazir sits twenty days, contracts tzara'at, shaves for it, and then completes the remaining thirty days, ensuring sufficient hair growth for the required offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by positing a case of extended nezirut (fifty days) where the nazir sits twenty days, contracts tzara'at, shaves for it, and then completes the remaining thirty days, ensuring sufficient hair growth for the required offerings.

items.text: Rami bar Hama raises a question
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama raises a question
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama introduces a case of a nazir who is uncertain whether he is tamei (ritually impure) and uncertain whether he is a confirmed metzora, posing a halakhic dilemma.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises an objection regarding a nazir who was טמא (ritually impure) with a ספק (doubt) and a confirmed leper with a ספק (doubt).

items.text: Opening baraita on nazirite restrictions
items.text_en: Opening baraita on nazirite restrictions
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a nazirite who took a short-term vow may eat sacrifices after 60 days and drink wine or become impure after 120 days, implying that days of impurity do not count toward the term.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a nazirite who took a short-term vow may eat sacrifices after 60 days and drink wine or become impure after 120 days.

items.text: Distinction between short and long nazirite terms
items.text_en: Distinction between short and long nazirite terms
items.desc_en: The baraita clarifies that the above applies only to a short nazirite term; for a year-long nazirite, he eats sacrifices after two years and drinks wine or becomes impure after four years, doubling the time due to impurity days not counting.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that the baraita applies only to a short nazirite vow, but for a year-long vow the nazirite eats sacrifices after two years and drinks wine or becomes impure after four years.
The baraita specifies that for a year-long nazirite, he eats sacrifices after two years and drinks wine or becomes impure after four years.

items.text: Gemara's objection: why not three years and thirty days?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: why not three years and thirty days?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if impurity days do not count, a year-long nazirite who became impure should only need three years and thirty days (360 + 30) rather than four years, since impurity days are only 30 days per year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if days of impurity count toward the term, then for a year-long vow the nazirite should be permitted after only three years and thirty days, not four years.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita that days of impurity do not count, and argues by kal vachomer that days of leprous confinement (חלוטו) also do not count, since both require shaving and bringing a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita that only days of impurity do not count toward the term, and argues by analogy that days of metzora confinement also should not count.
Rav Ashi asks: from where do we derive that days of leprous confinement (חלוטו) also do not count?
Rav Ashi argues by kal vachomer (a fortiori): just as days of impurity do not count, so too days of leprous confinement do not count, since both involve shaving and bringing a sacrifice.

items.text: Refutation of the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Refutation of the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer: impurity days cancel previous days, but leprous confinement days do not, so the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy: days of impurity cancel previous days, but days of metzora confinement do not, so the comparison fails.

items.text: Alternative kal vachomer from nazirite in a grave
items.text_en: Alternative kal vachomer from nazirite in a grave
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a different kal vachomer: a nazirite in a grave, whose hair is fit for nazirite shaving, still has impurity days not counting; leprous confinement, where hair is unfit for nazirite shaving, certainly should not count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a nazirite at a grave, whose hair is fit for nazirite shaving, does not have those days count, then days of metzora confinement, whose hair is unfit, certainly should not count.

items.text: Extension to days of counting (ימי ספרו)
items.text_en: Extension to days of counting (ימי ספרו)
items.desc_en: The baraita then asks about days of counting (ימי ספרו) for a leper, and begins a kal vachomer to include them as well, though the argument is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that days of counting (ימי ספרו) also do not count toward the term, and proposes an analogy.

items.text: Days of counting and completion do not count toward nazirite term
items.text_en: Days of counting and completion do not count toward nazirite term
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a kal vachomer that days of counting (ימי ספרו) for a metzora do not count toward his nazirite term, just as days of his quarantine (ימי חלוטו) do not. An objection is raised that days of closure (ימי הסגרו) might also not count, but the Gemara refutes this because closure lacks shaving and sacrifice. The Mishnah concludes that days of counting and completion do not count, but days of a zav, zavah, and closure of a metzora do count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): just as days of quarantine (ימי חלוטו) require shaving and sacrifice, so too days of counting (ימי ספרו) require them.
An objection is raised: perhaps days of closure (ימי הסגרו) should also not count, since they too involve impurity of bed and seat.
The Gemara refutes the objection: days of closure lack shaving and sacrifice, so they should count toward the nazirite term.
The Mishnah concludes: days of counting and completion do not count, but days of a zav, zavah, and closure of a metzora do count.

items.text: Clarification that days of quarantine do not count
items.text_en: Clarification that days of quarantine do not count
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a previous statement about days of impurity (ימי טומאה) and days of quarantine (ימי חלוטו), concluding that even in a case of extended naziriteship (נזירות מרובה), the days of quarantine do not count. This is proven from the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement by asking whether the comparison to days of impurity (ימי טומאה) applies to days of quarantine (ימי חלוטו), noting that impurity days nullify prior days while quarantine days do not.

The Gemara resolves that the case must be one of extended naziriteship (נזירות מרובה), and since the Mishnah rules that quarantine days do not count, it proves that they indeed do not count toward the nazirite period.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer's rule on corpse-tumah and Temple liability
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer's rule on corpse-tumah and Temple liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: any corpse-tumah for which a nazir shaves incurs liability for entering the Temple; any for which he does not shave does not incur liability. Rabbi Meir objects that this should not be more lenient than the tumah of a sheretz.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer citing Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer citing Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: any corpse-tumah for which a nazir shaves incurs liability for entering the Temple, and any for which he does not shave does not incur liability.
Rabbi Meir objects that this ruling should not be more lenient than the tumah of a sheretz (creeping animal).

items.text: Gemara: Source of Rabbi Eliezer's tradition
items.text_en: Gemara: Source of Rabbi Eliezer's tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer learned this from Rabbi Yehoshua directly, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer encountered Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peter Rosh discussing the same halakhah before Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Eliezer then confirmed from Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel that the tradition indeed came from Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer actually learned this tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua directly, given the baraita shows a different chain.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer recounts encountering Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peter Rosh discussing the halakhah before Rabbi Meir, and then confirming from Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel that the tradition indeed came from Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Principle about traditions transmitted in a chain of three
items.text_en: Principle about traditions transmitted in a chain of three
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives a principle: when a tradition is stated in a group of three, we mention the first and last transmitters but not the middle one. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this from a tradition of Nachum the scribe about a halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai, which lists a chain but omits Yehoshua and Calev.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: for any tradition transmitted in a chain of three, we mention the first and last transmitters but not the middle one.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports the principle by citing a tradition of Nachum the scribe about a halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai regarding sowing dill and mustard in multiple locations, which lists a chain but omits Yehoshua and Calev.
The Gemara concludes that since Yehoshua and Calev are omitted from the chain, this supports the principle that middle links in a tradition are not necessarily listed.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer and the halakhah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer and the halakhah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer: if a bone the size of a barley grain, which does not transmit tumah through a tent, requires a nazir to shave for contact and carrying, then a quarter-log of blood, which does transmit tumah through a tent, should also require shaving. Rabbi Eliezer rejects the kal vachomer, but Rabbi Yehoshua affirms Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, stating that the halakhah is as they said.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva presents a kal vachomer argument before Rabbi Eliezer: if a bone the size of a barley grain, which does not transmit tumah through a tent, requires a nazir to shave for contact and carrying, then a quarter-log of blood, which does transmit tumah through a tent, should also require shaving.
Rabbi Eliezer rejects the kal vachomer, stating that one cannot argue by means of a kal vachomer in this case.
Rabbi Yehoshua affirms Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, stating that the halakhah is as they said, but it is a halakhah transmitted to Moses from Sinai.

items.text: Query on derivation of bone and blood laws
items.text_en: Query on derivation of bone and blood laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: is the law of an olive-sized bone (עֶצֶם כִּשְׂעוֹרָה) a tradition (הֲלָכָה) and the quarter-log of blood derived by a fortiori reasoning (קַל וָחוֹמֶר), or vice versa? The Gemara cites a resolution that the bone law is a tradition and the blood law is a fortiori, and one cannot derive a fortiori from a tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: whether the law of a bone the size of a barley grain is a tradition and the quarter-log of blood is derived by a fortiori inference, or vice versa, and notes that one cannot derive a fortiori from a tradition.
The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing a baraita: the bone law is a tradition, the quarter-log of blood is a fortiori inference, and one does not derive a fortiori from a tradition.

items.text: Transition to new chapter
items.text_en: Transition to new chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל, indicating a return to the topic of the high priest, and transitions to the next mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל, indicating a return to the topic of the high priest, and transitions to the next mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Two nazirites with uncertain impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two nazirites with uncertain impurity
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case where two nazirites are told by a witness that one of them became impure, but the witness does not know which one. They both shave and bring a sin-offering and a peace-offering, stipulating that if they are the impure one, the offerings belong to them, and if pure, to the other. They then count thirty days and bring another peace-offering with similar stipulations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of two nazirites where a witness saw one become impure but does not know which, and details the procedure of shaving and bringing both impurity and purity offerings with conditional statements.

The mishnah describes the procedure: both nazirites shave and bring a sin-offering and a peace-offering, stipulating that if they are the impure one, the offerings belong to them, and if pure, to the other; then they count thirty days and bring another peace-offering with similar stipulations.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why is this not a public domain?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why is this not a public domain?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah: why is the impurity considered a doubt in a private domain (where impurity is stringent)? Since there are three people (two nazirites and the witness), it should be a doubt in a public domain, which is ruled pure. The Gemara explains that the law of doubt in a private domain is derived from the sotah, which involves two people, but here there are three, making it a public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah treats this as a doubt in a private domain, since the derivation from the sotah involves only two people, but here there are three (two nazirites and the witness), making it a public domain where doubt is ruled pure.

The Gemara explains the derivation: just as the sotah involves two people (the husband and the suspected adulterer), so too a doubt in a private domain requires only two people; here there are three, so it becomes a doubt in a public domain, which is ruled pure.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the difficulty by explaining that the witness said 'I saw impurity thrown between you,' implying the impurity was in a private domain between the two nazirites, excluding the witness. Rav Ashi adds that this is precisely the implication of the mishnah's language.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna resolves the difficulty by explaining that the witness said 'I saw impurity thrown between you,' which creates a private domain situation because the impurity is between the two nazirites alone.
Rav Ashi confirms that the language of the Mishnah is precise, implying that the witness's statement is about impurity thrown between them, not about seeing one of them impure.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that those who are uncertainly impure may shave and bring offerings, asking why this does not violate the prohibition of הקפה. Shmuel answers that it refers to a woman or a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that those uncertainly impure may shave and bring offerings, asking why this does not violate the prohibition of הקפה (rounding the corners of the head).
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah refers to a woman or a minor, who are exempt from the prohibition of הקפה.

items.text: Implication about Shmuel's view on הקפת כל הראש
items.text_en: Implication about Shmuel's view on הקפת כל הראש
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel could have answered that it refers to an adult, since הקפת כל הראש is not considered הקפה, but he did not, implying he holds that הקפת כל הראש is indeed forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shmuel could have explained the Mishnah as referring to an adult, since the prohibition of הקפת כל הראש (rounding the entire head) is not considered a violation.
The Gemara infers that Shmuel must hold that הקפת כל הראש (rounding the entire head) is indeed considered a violation, which is why he did not give that explanation.

items.text: Mar Zutra's version of Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's version of Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches this statement of Shmuel in the context of the latter part of the Mishnah, where a nazir who is uncertainly impure shaves four times, and the same question about הקפה arises, with Shmuel again answering that it refers to a woman or minor.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches that Shmuel's statement was said regarding the latter clause of the Mishnah, about a nazirite who is uncertainly impure and uncertainly confirmed, who shaves four shavings.
The Gemara again questions how this shaving does not violate the prohibition of הקפה.
Shmuel answers that the case involves a woman or a minor, who are exempt from the prohibition.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who shaves a minor is liable for הקפה. Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges him, asking who shaves his own children, and Rav Huna responds that his wife Chova does. The Gemara notes that Rav Adda bar Ahava never had children.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who rounds the head of a minor is liable for the prohibition of הקפה.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects to Rav Huna, asking who shaves his own children if he holds that one is liable for shaving a minor.
Rav Huna responds that a woman named Chova shaves them.
The Gemara notes that Rav Adda bar Ahava cursed Chova's children, and as a result, Rav Huna never had surviving children during Rav Adda's lifetime.

items.text: Explanation of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava agree that הקפת כל הראש is forbidden, but they disagree on the reason. Rav Huna derives from the verse that only those liable for השחתה (destruction of the beard) are liable for הקפה, excluding women. Rav Adda bar Ahava derives that the one who shaves and the one being shaved are linked, so a minor who is not punishable exempts the one who shaves him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that both Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava agree that הקפת כל הראש (shaving the entire head) is considered forbidden הקפה (rounding), and asks what they disagree about.
Rav Huna derives from the verse that only those liable for השחתה (destruction of the beard) are liable for הקפה (rounding), excluding women who are exempt from השחתה.
Rav Adda bar Ahava derives that the one who shaves (מקיף) and the one being shaved (ניקף) are linked, so a minor who is not punishable exempts the one who shaves him.

items.text: Attempt to present the dispute as a Tannaitic one
items.text_en: Attempt to present the dispute as a Tannaitic one
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute over whether הקפת כל הראש is forbidden is actually a Tannaitic dispute, citing a baraita that discusses the verse and asks what the word 'rosho' teaches.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about הקפת כל הראש is actually a dispute between Tannaim, citing a baraita that questions the meaning of the word 'ראשו' (his head) in the verse.

items.text: Opening baraitot on "his head"
items.text_en: Opening baraitot on "his head"
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one derives that a leprous nazirite may shave his head despite the prohibition, and the other questions the need for the word "his head" (ראשו) to teach that a leprous nazirite is permitted, implying a potential dispute.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita derives from the word 'ראשו' (his head) that a leprous nazirite may shave, countering the assumption that the prohibition applies to him as well.
The second baraita questions the need for the word 'ראשו' and similarly permits a leprous nazirite to shave, implying a potential dispute between the two baraitot.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is this a dispute about הקפת כל הראש?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is this a dispute about הקפת כל הראש?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the two baraitot reflect a dispute: one opinion holds that shaving the entire head (הקפת כל הראש) is not considered forbidden rounding, so the verse comes to override both a negative and positive command; the other holds it is forbidden rounding, so the verse only overrides a negative command.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the two baraitot reflect a dispute about whether shaving the entire head (הקפת כל הראש) is considered forbidden rounding, affecting whether the verse overrides both a negative and positive command or only a negative command.

items.text: Rava's first explanation: Everyone agrees הקפת כל הראש is not forbidden
items.text_en: Rava's first explanation: Everyone agrees הקפת כל הראש is not forbidden
items.desc_en: Rava argues that all agree shaving the entire head is not forbidden rounding; the verse is needed for a case where one first rounded (הקיף) and then shaved, since if done at once there would be no liability.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that everyone agrees that shaving the entire head (הקפת כל הראש) is not considered forbidden rounding (הקפה), and the verse addresses a case where one first rounded and then shaved, since if done simultaneously there would be no liability.

items.text: Objection from Reish Lakish's principle
items.text_en: Objection from Reish Lakish's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is the verse written that way? Reish Lakish stated that wherever there is a positive and negative command, if both can be fulfilled that is preferable; otherwise the positive overrides the negative. This principle seems to contradict Rava's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rava's explanation by citing Reish Lakish's principle that when a positive and negative command conflict, the positive overrides the negative only if both cannot be fulfilled.

items.text: Alternative: Everyone agrees הקפת כל הראש is forbidden
items.text_en: Alternative: Everyone agrees הקפת כל הראש is forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes instead that all agree shaving the entire head is forbidden rounding. The question then becomes: from where does the opinion that the verse only overrides a negative command derive the principle that a positive command overrides a negative one?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that everyone agrees shaving the entire head is called rounding, and then asks: for the opinion that the verse comes to override both a positive and negative command, from where does it derive the principle that a positive command overrides a bare negative command?

items.text: Derivation from "Gedilim" (fringes)
items.text_en: Derivation from "Gedilim" (fringes)
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the principle that a positive command overrides a negative command alone is derived from the verse about fringes (גדילים), where the positive command of tzitzit overrides the prohibition of shatnez.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the principle that a positive command overrides a negative command alone is derived from the verse about fringes (גדילים), where the positive command of tzitzit overrides the prohibition of shatnez.

items.text: Why not derive from "Gedilim"? Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Why not derive from "Gedilim"? Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the other opinion does not derive from "Gedilim". It answers that the verse is needed for Rava's teaching: Rava resolves a contradiction between verses about tzitzit, showing that wool and linen exempt both their own kind and other kinds, while other kinds only exempt their own kind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the opinion that derives the leniency from 'ראשו' (his head) does not derive it from 'גדילים' (fringes).
The Gemara answers that the verse 'גדילים' is needed for Rava's teaching.
Rava resolves a contradiction between verses about tzitzit, showing that wool and linen exempt both their own kind and other kinds, while other kinds only exempt their own kind.

items.text: Derivation from "his beard" (זקנו)
items.text_en: Derivation from "his beard" (זקנו)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the opinion which uses "his head" (ראשו) to teach that a positive command overrides both a negative and positive command derives the principle of overriding a negative command alone from "his beard" (זקנו), where a leprous priest may shave despite the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Tanna who uses 'his head' (ראשו) to teach that a positive command overrides a negative command alone, from where does he derive that a positive command overrides both a negative and a positive command? It answers: he derives it from 'his beard' (זקנו).
A baraita is cited: the verse 'his beard' (זקנו) teaches that a leprous priest may shave despite the prohibition, showing that a positive command overrides both a negative and a positive command.

items.text: Question: Why not derive from "his beard"?
items.text_en: Question: Why not derive from "his beard"?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why doesn't the other opinion derive the principle from "his beard" (זקנו) instead? The daf cuts off with "וליטעמיך דקיימא לן בעלמא", indicating the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why doesn't the opinion that derives from 'ראשו' (his head) the principle of a positive commandment overriding both a negative and a positive commandment instead derive this from 'זקנו' (his beard)? The daf cuts off with 'וליטעמיך דקיימא לן בעלמא' (and according to your reasoning, since we hold generally...), indicating the discussion continues.

items.text: Gemara's question: Can a positive commandment override a prohibition with a positive commandment?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Can a positive commandment override a prohibition with a positive commandment?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a positive commandment can override a prohibition that also includes a positive commandment, and attempts to derive this from the case of a priest. It concludes that a priest cannot serve as a source because his prohibition is not universal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a positive commandment can override a prohibition that includes a positive commandment, and proposes to derive this from the case of a priest, where the positive commandment overrides such a prohibition.
The Gemara rejects the derivation from the priest, because the priest's prohibition is not universal (שֶׁאֵינוֹ שָׁוֶה בַּכֹּל), and therefore the nazirite cannot learn from it either.

items.text: Derivation of the word 'his beard' for a priest with tzaraat
items.text_en: Derivation of the word 'his beard' for a priest with tzaraat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'his beard' in the verse is needed to teach that a priest with tzaraat is permitted to shave his beard, unlike the general prohibition. It then derives that the prohibition of shaving applies only with a razor, not with scissors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that the word 'רֹאשׁוֹ' (his head) in the verse refers to a nazirite, why is the word 'זְקָנוֹ' (his beard) also needed?

The Gemara answers: it is needed for what was taught in a baraita — the word 'זְקָנוֹ' (his beard) teaches that a priest with tzaraat (צרעת) is permitted to shave his beard, unlike the general prohibition.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verses that the prohibition of shaving the beard applies only with a razor (תער), not with scissors (מספריים).

items.text: The need for both 'his head' and 'his beard'
items.text_en: The need for both 'his head' and 'his beard'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both 'his head' and 'his beard' are written if 'his head' is used for a mere prohibition. It answers that one indicates overriding a simple prohibition and the other indicates overriding a prohibition with a positive commandment, and since they are equal, both apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both 'his head' and 'his beard' are written if 'his head' is used for a mere prohibition.
The Gemara answers that one indicates overriding a simple prohibition and the other indicates overriding a prohibition with a positive commandment, and since they are equal, both apply.

items.text: Conclusion: No derivation between priest and nazirite
items.text_en: Conclusion: No derivation between priest and nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a priest cannot be derived from a nazirite because a nazirite can be released from his vow, and a nazirite cannot be derived from a priest because the priest's prohibition is not universal. Therefore, no general derivation is made from either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a priest cannot be derived from a nazirite because a nazirite can be released from his vow, and a nazirite cannot be derived from a priest because the priest's prohibition is not universal, so no general derivation is made from either.

items.text: Rav's statement on shaving the entire body with a razor
items.text_en: Rav's statement on shaving the entire body with a razor
items.desc_en: Rav states that a person may shave his entire body with a razor. An objection is raised from a baraita that one who shaves the armpit and pubic area is liable. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a razor, while Rav refers to scissors-like instruments.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a person may shave his entire body with a razor (תער).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that one who shaves the armpit and pubic area is liable to lashes, contradicting Rav's leniency.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a razor (תער), while Rav permits shaving with scissors-like instruments (מספרים).
The Gemara objects that Rav himself said 'with a razor' (בתער), not with scissors.
The Gemara explains that Rav meant a razor-like instrument (כעין תער), i.e., scissors that cut like a razor, not a literal razor.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on shaving armpit and pubic area
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on shaving armpit and pubic area
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who shaves the armpit and pubic area is liable. An objection is raised that this is only a rabbinic prohibition. The Gemara explains that the 'liable' mentioned is a rabbinic punishment.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who shaves the armpit and pubic area is liable to lashes.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that shaving body hair is only a rabbinic prohibition, not a Torah one.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's 'liable' refers to a rabbinic punishment, not a Torah one.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on hair removal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on hair removal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who removes armpit and pubic hair violates the prohibition of 'lo yilbash gever simlat isha'. The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that such removal is only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who removes armpit and pubic hair is liable to lashes for violating the prohibition of cross-dressing.
The Gemara objects from a baraita that hair removal is only a rabbinic prohibition, not a Torah one.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan follows a specific Tanna who holds that such removal is a Torah violation.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse by Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse by Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interpret the verse 'lo yihyeh kli gever al isha' to prohibit cross-dressing for deceptive purposes and women bearing weapons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the first Tanna (who disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan) interprets the verse 'lo yilbash gever'.
The baraita explains that the verse prohibits a man wearing a woman's garment only when it leads to sitting among women, not when there is no abomination.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives from the verse that a woman may not go to war with weapons and a man may not adopt feminine grooming.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives from the verse that a woman may not go out with weapons of war, and a man may not adorn himself with women's cosmetics.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman permits a nazir to remove such hair, but the Gemara rejects his ruling. Rabbis testify that Rabbi Yochanan himself had no hair, and Rabbi Shimon bar Abba explains it fell out due to old age.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a nazirite is permitted to remove armpit and pubic hair, but the Gemara states the halacha does not follow him.

sub.text: Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Shimon bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Shimon bar Abba
sub.desc_en: The rabbis object to Rabbi Shimon bar Abba that they saw Rabbi Yochanan without armpit hair, and he explains it fell out due to old age.
The rabbis testify to Rabbi Shimon bar Abba that they saw Rabbi Yochanan had no armpit hair.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba explains that Rabbi Yochanan's hair fell out due to old age, not from shaving.

items.text: Incident with Rabbi Ami
items.text_en: Incident with Rabbi Ami
items.desc_en: A man liable for lashes was found not to have shaved his armpit hair; Rabbi Ami recognized him as a scholar and released him.

sub.desc_en: A man liable for lashes before Rabbi Ammi was found without shaved armpit hair, and Rabbi Ammi released him, identifying him as a colleague who follows the prohibition.
Rabbi Ami recognized the man as a scholar and ordered his release.

items.text: Rav's question about shaving
items.text_en: Rav's question about shaving
items.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya whether a nazir may shave his hair; Rabbi Chiyya forbids it, explaining that hair that grows will eventually fall out on its own.

sub.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya whether one may shave armpit hair, and Rabbi Chiyya answers it is forbidden.
Rav objects that the hair grows long, and Rabbi Chiyya explains that it has a set time and eventually falls out on its own.
Rav objects that the hair is still growing, implying it should be permitted.
Rabbi Chiyya explains that hair which grows will eventually fall out on its own, so shaving is unnecessary and forbidden.

items.text: Rav's question about plucking and rubbing
items.text_en: Rav's question about plucking and rubbing
items.desc_en: Rav asks about plucking hair; Rabbi Chiyya forbids it but permits rubbing with a garment. An alternative version says rubbing in prayer is forbidden, but the Gemara rejects that ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya whether one may rub armpit hair, and Rabbi Chiyya answers it is forbidden.
Rav asks whether rubbing through one's garment is permitted, and Rabbi Chiyya answers it is permitted.
An alternative version: Rav asks about rubbing through one's garment during prayer, and Rabbi Chiyya answers it is forbidden, but the halacha does not follow him.
Rabbi Chiyya permits rubbing with a garment.
An alternative version reports that Rav asked about rubbing with a garment during prayer (תפילה).
In the alternative version, Rabbi Chiyya forbids rubbing even with a garment during prayer.
The Gemara rules that the alternative version's prohibition is not the binding law (הלכה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua's proposal
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua's proposal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yehoshua's solution for a nazirite who died in impurity: find another person to vow as a nazirite opposite him, with conditional statements to cover both possibilities of who was impure, and then bring offerings accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehoshua's proposal: find a volunteer nazirite who makes conditional vows to cover both possibilities of who was impure.
The Mishnah details the first stage: they count thirty days, bring both impurity and purity offerings, and the original nazirite makes conditional statements about whose offering is whose.
The Mishnah concludes the procedure: after another thirty days they bring a purity offering, and the original nazirite makes final conditional statements to resolve the uncertainty.

items.text: Ben Zoma's objection and alternative
items.text_en: Ben Zoma's objection and alternative
items.desc_en: Ben Zoma questions who would agree to vow as a nazirite opposite him, and instead proposes bringing a bird sin-offering and a burnt-offering, with conditional statements, and then after thirty days bringing the purification offering. Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that this results in bringing offerings in halves, but the Sages agree with Ben Zoma.

sub.desc_en: Ben Zoma objects that no one would agree to vow as a nazirite opposite him, and proposes an alternative procedure involving a bird sin-offering and a burnt-offering with conditional statements.
Ben Zoma details the second stage of his alternative: after thirty days, the nazirite brings the purification offering with further conditional statements.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's concession and Sages' agreement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's concession and Sages' agreement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that Ben Zoma's method results in bringing offerings in halves, but the Sages agree with Ben Zoma's position.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehoshua didn't bring a bird offering. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that Rabbi Yehoshua only said his proposal to sharpen the students. Rav Nachman adds that Rabbi Yehoshua did this to prevent them from being prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua didn't simply bring a bird offering himself instead of proposing the complicated arrangement.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that Rabbi Yehoshua only said his proposal to sharpen the students' understanding, not as a practical ruling.
Rav Nachman adds that Rabbi Yehoshua did this to prevent the students from being prohibited (from eating קדשים or drinking wine) due to uncertainty.

items.text: New Mishnah: Nazirite with uncertain impurity
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Nazirite with uncertain impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of a nazirite who is uncertainly impure and uncertainly a leper: he may eat sacred food after sixty days, and drink wine and become impure from the dead after one hundred and twenty days, because the leper's shaving overrides the nazirite's shaving only when certain, not when uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a nazirite who is uncertainly impure and uncertainly a leper, stating he may eat sacred food after sixty days.
The Mishnah adds that he may drink wine and become impure from the dead only after one hundred and twenty days.
The Mishnah explains that the leper's shaving overrides the nazirite's shaving only when the leprosy is certain, not when it is uncertain.

items.text: Baraita on the timeline for a nazirite with a year-long term
items.text_en: Baraita on the timeline for a nazirite with a year-long term
items.desc_en: The baraita states that the previous ruling applies only to a short nazirite term, but for a full year, the nazirite eats sacrifices after two years and drinks wine and becomes impure after four years.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the previous ruling applies only to a short nazirite term, but for a full year, the nazirite eats sacrifices after two years and drinks wine and becomes impure after four years.

items.text: Baraita on the four shavings and their offerings
items.text_en: Baraita on the four shavings and their offerings
items.desc_en: A second baraita is taught alongside: the nazirite performs four shavings. The first involves bringing birds, a bird sin-offering, and a burnt animal offering; the second and third involve a bird sin-offering and a burnt animal offering; the fourth brings a purification offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the nazirite performs four shavings.

The baraita details the offerings for each of the four shavings: the first includes birds, a bird sin-offering, and a burnt animal offering; the second and third include a bird sin-offering and a burnt animal offering; the fourth brings a purification offering.

items.text: Analysis of the first shaving's offerings
items.text_en: Analysis of the first shaving's offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the first shaving's offerings, analyzing each possibility: if he is a definite leper but not impure, the birds are his obligation, the bird sin-offering goes to burial, and the burnt offering is a donation; if he is not a definite leper but is impure, the bird sin-offering is his obligation, the birds are external, and the burnt offering is a donation; if he is neither, the birds are external, the bird sin-offering goes to burial, and the burnt offering is his obligation. The Gemara notes that a guilt-offering is needed, but this follows Rabbi Shimon who says he brings and stipulates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the first shaving's offerings are valid, given the uncertainty of the nazirite's status.
The Gemara proposes that if he is a definite leper but not impure, the birds are his obligation, the bird sin-offering goes to burial, and the burnt offering is a donation.
The Gemara objects that shaving within seven days is impossible, because if he is not a confirmed leper, the Torah forbids shaving before the completion of his nazirite term.
The Gemara proposes that if he is not a definite leper but is impure, the bird sin-offering is his obligation, the birds are external, and the burnt offering is a donation.
The Gemara proposes that if he is neither a leper nor impure, the birds are external, the bird sin-offering goes to burial, and the burnt offering is his obligation.
The Gemara objects that a guilt-offering (אשם) is required, but it is missing from the list.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one brings the offerings and stipulates about their status.

items.text: Explanation of the second and third shavings and the fourth
items.text_en: Explanation of the second and third shavings and the fourth
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second and third shavings do not require birds because they were already done: one for the uncertainty of his leprosy and one for the uncertainty of his impurity. The fourth shaving involves bringing a purification offering and stipulating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second and third shavings do not require birds because they were already performed: one for the uncertainty of his leprosy and one for the uncertainty of his impurity.
The Gemara states that the fourth shaving involves bringing a purification offering and stipulating.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of a safek nazir and a definite metzora
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of a safek nazir and a definite metzora
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents four cases involving a person who is a safek nazir and a definite metzora, detailing when they may eat sacrifices and drink wine or become impure. Each case specifies different waiting periods based on the combination of certainties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: if the person is a definite nazir and a definite metzora, the first offering is obligatory and the second is a voluntary gift, with the reverse if he is a definite metzora and a safek nazir.
The Mishnah states the second case: a safek tamei and a definite metzora may eat sacrifices after eight days and drink wine and become impure after sixty-seven days.
The Mishnah states the third case: a safek metzora and a definite tamei may eat sacrifices after thirty-seven days and drink wine and become impure after seventy-four days.
The Mishnah states the fourth case: a definite tamei and a definite metzora may eat sacrifices after eight days and drink wine and become impure after forty-four days.

items.text: Students' question to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.text_en: Students' question to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai whether a pure nazirite who is also a leper can have one haircut that counts for both his nazirite and leprosy obligations. Rabbi Shimon answers that he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai whether a pure nazirite who is also a leper can have one haircut that counts for both his nazirite and leprosy obligations.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers that the nazirite cannot have one haircut count for both obligations.

items.text: First reason: Growth vs. removal
items.text_en: First reason: Growth vs. removal
items.desc_en: The students ask why, and Rabbi Shimon explains that if both required growth or both required removal, it would work. But the nazirite's haircut is for removal (of hair), while the leper's is for growth (of hair), so they conflict.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai why a nazirite who is also a leper cannot perform one haircut that fulfills both obligations.
Rabbi Shimon explains that the nazirite's haircut is for removal (להעביר) of hair, while the leper's is for growth (לגדל), so they conflict and cannot be combined.

items.text: Second reason: Timing relative to blood sprinkling
items.text_en: Second reason: Timing relative to blood sprinkling
items.desc_en: The students propose that the haircut might count for the leper's days of counting (s'faro) even if not for his days of isolation (chiluto). Rabbi Shimon responds that the leper's haircut is before blood sprinkling, while the nazirite's is after, so they cannot be combined.

sub.desc_en: The students propose that the haircut might count for the leper's days of counting (s'faro) even if not for his days of isolation (chiluto).
Rabbi Shimon responds that the leper's haircut is before blood sprinkling, while the nazirite's is after, so they cannot be combined.

items.text: Third reason: Timing relative to water immersion
items.text_en: Third reason: Timing relative to water immersion
items.desc_en: The students suggest the haircut might count for the leper's days of leprosy and impurity. Rabbi Shimon explains that the impure person's haircut is after water immersion, while the leper's is before, so they cannot be combined.

sub.desc_en: The students object that if the haircut cannot count for both leprosy and nazirite days, it should at least count for leprosy and impurity days, since both require haircut after impurity.
Rabbi Shimon explains that the impure nazirite's haircut is after water immersion (ביאת מים), while the leper's haircut is before water immersion, so they cannot be combined.

items.text: Students' counterproposal: Counting for days of isolation and impurity
items.text_en: Students' counterproposal: Counting for days of isolation and impurity
items.desc_en: The students acknowledge that the haircut cannot count for the leper's days of counting and naziriteship, but propose it might count for his days of isolation and impurity, since both require growth. Rabbi Shimon rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The students concede that the haircut cannot count for the leper's days of counting and naziriteship, but propose it might count for his days of isolation and impurity, since both require growth.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's final answer: Distinction between pure and impure nazirite
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's final answer: Distinction between pure and impure nazirite
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon explains that for a pure nazirite who is a leper, one requires growth and the other removal, so they conflict. For an impure nazirite who is a leper, one is before water immersion and the other after, so they also conflict.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon gives his final answer: for a pure nazirite who is a leper, one requires growth and the other removal, so they conflict; for an impure nazirite who is a leper, one is before water immersion and the other after, so they also conflict.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita distinguishing between two cases: one before the application of living water and one after, one before the sprinkling of blood and one after, in the context of the nazirite's shaving.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita distinguishing between two cases in the nazirite's shaving: one before the application of living water and one after, one before the sprinkling of blood and one after.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question on the four shavings
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question on the four shavings
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the four shavings mentioned are for the mitzvah or for removing impure hair. The practical difference is whether a non-nazirite can shave for him. Rava resolves the question from the mishnah's wording, concluding they are for the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the four shavings mentioned are for the mitzvah or for removing impure hair.
The gemara clarifies the practical difference: if for the mitzvah, a non-nazirite cannot shave for him; if for removing impure hair, even a non-nazirite may shave for him.
Rava resolves the question from the mishnah's wording: if it were for removing impure hair, three shavings would suffice, so the fourth must be for the mitzvah.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach Shnei Nezirim' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter 'Two Nazirites' with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Opening mishnah: Gentiles and naziriteship
items.text_en: Opening mishnah: Gentiles and naziriteship
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that gentiles cannot take nazirite vows, while women and slaves can. A stringency for women over slaves is that a master can coerce his slave but not his wife.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that gentiles cannot take nazirite vows, while women and slaves can, and a master can coerce his slave but not his wife.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for gentiles and slaves
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for gentiles and slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from 'Speak to the children of Israel' that gentiles are excluded, and 'and say to them' includes slaves. Rava explains that the verse 'to bind a bond upon his soul' excludes a slave whose soul is not his own, but the inclusion teaches that a slave can still take a vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah that gentiles have no nazirite vow and derives from the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel' that gentiles are excluded, and 'and say to them' includes slaves.
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to include slaves, given the principle that any מצוה (commandment) a woman is obligated in, a slave is also obligated.
Rava explains that the verse 'לאסור אסר על נפשו' (to bind a bond upon his soul) excludes a slave whose soul is not his own, but the inclusion teaches that a slave can still take a vow.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding gentiles
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding gentiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'Israel' elsewhere includes gentiles in some contexts, citing valuations. It then distinguishes naziriteship by the verse 'to his father and mother he shall not become impure', which applies only to one who has a father in the sense of being commanded to honor him, excluding gentiles. The discussion concludes with the principle that a gentile has impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the principle that 'דַּבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' excludes gentiles, and then objects that in the context of valuations (ערכין) the same phrase appears yet gentiles are included in some capacity.
A baraita is cited showing that regarding valuations, the verse 'אִישׁ' includes gentiles as subjects who can be evaluated, contradicting the simple exclusion.

The Gemara distinguishes naziriteship by the verse 'לְאָבִיו וּלְאִמּוֹ לֹא יִטַּמָּא', which applies only to one who has a father, and then clarifies that this does not refer to inheritance, citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a gentile inherits his father by Torah law.

The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to one who is commanded regarding honoring his father, and since a gentile is not commanded in this, he is excluded; the discussion concludes with the principle that a gentile has impurity (טומאה), so the nazirite prohibition applies only to one who has impurity.

items.text: First derivation: gentiles lack impurity because they lack purification
items.text_en: First derivation: gentiles lack impurity because they lack purification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a gentile has no impurity. It cites the verse 'And a man who becomes impure and does not purify himself' to argue that only those who have a congregation (Israel) are subject to impurity. It then raises a challenge: perhaps they are exempt from karet but still become impure? The Gemara answers with another verse: 'The pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure' — only those who can become pure can become impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a gentile has no impurity and asks how we know this, citing the verse 'וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִטְמָא וְלֹא יִתְחַטָּא' to argue that only those who have a congregation (Israel) are subject to impurity.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the gentile is only exempt from karet (spiritual excision) but still becomes impure.
The Gemara answers with the verse 'וְהִזָּה הַטָּהוֹר עַל הַטָּמֵא' (the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure), establishing that only those who can become pure can become impure.

items.text: Rejection and alternative verse
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps a gentile has impurity but no purification? It responds by citing the verse 'And a man who becomes impure and does not purify himself' to show that impurity and purification are linked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps a gentile has impurity (טומאה) but lacks purification (טהרה)?
The Gemara responds by citing the verse 'וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִטְמָא וְלֹא יִתְחַטָּא' (And a man who becomes impure and does not purify himself) to show that impurity and purification are linked.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from inheritance
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from inheritance
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers a different derivation: the verse 'You shall bequeath them to your children after you' implies that only those who have inheritance (Israelites) have impurity, excluding gentiles. The Gemara objects that this would also exclude slaves, who do inherit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov introduces a new derivation from the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אֹתָם לִבְנֵיכֶם אַחֲרֵיכֶם' (You shall bequeath them to your children after you).
