Rav Acha bar Yaakov states the principle: whoever has inheritance (Israelites) has impurity, and whoever lacks inheritance (gentiles) lacks impurity.
The Gemara objects that according to this principle, slaves (עבדים) would also lack impurity, since they do not inherit.

items.text: Rava's analogy to valuations and naziriteship
items.text_en: Rava's analogy to valuations and naziriteship
items.desc_en: Rava explains that just as with valuations (arakhin), where the verse 'Children of Israel' excludes gentiles from making valuations but 'a man' includes them as being valued, similarly with naziriteship: 'Children of Israel' excludes gentiles from vowing and bringing a sacrifice, but 'a man' includes them in naziriteship itself.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by drawing an analogy to valuations (ערכין), where the verse 'בני ישראל' excludes gentiles from making valuations but 'איש' includes them as being valued.
Rava applies the same logic to naziriteship: 'בני ישראל' excludes gentiles from vowing and bringing a sacrifice, but 'איש' includes them in naziriteship itself.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yossi HaGelili's verse
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yossi HaGelili's verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the exclusion from bringing a sacrifice is not derived from here but from the verse 'for a burnt offering' which excludes naziriteship, according to Rabbi Yossi HaGelili.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the exclusion of a gentile from bringing a nazirite offering is not derived from the phrase 'the children of Israel' in the nazirite passage, but rather from the verse 'for a burnt offering' which excludes naziriteship, according to Rabbi Yossi HaGelili.

items.text: Attempted derivation for permanent naziriteship
items.text_en: Attempted derivation for permanent naziriteship
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from permanent naziriteship (nezirut olam), but Rabbi Yochanan objects that the Torah does not write 'permanent nazirite'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from permanent naziriteship (נזירות עולם), but a baraita could teach that they are included by the word 'איש'.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that the Torah does not write the term 'נזיר עולם' (permanent nazirite), so the derivation is invalid.

items.text: Attempted derivation for fathers dedicating sons
items.text_en: Attempted derivation for fathers dedicating sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from the law that fathers can dedicate their sons as nazirites, but Rabbi Yochanan says this is a halakha (tradition) in naziriteship, not derived from a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from the law that fathers can dedicate their sons as nazirites, but then proposes that the word 'איש' (a man) includes them.
Rabbi Yochanan rejects the derivation, stating that the rule that a father can dedicate his son as a nazirite is a halakha (tradition) in naziriteship, not derived from a verse.

items.text: Attempted derivation for shaving on father's naziriteship
items.text_en: Attempted derivation for shaving on father's naziriteship
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from shaving on their father's naziriteship, but this is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might exclude gentiles from shaving on their father's naziriteship, but this is left unresolved.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's halakhic principle
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's halakhic principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the word "איש" in the context of naziriteship teaches that gentiles can become nazirites, as it is a halakhic tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rabbi Yochanan's tradition that the word 'איש' in the nazirite context includes gentiles.

items.text: Question on the need for "איש" in valuations
items.text_en: Question on the need for "איש" in valuations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needs the word "איש" in the context of valuations (ערכין), since valuations are already linked to vows. It suggests that "איש" in valuations might come to include a minor close to adulthood (מופלא סמוך לאיש), and then addresses the views of those who hold this inclusion is biblical or rabbinic, and for gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the word 'איש' is needed in the context of valuations (ערכין), since valuations are already linked to vows, and notes that a baraita already uses 'איש' in vows to include gentiles.
The Gemara answers that the word 'איש' in valuations comes to include a minor close to adulthood (מופלא סמוך לאיש).

The Gemara objects that this works only for the view that the inclusion of a minor close to adulthood is biblical (דאורייתא), but for the view that it is rabbinic (דרבנן), the word 'איש' must include a gentile minor close to adulthood.

items.text: Two views on gentiles and valuations
items.text_en: Two views on gentiles and valuations
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two opposing views: one that Israelites can be evaluated but gentiles cannot, and another that Israelites can evaluate but gentiles cannot. It then questions the need for the phrase "כי יפליא" in the latter view.

sub.text: First view (Israelites are evaluated, gentiles are not)
sub.text_en: First view (Israelites are evaluated, gentiles are not)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the first view: Israelites can be evaluated (נֶעֱרָכִין) but gentiles cannot, and the verse 'אִישׁ' resolves the concern that they might not be able to evaluate.

sub.text: Second view (Israelites evaluate, gentiles do not)
sub.text_en: Second view (Israelites evaluate, gentiles do not)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the second view: Israelites can evaluate (מַעֲרִיכִים) but gentiles cannot, and then questions the need for the phrase 'כִּי יַפְלִיא' in this context.

items.text: Answer: Including an adult gentile who cannot articulate
items.text_en: Answer: Including an adult gentile who cannot articulate
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that the phrase "כי יפליא" in valuations comes to include an adult gentile who, despite being old, does not know how to articulate a vow.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava answers that 'כי יפליא' includes an adult gentile who does not know how to make a vow.

items.text: Question on "כי יפליא" in naziriteship and the dispute about non-indicative actions
items.text_en: Question on "כי יפליא" in naziriteship and the dispute about non-indicative actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah writes "כי יפליא" in the context of naziriteship, since naziriteship is linked to vows. It suggests it comes to include non-indicative actions (ידים שאינן מוכיחות), and cites the dispute between Abaye and Rava on this matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'כי יפליא' (when he expresses a vow) specifically in the context of naziriteship, since naziriteship is linked to vows in general.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include non-indicative actions (ידים שאינן מוכיחות) as valid expressions of naziriteship.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding non-indicative actions: Abaye holds they are valid, Rava holds they are not.
The Gemara objects that this answer works for Abaye, but for Rava who rejects non-indicative actions, what purpose does 'כי יפליא' serve?

items.text: Alternative: Rabbi Tarfon's view on naziriteship requiring articulation
items.text_en: Alternative: Rabbi Tarfon's view on naziriteship requiring articulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that "כי יפליא" might be needed for Rabbi Tarfon's ruling that naziriteship requires explicit articulation, and then questions what the Rabbis would say.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that 'כי יפליא' is needed for Rabbi Tarfon's view that naziriteship requires explicit specification, but questions what the rabbis would say.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon: none of them is a nazirite because naziriteship is only given through explicit articulation (הפלאה).
The Gemara notes that this works for Rabbi Tarfon, but then asks: what can be said for the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Tarfon?

items.text: Final answer: The double "כי יפליא" for permission of vows
items.text_en: Final answer: The double "כי יפליא" for permission of vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that "כי יפליא" is needed for the principle that the permission of vows (התרת נדרים) has a scriptural basis, as taught by Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the double occurrence of "כי יפליא" one for prohibition and one for permission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the double "כי יפליא" is needed for the principle that the permission of vows (התרת נדרים) has no scriptural basis, as taught in a baraita.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the permission of vows does have a scriptural basis, deriving from the double occurrence of "כי יפליא" — one for prohibition and one for permission.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a master can annul his wife's vows but not his slave's, and if he annuls his slave's vow, the slave goes free and completes his naziriteship.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a master can annul his wife's vows but not his slave's, and if he annuls his slave's vow, the slave goes free and completes his naziriteship.

items.text: Baraita on Master's Coercion
items.text_en: Baraita on Master's Coercion
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a master can coerce his slave into naziriteship but not into other vows or valuations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a master can coerce his slave into naziriteship but not into other vows or valuations.

items.text: Gemara's Question on the Distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's Question on the Distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why naziriteship is different, citing the verse 'to bind a binding upon his soul'—only one whose soul is his own, excluding a slave. It then asks why the same logic wouldn't apply to other vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the master's coercion applies specifically to naziriteship, citing the verse 'to bind a binding upon his soul' to exclude a slave, and then challenges why the same logic would not apply to other vows.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's First Answer
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's First Answer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the case involves a cluster of grapes before the slave. For other vows, abstaining from this cluster does not forbid other grapes, so the master cannot coerce. For naziriteship, abstaining from this cluster forbids all grapes, so coercion is possible. The Gemara objects: what if there is only this cluster and the slave would become ill?

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the case involves a cluster of grapes before the slave; for other vows, abstaining from this cluster does not forbid other grapes, so the master cannot coerce.
The Gemara objects: for naziriteship, abstaining from this cluster forbids all grapes, so coercion is possible; but what if there is only this cluster and the slave would become ill?

items.text: Rava's Second Answer
items.text_en: Rava's Second Answer
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the case involves a single pit (of grapes) before the slave. For other vows, only this pit is forbidden, so coercion is impossible. For naziriteship, all pits are forbidden, so coercion is possible. The Gemara again objects: what if there is only this pit and the slave would become ill?

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case involves a grape seed before the slave; for other vows, only this seed is forbidden, so the master cannot coerce; for naziriteship, all grapes are forbidden, so coercion is possible.
The Gemara objects: what if there is only this grape seed and the slave would become ill?

items.text: Abaye's Final Answer
items.text_en: Abaye's Final Answer
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the master need only coerce the slave for naziriteship, not for other vows or oaths. The reason is derived from the verse 'to do evil or to do good'—just as doing good is discretionary, so is doing evil discretionary, excluding causing evil to others, which is not in his power.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the master needs to coerce the slave only for naziriteship, not for other vows or oaths.
Abaye cites the verse 'לְהָרַע אוֹ לְהֵיטִיב' (to harm or to benefit) to derive that just as benefiting is discretionary, harming others is not in the master's authority.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Slave Who Passed Before His Master
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Slave Who Passed Before His Master
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if a slave passed before his master (i.e., left), Rabbi Meir says he may not drink wine, while Rabbi Yosei says he may drink.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a slave passed before his master, Rabbi Meir says he may not drink wine, and Rabbi Yosei says he may drink.

items.text: Gemara's Analysis of the Dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's Analysis of the Dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara first suggests the dispute is about Shmuel's ruling that an owner who abandons his slave frees him without a writ. It then rejects this, saying all agree with Shmuel. The real dispute is: Rabbi Yosei holds the slave will eventually return, so let him drink to avoid illness; Rabbi Meir holds he should suffer to encourage his return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is based on Shmuel's principle that one who abandons his slave frees him without a writ of manumission.
The Gemara initially explains that Rabbi Meir accepts Shmuel's view, so the slave is free and may drink, while Rabbi Yosei rejects it, so the slave remains bound and may not drink.

The Gemara rejects that explanation, stating that everyone accepts Shmuel's view; rather, the dispute is about whether the master wants the slave to drink wine so he does not weaken, or to suffer so he returns.
The Gemara concludes that the one who says the slave may not drink holds that the master wants him to suffer so he returns to him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a nazirite shaved and then discovered he was impure, if the impurity was known, it cancels his days; if it was impurity of the deep, it does not. It then gives examples of finding a corpse in a cave, distinguishing between cases where the nazirite went to immerse or to cool off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: if a nazirite shaved and then discovered impurity, known impurity cancels his days, but טומאת תהום (impurity of the deep) does not; if he shaved after discovery, it always cancels.
The Mishnah gives an example: one who descended to immerse in a cave and found a corpse floating at the entrance is impure; if the corpse was sunk in the cave floor, the case is different.
The Mishnah concludes: if he descended to cool off, he is pure; if to purify from corpse impurity, he is impure, based on the principle that a person's status follows their presumed state.

items.text: Gemara's Scriptural Sources for Impurity of the Deep
items.text_en: Gemara's Scriptural Sources for Impurity of the Deep
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of this law. Rabbi Eliezer derives it from the word 'עליו' in the verse, implying impurity that is 'clear to him'. Resh Lakish derives it from the word 'דרך', comparing it to a road which is visible, so only revealed impurity counts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the distinction between known impurity and טומאת תהום) derived?
Rabbi Eliezer answers: the verse 'וְכִי יָמוּת מֵת עָלָיו בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם' uses 'עָלָיו' (upon him) to indicate impurity that is clearly visible to him.
Reish Lakish answers: the verse 'כִּי יִהְיֶה טָמֵא לָנֶפֶשׁ אוֹ בְדֶרֶךְ רְחֹקָה' teaches that just as a 'דרך' (road) is exposed, so too the impurity must be exposed (known).

items.text: Definition of טומאת תהום and Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Definition of טומאת תהום and Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining impurity of the deep as one that no one in the world recognizes. It then challenges Rabbi Eliezer's view: if even one person at the end of the world recognizes it, why is it not considered revealed? It then brings another baraita about a corpse found across the road, which is treated differently for terumah versus nazirite and Passover, concluding that the law of טומאת תהום is a tradition.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited defining טומאת תהום as impurity that no one at the end of the world recognizes; if even one person recognizes it, it is not טומאת תהום.

The Gemara objects: for Reish Lakish's view (like a road) the baraita works, but for Rabbi Eliezer's view (clearly visible to him), what difference does it make if someone at the end of the world recognizes it?

The Gemara digresses to cite another baraita about finding a corpse lying across a road, where the rule differs for תרומה (priestly portion) versus nazirite and פסח (Passover), concluding that the law of טומאת תהום is a received tradition.
The Gemara resolves: the distinction is not derived from a verse but is a received tradition (גמירא) that the law of טומאת תהום (impurity of the deep) is a halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna and a Question on Timing
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna and a Question on Timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah's second clause as Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that shaving is an impediment. Then Rami bar Chama asks: if a nazirite became impure during his term but only discovered it after the term ended, does the discovery cancel his days?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's second clause.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that shaving is an impediment (מעכבת).
Rami bar Chama asks: if a nazirite became impure during his term but only discovered it after the term ended, does the discovery cancel his days?
The Gemara clarifies that the question is whether the discovery cancels the days (למיסתר).

items.text: Rava's proof and the unresolved question
items.text_en: Rava's proof and the unresolved question
items.desc_en: Rava cites a mishnah to argue that impurity after the term (after melot) causes a full setback, but the Gemara questions whether this applies to all opinions or only to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that after melot only seven days are set back. The Gemara then considers whether the case involves knowledge after melot or before.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a mishnah to prove that impurity after melot causes a full setback, arguing that the mishnah's case must be after melot.
The Gemara questions whether the setback is full or only seven days, and notes that for Rabbi Eliezer, after melot only seven days are set back.
The Gemara considers two possibilities: that the case involves impurity before melot, or that the knowledge after melot changes the ruling.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah states 'in either case it sets back' without distinguishing, implying a full setback.

items.text: Baraita on tum'at hatehom for a nazirite
items.text_en: Baraita on tum'at hatehom for a nazirite
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: one who finds a corpse lying across the road is impure for terumah but pure for nazirite and Passover sacrifices, provided there is no alternative path. This is defined as tum'at hatehom (unknown impurity), which applies only to a corpse, not to a creeping thing. Various conditions are given regarding the corpse's condition and the traveler's mode of transport.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens: one who finds a corpse lying across the road is impure for תרומה (priestly portion) but pure for nazirite and Passover, provided there is no alternative path.
The baraita adds: if there is an alternative path, even for תרומה (priestly portion) he is pure.

The baraita specifies: the leniency applies only to a whole corpse; if broken or dismembered, we suspect he passed between the limbs, and in a grave even broken limbs are impure because the grave joins them.
The baraita adds: the leniency applies only to a pedestrian; one who is laden or riding is impure, because a pedestrian can avoid contact, but a laden or riding person cannot.
The baraita specifies: all these leniencies apply only to טומאת התהום (unknown impurity); but for known impurity, all three (terumah, nazirite, Passover) are impure.
The baraita defines טומאת התהום (unknown impurity): any impurity that no one at the end of the world recognizes; if even one person recognizes it, it is not טומאת התהום.
The baraita gives examples: impurity buried in straw or pebbles is טומאת התהום; but in seas, darkness, or crevices of rocks, it is not.
The baraita concludes: the rule of טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) was stated only for a corpse, not for a creeping thing.

items.text: Clarification regarding floating impurity
items.text_en: Clarification regarding floating impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that floating impurity (tsafah) does not apply to a creeping thing, citing a baraita where a doubt about floating impurity is pure on the ground but Rabbi Shimon deems it impure for vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that floating impurity (צָפָה) does not apply to a creeping thing (שֶׁרֶץ).
A baraita is cited stating that a doubt about floating impurity is pure (טְהוֹרָה) both for vessels and for the ground.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, ruling that floating impurity is impure (טְמֵאָה) for vessels but pure (טְהוֹרָה) for the ground.

items.text: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon's reasons for their rulings on floating impurity
items.text_en: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon's reasons for their rulings on floating impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains the Tanna Kamma's view that a creeping creature's certain contact with a vessel imparts impurity, but doubtful contact does not, based on the verses 'in all the creeping things that creep' and 'upon the earth'. Ulla explains Rabbi Shimon's view that a creeping creature floating on vessels imparts impurity, but on the ground it does not, based on the verses 'but a spring' and 'it shall be impure'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Tanna Kamma's ruling on floating impurity.

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains that the Tanna Kamma derives from the verses 'בכל השרץ השורץ' (in all the creeping things that creep) and 'על הארץ' (upon the earth) that certain contact with a creeping creature imparts impurity, but doubtful contact does not.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Shimon's ruling on floating impurity.

Ulla explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from the verses 'אך מעין' (but a spring) and 'יטמא' (it shall be impure) that a creeping creature floating on vessels imparts impurity, but on the ground it does not.

items.text: Baraita on the status of floating items
items.text_en: Baraita on the status of floating items
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: Items that are carried or dragged, their doubtful impurity is impure because they are considered as if placed; items that are thrown, their doubtful impurity is pure. Exceptions include an olive's bulk of a corpse, anything that overshadows impurity, and anything that imparts impurity from above as from below, which includes a zav and a zavah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the general rule: items carried or dragged have impure doubtful status, while thrown items have pure doubtful status.
The baraita lists exceptions to the rule: an olive's bulk of a corpse, anything that overshadows impurity, and anything that imparts impurity from above as from below, including a zav and a zavah.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's first query: corpse in a vessel floating on water
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's first query: corpse in a vessel floating on water
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: If a corpse is in a vessel and the vessel floats on water, do we follow the vessel (which is floating) or the corpse (which is inside)? This is a single-segment query.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether, when a corpse is inside a vessel floating on water, we follow the vessel's status or the corpse's status.

items.text: Second query: corpse on a creeping creature
items.text_en: Second query: corpse on a creeping creature
items.desc_en: If we assume we follow the vessel, Rami bar Chama asks: If a corpse is on top of a creeping creature (which is floating), what is the ruling? Since the creeping creature imparts impurity for one day and the corpse for seven, is it considered as if impurity is placed in a vessel (making it definitely impure) or is it a light impurity?

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if a corpse is on top of a creeping creature (which is floating), is the impurity considered as if placed in a vessel (making it definitely impure) or is it a light impurity?

items.text: Third query: creeping creature on a neveilah
items.text_en: Third query: creeping creature on a neveilah
items.desc_en: If we assume it is as if impurity is placed in a vessel and is definitely impure, Rami bar Chama asks: If a creeping creature is on top of a neveilah (carcass) and the neveilah floats, what is the ruling? Since both impart impurity for one day, is it a light impurity, or does the difference in size (an olive's bulk vs. a lentil's bulk) matter?

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if a creeping creature is on a floating neveilah, is the impurity considered light because both impart one-day impurity, or does the difference in size (an olive's bulk vs. a lentil's bulk) matter?

items.text: Fourth query: creeping creature on another creeping creature
items.text_en: Fourth query: creeping creature on another creeping creature
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: If a creeping creature is on top of another creeping creature (both floating), what is the ruling? Are they certainly the same measure (both require a lentil's bulk), or since they are separate from each other, is it not considered as placed?

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a creeping creature on top of another creeping creature (both floating) is considered a certain source of טומאה (impurity) since both require the same lentil-bulk measure, or whether they are separate and thus not considered as placed.

items.text: Fifth query: creeping creature on a melted neveilah
items.text_en: Fifth query: creeping creature on a melted neveilah
items.desc_en: If we assume that a creeping creature on another creeping creature is like being placed in a vessel, Rami bar Chama asks: If a creeping creature is on top of a melted neveilah, what is the ruling? Since it melted, it becomes a liquid, or is it still food?

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if a creeping creature is on top of a melted neveilah, is the neveilah considered a liquid (משקה) or still food (אוכל), affecting whether the creeping creature transmits impurity to what is beneath it.

items.text: Final queries and teiku
items.text_en: Final queries and teiku
items.desc_en: If we assume it is food, Rami bar Chama asks about a creeping creature on seminal fluid, and if that is considered food, about a creeping creature on waters of purification floating on water. The answer is unknown, so the matter stands unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if we assume the melted neveila is considered food (אוכל), what is the status of a creeping creature (שרץ) on seminal fluid (שכבת זרע) floating on water — does it convey impurity or not?
Rami bar Chama asks: if we assume seminal fluid becomes like food after being detached, what is the status of a creeping creature on the waters of purification (מי חטאת) that float on water?
The Gemara concludes that the answer is unknown, so the matter stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's ruling on nazirite and Passover participant
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's ruling on nazirite and Passover participant
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that a nazirite and a Passover participant who walk over a grave in the deep on their seventh day are pure, because the impurity of the deep is not strong enough to override their status.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna rules that a nazirite and a Passover participant who walk over a grave in the deep on their seventh day are pure, because the impurity of the deep is not strong enough to override their status.

items.text: Rava's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita that states one who descends to purify from corpse impurity is impure, implying that the deep grave impurity is effective.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a baraita that one who descends to purify from corpse impurity remains impure, because a person with a חזקה (presumption) of impurity stays impure, and one with a presumption of purity stays pure.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's response and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's response and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna concedes regarding the nazirite because he lacks shaving, but Rava concedes regarding the Passover participant. Abaye objects that the Passover participant still lacks sunset, but Rav Hamnuna replies that sunset occurs automatically.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna concedes to Rava regarding the nazirite case because the nazirite lacks shaving (תגלחת), which is a required act.
Rava concedes to Rav Hamnuna regarding the Passover participant because he lacks nothing required for completion.
Abaye objects that the Passover participant still lacks sunset (הערב שמש), which is a required condition for purity.
Rav Hamnuna replies that sunset occurs automatically (ממילא) and does not require human action, so it is not a deficiency.

items.text: Abaye's retraction and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's retraction and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his objection, as taught in a baraita about a woman bringing an offering on the day of completion. Rav Kahana distinguishes the cases, but Abaye again notes that sunset occurs automatically, supporting the original ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Abaye retracted his objection, as taught in a baraita.
The baraita teaches that a woman brings an offering on the day of completion (יוֹם מְלֹאת), but not within the completion period, establishing that sunset occurs automatically.
Rav Kahana distinguishes the baraita's case, arguing that there the woman is lacking a sacrifice, unlike the nazir who lacks only sunset.
Abaye objects that even in the baraita, the woman is lacking sunset, just like the nazir.
Abaye resolves that sunset occurs automatically (שִׁימְשָׁא מִמֵּילָא עָרְבָא), so the nazir's lack of sunset is not a true deficiency, supporting the original ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Finding a corpse initially
items.text_en: Mishnah: Finding a corpse initially
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who finds a corpse lying in its normal manner takes it and its surrounding soil. If two are found, they are taken with their soil. If three are found within four to eight cubits of each other, it is a burial ground.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who finds a corpse lying in its normal manner takes it and its surrounding soil.
The Mishnah adds that if two corpses are found, they are taken with their soil; if three are found within four to eight cubits of each other, it is a burial ground.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Checking for a corpse
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Checking for a corpse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds a corpse, he checks twenty cubits in each direction. If he finds one at the end of twenty cubits, he checks another twenty cubits, because there is a presumption of a burial ground. If he found it at the beginning, he takes it and its תפוסה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for checking twenty cubits from a found corpse, and that if found at the start, one takes it and its תפוסה (surrounding area).

items.text: Gemara: Exclusions and the reason for lack of תפוסה
items.text_en: Gemara: Exclusions and the reason for lack of תפוסה
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah's terms exclude certain cases: 'found' excludes a corpse that is already known, 'dead' excludes a murdered person, 'lying' excludes a sitting corpse, 'in its way' excludes one whose head is between his thighs. Ulla bar Chanina teaches that a corpse missing a limb has no תפוסה and does not create a burial ground, because we suspect it might be a gentile.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that each term in the Mishnah excludes a specific case: 'found' excludes a known corpse, 'dead' excludes a murdered person, 'lying' excludes a sitting corpse, 'in its way' excludes one whose head is between his thighs.
Ulla bar Chanina teaches that a corpse missing a limb has no תפוסה (attached earth) and does not create a burial ground, because we suspect it might be a gentile.

items.text: Cases of multiple corpses and the story of Rabbi Yeshevav
items.text_en: Cases of multiple corpses and the story of Rabbi Yeshevav
items.desc_en: If one finds two corpses with their heads at each other's feet, they have no תפוסה and do not create a burial ground. If one finds three, with one known and two unknown, or two known and two unknown, they also have no תפוסה. A story is told of Rabbi Yeshevav who found two known and one unknown and wanted to make them a burial ground, but Rabbi Akiva told him that burial grounds are only for three known or three unknown corpses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds two corpses with their heads at each other's feet, or three with a mix of known and unknown, they have no תפוסה (attached burial space) and do not create a burial ground.

A story is told of Rabbi Yeshevav who found two known and one unknown corpse and wanted to make them a burial ground, but Rabbi Akiva told him that burial grounds are only for three known or three unknown corpses.

items.text: Definition and measurement of תפוסה
items.text_en: Definition and measurement of תפוסה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the definition of תפוסה. Rav Yehuda derives from the verse 'and you shall carry me up from Egypt' that one takes the surrounding earth with the corpse. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok teaches that one takes loose earth and digs three fingerbreadths into the virgin soil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the definition of תפוסה (the surrounding earth taken with a corpse).
Rav Yehuda derives from the verse 'וּנְשָׂאתַנִי מִמִּצְרַיִם' (and you shall carry me up from Egypt) that one takes the surrounding earth with the corpse.
The Gemara asks what is the measure of תפוסה (the surrounding earth).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok teaches that one takes loose earth and digs three fingerbreadths into the virgin soil.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the measurement
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the measurement
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok says one takes the chips and splinters, throws away the definite ones and leaves the doubtful ones, and the rest combines for the majority of the corpse's structure and for a quarter-log of bones. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok holds like the tanna who says one takes loose earth and digs three fingerbreadths, as taught by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Ben Azzai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok defines the measure of תפוסה (the surrounding area taken with a corpse) as taking the chips and splinters, discarding the definite ones and leaving the doubtful ones.
The baraita continues that the remaining material combines for the majority of the corpse's structure and for a quarter-log of bones and a full tarvad of decay.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok holds like the tanna who says one takes loose earth and digs three fingerbreadths, as taught by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Ben Azzai.

items.text: Conclusion: Checking from the corpse
items.text_en: Conclusion: Checking from the corpse
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with the Mishnah's rule that one checks from the corpse outward.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes with the phrase 'בּוֹדֵק הֵימֶנּוּ' (he checks from it), likely a continuation of the Mishnah's rule.

items.text: Rava's dispute about checking and clearing graves
items.text_en: Rava's dispute about checking and clearing graves
items.desc_en: Rava presents two versions of a case where one checked and cleared graves. The first version holds that the cleared bones are not joined with the others; the second version holds that once permission is given to clear, one clears them all. Reish Lakish explains that this is because they found and purified Eretz Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents the first version of a case where one checked and cleared graves: the cleared bones are not joined with the others.
Rava presents the second version: once permission is given to clear, one clears them all.
The gemara objects: why not consider them a burial ground (שכונת קברות)?
Reish Lakish explains that the reason is because they found and purified Eretz Yisrael.
The gemara asks: if one checked twenty cubits and found nothing, what is the law?

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya in the name of Rav rules that it is considered a burial ground (שכונת קברות).
Reish Lakish provides the reason: because they found and purified Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Mishnah: Doubt in nega'im at the outset
items.text_en: Mishnah: Doubt in nega'im at the outset
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any doubt regarding nega'im at the beginning is pure, but once one is committed to impurity, his doubt is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: all doubtful cases of skin afflictions (נגעים) at the outset are pure; once examined, doubtful cases are impure.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Rav that the verse 'to purify him or to defile him' teaches that the Torah begins with purity. The Gemara initially questions this, then clarifies that the statement was made regarding a different case: if a bright spot preceded white hair, it is impure; if white hair preceded, it is pure; doubt is impure. Rabbi Yehoshua says it is dim, and Rav Yehuda explains that dim means pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the Mishnah's rule) derived?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that the verse 'לְטַהֲרוֹ אוֹ לְטַמְּאוֹ' (to purify him or to defile him) teaches that since the verse opened with purity first, any uncertainty is deemed pure.
The Gemara objects: If so, even after being established as impure, uncertainty should still be deemed pure.

The Gemara clarifies that Rav Yehuda's statement was actually said regarding a different case: if a bright spot preceded white hair, it is impure; if white hair preceded, it is pure; doubt is impure; Rabbi Yehoshua says it is dim.
The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of 'dim'?
Rav Yehuda explains: 'Dim' means it is pure.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps 'dim' means it is impure?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that the verse 'לְטַהֲרוֹ אוֹ לְטַמְּאוֹ' (to purify him or to defile him) teaches that since the verse opened with purity first, any uncertainty is deemed pure.

items.text: Mishnah: Seven ways to check a zav
items.text_en: Mishnah: Seven ways to check a zav
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists seven ways to check a zav before he becomes subject to zivah: through food, drink, carrying, jumping, illness, sight, and thought. Once subject to zivah, he is not checked. His ones, doubt, and semen are impure, as there is a basis for the matter. The Mishnah also discusses a case of one who struck another and was assessed for death, then improved and later worsened and died.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing seven ways to check a זב (zav) before he is confirmed as a זב (zav): through food, drink, carrying, jumping, illness, sight, and thought.
The Mishnah states that once a זב (zav) is confirmed, he is not checked; his ones, doubt, and semen are impure because there is a basis for the matter.

The Mishnah presents a case of one who struck another and was assessed for death, then improved and later worsened and died: the striker is liable, but Rabbi Nechemya says he is exempt because there is a basis for the matter.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the zav's checking and the dispute about אתים
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the zav's checking and the dispute about אתים
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan derives from the verse 'and the zav with his flow' that the third sighting is linked to a female. The Gemara notes a beraita where Rabbi Eliezer says they check him on the third, but not on the fourth. The dispute is about whether to expound the word 'את'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived, that one examines a zav before he has been confirmed as having a ziva, but not after?
Rabbi Natan answers that the verse 'וְהַזָּב אֶת זוֹבוֹ' (and the zav with his flow) teaches that the third sighting is juxtaposed to a female, so after two discharges one no longer examines him.
The Gemara objects: But isn't it taught in a beraita that Rabbi Eliezer says they examine him on the third discharge, and only on the fourth they do not examine him?

The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about whether to expound the word 'את' (et): Rabbi Eliezer expounds instances of 'את', counting three discharges from the verse, while the Rabbis do not expound 'את', counting only two.
The Gemara cites the continuation of the mishnah: his discharge due to circumstances beyond his control and his uncertain discharge are impure.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a doubtful emission
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a doubtful emission
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the case is not one of doubt whether he saw an emission, but rather certainty that he saw, with doubt whether it was due to semen or a zivah discharge. Once he is subject to impurity, his doubtful case is impure.

sub.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the case is not one of doubt whether he saw an emission, but rather certainty that he saw, with doubt whether it was due to semen or a zivah discharge. Once he is subject to impurity, his doubtful case is impure.

items.text: The impurity of a zav's semen
items.text_en: The impurity of a zav's semen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of the statement that a zav's semen is impure: is it for contact or for carrying? It cites a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, concluding that even Rabbi Yehoshua only permits impurity due to traces of zivah, not the semen itself. Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the statement means that one does not attribute the emission to the zav's semen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what impurity the mishna's statement about a zav's semen refers to, and suggests it must be impurity by carrying, not contact.
The Gemara objects that even Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds the semen of a zav imparts impurity by carrying, only says so because of droplets of ziva, not the semen itself.
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the mishna's statement means one does not attribute a subsequent ziva discharge to the earlier seminal emission.

items.text: Rav Pappa's suggestion and Rava's refutation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's suggestion and Rava's refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa thought to say that the emission is due to weakness, but Rava refuted him with a mishnah: a convert who converts is immediately impure with zivah. Rav Pappa replied that there is no greater illness than that.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa suggests that the emission is due to weakness from the previous ziva.
Rava refutes Rav Pappa by citing a mishnah that a convert who converts is immediately impure with zivah, showing that weakness is not a factor.
Rav Pappa responds that there is no greater illness than the acceptance of mitzvot, so the convert's zivah is still attributable to weakness.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the duration of impurity
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the duration of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute: the first tanna says a zav's semen conveys impurity through carrying for a full day (מעת לעת), while Rabbi Yosei says only for his day (יומו). They argue over the interpretation of verses about one who has a nocturnal emission: one derives from 'toward evening' and the other from 'a nocturnal emission'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute: the first tanna says a zav's semen conveys impurity through carrying for a full day (מעת לעת), while Rabbi Yosei says only for his day (יומו).
The gemara asks what underlies their dispute, and answers that it is based on a contradiction raised by Shmuel between two verses.
Shmuel raises a contradiction: one verse says impurity from a nocturnal emission lasts until evening, and another says he must bathe toward evening, implying a full day.
The gemara explains: the first tanna focuses on the phrase 'toward evening' (implying a full day), while Rabbi Yosei focuses on 'a nocturnal emission' (implying only the day of the event).

The gemara objects: how can the first tanna ignore the verse 'a nocturnal emission'? The answer is that the first tanna explains that the natural way for a nocturnal emission to occur is at night, so the verse merely describes the typical case.

items.text: Mishnah: Samuel was a nazirite
items.text_en: Mishnah: Samuel was a nazirite
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that Samuel was a nazirite according to Rabbi Nehorai, based on a verbal analogy between 'מורה' in Samson and 'מורה' in Samuel. Rabbi Yosei objects that 'מורה' only refers to fear of flesh and blood, but Rabbi Nehorai responds that Samuel already had fear of flesh and blood (Saul).

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that Samuel was a nazirite according to Rabbi Nehorai, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'מורה' used for Samson and for Samuel.
Rabbi Yosei objects that the word 'מורה' in the verse only refers to fear of flesh and blood, not to a nazirite vow.
Rabbi Nehorai responds that Samuel already had fear of flesh and blood (Saul), as the verse shows he feared Saul would kill him, so the 'מורה' in his verse must refer to the nazirite prohibition.

items.text: Gemara: Rav to his son Chiyya
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav to his son Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with Rav speaking to his son Chiyya, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins: Rav said to his son Chiyya (the continuation is cut off in the source).

items.text: Opening statement: 'Grab and bless'
items.text_en: Opening statement: 'Grab and bless'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna instructs his son Rabba to 'grab and bless', implying that the one who recites the blessing is superior.

sub.text: Rav Huna to his son Rabba
sub.text_en: Rav Huna to his son Rabba
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna instructs his son Rabba to 'grab and bless', implying that the one who recites the blessing is superior.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita: Responding 'Amen' is greater
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita: Responding 'Amen' is greater
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the blesser is indeed superior, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says the one who answers 'Amen' is greater, and Rabbi Nehorai confirms this with a parable of soldiers and warriors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the blesser is indeed superior, based on the previous statement.
Rabbi Yosei states that the one who answers 'Amen' is greater than the one who blesses.
Rabbi Nehorai confirms Rabbi Yosei's statement with a parable: soldiers engage in battle but warriors are victorious.

items.text: Resolution: It is a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: It is a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by presenting a baraita where both the blesser and the responder are equally important, but the blesser is given precedence in timing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that the dispute is between Tannaim, citing a baraita that equates the blesser and responder but gives the blesser precedence in timing.

items.text: Concluding statement: Torah scholars increase peace
items.text_en: Concluding statement: Torah scholars increase peace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina concludes that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'
